0.title: Christ Is All: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
0.overview:
The message. Few letters of Paul’s are so concentrated on who Christ is, and its argument fits in five words: Christ is all you need. The church at Colossae was being offered something more: a “philosophy” of food laws and holy days, harsh treatment of the body, the honouring of angels and the pursuit of visions. The teachers were not asking the Colossians to abandon Christ, only to add to him, as though he alone could not give them everything. Paul answers with a bigger Christ: “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (2:9–10). There is nothing to add. He is enough.

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul three times (1:1, 23; 4:18), writing with Timothy (1:1) and closing in his own hand: “Remember my chains” (4:18). He was in prison (4:3, 10, 18), most likely under house arrest in Rome about AD 60–62 (Acts 28:16, 30–31); some place the letter earlier, in an imprisonment at Ephesus or Caesarea. It was written at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon, and Tychicus carried it, with Onesimus going home beside him (4:7–9; Ephesians 6:21–22).

Colossae. Colossae lay in the Lycus valley in Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, about a hundred miles (160 km) east of Ephesus, in what is now western Turkey. Once a large city on the main road east, by Paul’s day it was overshadowed by its neighbours, wealthy Laodicea about ten miles away and Hierapolis with its hot springs, both mentioned in the letter (2:1; 4:13–16). The valley was known for its wool, and for earthquakes. Most people worshipped the gods of Greece and Phrygia, but Jewish communities had lived in the region for generations, and religions mingled freely.

The church there. Paul had never visited (2:1). The church was planted by Epaphras, “one of you” (4:12), probably during Paul’s long ministry at Ephesus, when “all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord” (Acts 19:10). The believers were mostly converted Gentiles, once “alienated and hostile in mind” (1:21). At least one congregation met in the home of Philemon, whose runaway slave Onesimus now returned as “our faithful and beloved brother” (4:9; Philemon 1–2). Epaphras had brought Paul news of their faith and love (1:7–8), and evidently of a danger.

What prompted the letter. We see the false teaching only through Paul’s reply. It was a “philosophy” passed on as “human tradition” (2:8). It judged believers over food and drink, festivals, the new moon and the Sabbath, all Jewish practices (2:16). It insisted on “asceticism and worship of angels”, visions and rules such as “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (2:18, 21), and it spoke of “the elemental spirits of the world” (2:8, 20). Scholars still debate whether this was chiefly a form of Jewish mysticism, a local blend of Jewish and pagan ideas, or an early form of the secret-knowledge teaching later called Gnosticism. This commentary thinks it was most likely a local mixture with strong Jewish elements. What matters more is its shape, which all agree on: Christ plus.

Did Paul really write it? A good number of modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to vocabulary and style unlike his undisputed letters, to the soaring passage of 1:15–20, and to its close relation to Ephesians. But the letter names Paul three times, closes with his signature, and is tied by its list of names to Philemon, which almost no one doubts is his: the same Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke appear in both. Differences of style are well explained by the subject (a new error to answer) and by Timothy’s share in the writing. The church received it as Paul’s from the beginning, and the more likely conclusion is that he wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. The letter has two halves. Chapters 1–2 teach who Christ is. Chapter 1 moves from thanks and prayer (1:3–14) to the great passage on Christ as Creator, sustainer and reconciler of all things (1:15–20), then to the readers, enemies reconciled (1:21–23), and to Paul’s labour for the mystery now revealed, “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:24–29). Chapter 2 names the danger. Since all “the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” are hidden in Christ (2:3), “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (2:6). In him they are already filled, circumcised without hands, buried and raised, forgiven, and freed from the powers (2:9–15), so no one may judge or disqualify them by rules that have “an appearance of wisdom” but are “of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (2:16–23). Chapters 3–4 show how to live. The hinge is 3:1: “If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above.” Because their life is hidden with Christ in God (3:1–4), they put to death what is earthly and put on the new self, where “Christ is all, and in all” (3:5–17). His lordship reaches the home, wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (3:18–4:1), and then outsiders (4:2–6). A page of names closes the letter (4:7–18), and it shows the gospel in human form: a runaway slave now a brother, the restored Mark, “Luke the beloved physician”, and Demas, who would later leave.

Where it leads: to Christ. The whole letter is built on 1:15–20, among the fullest statements of who Christ is in Paul’s letters. He is “the image of the invisible God”, “the firstborn of all creation”, meaning first in rank, not first created; all things were made by him, through him and for him, and in him they hold together. He is head of the church, “the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent” (1:18), and through his cross God reconciles all things, making peace by his blood. So the things the false teachers prized were shadows: food laws, festivals and Sabbaths were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (2:17). The true circumcision is union with him (2:11), the record of debt is nailed to his cross (2:14), and the powers they feared he has disarmed and led in triumph (2:15). The new self is renewed “after the image of its creator” (3:10), so in Christ God restores the image first given in Genesis 1. If Christ is who this letter says he is, every attempt to add to him is not only unnecessary but foolish.

For us. Colossians answers every form of Christianity that adds to Christ. It speaks to the believer who feels that faith in Christ alone is not quite enough, and that extra experiences, extra rules or extra revelations are needed to come fully to God. The letter says: you have been filled in him. The fullness you are seeking is already yours, in the one in whom all fullness dwells. It frees you from anyone who would judge you by rules of their own making, and sends you into ordinary life, at home, at work and among neighbours, doing “everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). Seek more of him, not something more beyond him.

1.title: The Supremacy of Christ: Hymn, Mystery, and Ministry
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 lays the foundation of the letter: before Paul names the false teaching in chapter 2, he shows a church he has never visited the Christ it already has.

The message. Christ is first over everything, and he is enough. The Son into whose kingdom the Father has rescued them is the image of the invisible God, the maker and goal of all things, the head of the church and the first to rise from the dead, the one in whom all God’s fullness lives and through whose cross God has made peace. And he is not far off, reached through angels and secrets: he lives in them, the hope of glory. They lack nothing.

Why it was said. Teachers at Colossae were offering something more: secret knowledge, angelic powers, food laws, festivals and harsh treatment of the body (2:8–23; see the introduction). They did not ask the believers to give up Christ, only to add to him. Paul’s answer is not a better technique but a bigger Christ.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul thanks God for what the gospel has produced in them (vv. 1–8), and prays that they will know God’s will, live to please the Lord, and thank the Father who has qualified, rescued and redeemed them in his Son (vv. 9–14). Then he turns wholly to the Son, first over creation and first over the new creation, the dwelling of God’s fullness and the maker of peace by his blood (vv. 15–20). He brings that home to the readers, once enemies and now reconciled, if they hold to the gospel (vv. 21–23), and to his own labour as servant of the mystery now open to the Gentiles: Christ in you, the hope of glory (vv. 24–29).

Where it leads. The chapter climbs to one of the highest passages about Christ in the Bible, then brings it down to earth: the one who made the galaxies made peace by a death outside a city wall, and now lives in ordinary believers in a small town. The firstborn of creation became the firstborn from the dead, so that a great family could follow him through the grave. Creation and redemption alike serve one purpose: “that in everything he might be preeminent” (v. 18).

For us. Whenever Christianity is offered with something added, a deeper experience, a stricter rule, a secret teaching, this chapter says: look again at Christ. In him you are qualified, rescued, forgiven and reconciled, and he lives in you. Grow deeper into him, never beyond him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel the Colossians received is already doing God’s work in them, and what they need is more of what they already have. Paul thanks God for the faith, love and hope the gospel has produced, as it bears fruit across the world and came to them through Epaphras (vv. 1–8). Then he prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God’s will, so as to live lives that please the Lord, strengthened to endure with joy and thankful to the Father who has qualified them, rescued them from darkness and brought them into the kingdom of his Son, in whom they have redemption (vv. 9–14). The prayer ends at the Son, and the next section turns wholly to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Knowledge of God’s Will: Wisdom, Not Secrets

Paul’s prayer for knowledge of God’s will (v. 9) counters the false teachers’ offer of special knowledge; the knowledge he seeks is meant to be walked (see the notes on vv. 9–10). The wisdom from above, as James says, is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits” (James 3:17). It is visible in a life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered a spiritual wisdom that was speculative and attainable only through special initiation. Now: Knowledge of God’s will is measured not by the height of its claims but by the life it produces: does it make you fruitful, enduring and thankful?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, sent by the risen Christ, greets a church he has never seen as God’s holy people, and speaks God’s grace and peace over them. Before a word of correction, they hear who is writing and who they are.

An apostle by the will of God. Paul roots his authority not in achievement or recognition but in calling: the risen Christ stopped him on the Damascus road while he was hunting Christians (Acts 9:5). An apostle is a sent man, and the sender is the point. The letter that will set Christ above every power in heaven begins by putting its own writer under him.

And Timothy our brother. Timothy was with Paul in prison and is named as co-sender, though Paul is the writer (see the “I” of 1:23–25). Paul’s word for him is not assistant but brother: family before team.

Saints and faithful brothers. Saints are set apart for God by his action; faithful brothers are believing and trustworthy. Paul gives them two addresses. In Christ is their true location, where their life is hidden (3:3): joined to him by faith, so that his death counts as their death to sin’s penalty and his risen life is their life (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 2:12). At Colossae is their earthly address, with its markets, temples and ordinary pressures. Every believer has both, and the whole letter is about living at the second address as someone who belongs to the first.

The setting. Paul had never visited Colossae, a small town in the Lycus Valley overshadowed by its wealthier neighbours; Epaphras had planted the church, and Paul writes from prison (see the introduction). So the greatest description of Christ’s lordship over the universe was written by a man in chains, to a small church in a fading town that he had never seen.

Grace and peace. Grace (charis) takes the ordinary Greek hello, chairein, and fills it with the gospel: God’s free, undeserved favour. Peace is the Hebrew shalom, everything set right with God: grace the source, peace the fruit. The God who could have written as a judge writes as a Father, and before a line of argument he pronounces grace and peace over a little church in a declining town, and calls them holy.

What it does not mean. Saint is not a level reached by a few but what God has done for all believers in setting them apart.

Why is Paul so formal with people he loves? Because a rival teaching was claiming a higher authority than the gospel the Colossians first received, and a church that does not know Paul’s face needs to know that this letter is not one man’s view. Apostolic letters were read aloud in church as the word of the Lord (4:16), and they still are. When you open Colossians, you are not reading a pious friend’s advice but receiving what Christ’s appointed envoy was given to say.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and the Lord Jesus Christ; the earliest do not.
verseByVerse.note: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited; the church was founded by Epaphras. Paul wrote from prison, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.

verseByVerse.quote: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God, the Father of the Lord Jesus, for what the gospel has done in the Colossians, and he does it every time he prays for them.

We always thank God. Paul thanks God not for the church’s success but for the faith, love and hope the gospel produced (vv. 4–5), because every evidence of grace is God’s doing. Thanksgiving runs through the letter (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17; 4:2), and a church that has forgotten how to give thanks is already open to teachers who say it does not yet have enough. And his praying was not vague goodwill; it had names and places in it, for people whose faces he had never seen.

The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The full title identifies which God Paul addresses: not one deity among many in the crowded religious marketplace of Asia Minor, but the God who has revealed himself in Jesus Christ. It also names the ground on which we approach him: the God who is Father of the Lord Jesus is, by adoption, Father of all who are in him (John 14:6; 20:17).

Should I thank God for Christians I find difficult? Yes, and Paul shows how. You need not approve of everything they do or pretend their faults are not there. You thank God for what he has truly given them: their faith in Christ, the love they do show, the hope they hold. That is not flattery, because the gifts are real and the credit goes to God. And it changes you. It is very hard to keep resenting someone you have honestly thanked God for that morning.

verseByVerse.quote: since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has heard that the Colossians trust Christ and love all his people, the two marks of a living church.

Your faith in Christ Jesus. Faith looks upward: it is the soul resting its weight on Christ. Its value lies in its object. Faith is not strong because the believer is strong but because Christ is; weak faith in a strong Saviour is safe, because it is the Saviour who saves.

Love for all the saints. Love looks outward. It is the evidence that the faith is real, and it is for all of them, not only the believers who are like us or easy to be with. The two are inseparable in Paul: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6). Faith that produces no love is not the genuine article (1 John 4:20), and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Does loving all the saints mean I have to like them all? No. Love in the New Testament is not first a feeling of warmth but a settled commitment to another person’s good. You may never find a particular believer easy company, and that is not a sin. But you can pray for him, speak well of him, help him when he is in need, forgive him when he wrongs you, and refuse to join in when others run him down. That is love, and over time God often adds the warmth to the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their faith and love spring from a sure hope kept in heaven, first heard in the true message of the gospel.

The hope laid up for you. Biblical hope is not a wish but confident expectation grounded in God’s promise: certain, though not yet received. “Laid up” is the language of a secured deposit, kept where nothing can spoil or steal it (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 1:4). No thief breaks in there, no market crashes there, no diagnosis reaches there.

Hope is the fuel. Faith and love springing from hope seems backwards, but Paul is describing what keeps them going day by day (1 Corinthians 13:13). Lose sight of what is coming, and faith shrinks and love grows cold. Those sure of heaven can afford to love sacrificially on earth.

The word of the truth. Against a teaching that paraded itself as higher wisdom, Paul offers no competing philosophy. The gospel is the word of the truth, not one opinion among many, because it tells what God has actually done in Christ. “Gospel” (euangelion) was the word for an emperor’s public announcement of good news; this one announces that a King has won the decisive victory (Isaiah 52:7).

A hope with a face. What is laid up in heaven is finally not a thing but a Person: Christ in you, the hope of glory (1:27), with whom your life is hidden in God (3:3). It is kept in heaven because Christ is there, and it is as safe as he is. And it will not be posted to us from a distance. It arrives when he does.

In everyday life. When love feels too costly, look up before you look in: is what you hope for big enough to pay for what Christ asks of you today? A forgiven grudge, a hard kindness, a long patience: none of them can bankrupt someone whose inheritance is kept in heaven.

Is heaven a place I go to, or something that comes here? Both, in their order. A believer who dies goes to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). But the final hope is larger: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will make a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4), and what is kept in heaven will be revealed when he appears (3:4). You are not hoping to float away from creation for ever, but to live in it renewed, with God.

verseByVerse.quote: which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is alive and growing all over the world, and it has been doing the same among the Colossians since the day they truly grasped God’s grace.

Bearing fruit and increasing. They did not go looking for the gospel in some distant shrine; it came to them, carried by a man from their own town (v. 7). And it is a living plant: not an idea spread by human energy but God’s word, with the power to produce what it announces. The farmer only sows; the seed has life in itself (Mark 4:26–29; 1 Corinthians 3:6–7). “In the whole world” means this is no local cult or secret teaching but a message for all nations. The word that came to a small town in the Lycus Valley is still running across the earth, alive with the life of the God who spoke it, and it has never yet returned to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

Understood the grace of God in truth. “Understood” is a strong word: coming to know fully, that you brought nothing, deserved nothing, and received everything. “In truth” (en alētheia) probably carries two ideas. Truly: their understanding was real, and it showed in the fruit growing since that day. And as it really is: they grasped grace accurately, from the word of the truth (v. 5) taught by a faithful minister (v. 7). That mattered, because false teachers were now offering plausible arguments (2:4, 8) and rules about food, festivals and self-denial (2:16–23). Those who have simply received the gospel are missing nothing (Galatians 1:6–9).

Why it matters. Grace can be misunderstood in two opposite ways. Some turn it into permission to sin: if God forgives, why not carry on? (Romans 6:1; Jude 4). Others add something to it, so that Christ is not quite enough without extra rules, rituals or experiences: the very danger in Colossae (2:20–23; Galatians 5:4). Grace in truth is entirely free, and it changes those who receive it, “training us to renounce ungodliness” (Titus 2:11–12).

Grace with a name. Grace is not a general mood of kindness in heaven; it has a name. John says that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), and Paul that the rich Son became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is why grace cannot be topped up with rules or experiences. It is not a quantity God measures out but the gift of his Son, and the Son is not given in part.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel, remember whose seed it is: you sow; you do not make it grow. That frees you to speak without pressure and to wait without despair.

How can I tell whether I have understood grace in truth? Look at both halves. Do you rest your hope before God on Christ alone, with nothing of your own added: not church attendance, record, feelings or experiences? And is that grace changing you, so that you hate the sins you once excused and want to please the God who forgave you? If you think God accepts you because you are doing well, grace has been distorted one way. If you think it does not matter how you live because you are forgiven, it has been distorted the other. Grace in truth gives you peace and makes you new.

verseByVerse.quote: just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Colossians learned this gospel from Epaphras, a faithful servant of Christ whom Paul loves and fully endorses. They did not receive a beginner’s version that now needs upgrading; they received the real thing from a faithful man.

Epaphras. A native of Colossae (4:12), Epaphras probably heard the gospel from Paul in Ephesus and took it home to the Lycus Valley.

Our beloved fellow servant. Literally fellow slave (syndoulos), one whose whole existence belongs to a master. Paul calls himself a slave of Christ (Romans 1:1) and names Epaphras his equal in that service; “beloved” shows that the praise comes from real affection, not tactics.

A faithful minister of Christ. “Minister” (diakonos) is the word for a table servant, who brings what his Master gives him, not a message of his own (Mark 10:44–45). And he is a minister of Christ: when Paul speaks of the source and purpose of salvation he tends to name the Father (v. 3), but when he speaks of the ministry he names Christ, who commissions his servants, whose death and resurrection is the message, and who sends them with all authority (Matthew 28:18–20).

Following his Master to the table. Christ the Lord took the form of a servant and came among us as one who serves (Philippians 2:7; Luke 22:27). Every faithful Epaphras is only following his Master to the table.

In everyday life. Thank God for the person who first brought you the gospel, and if you can, write and thank them. Faithful servants are rarely told what their faithfulness did.

What if the person who brought me the gospel later failed badly? It happens, and it is painful. But the gospel does not stand or fall with the messenger: what saved you was Christ, not the person who told you of him. Paul could rejoice that Christ was preached even when the preachers had poor motives (Philippians 1:15–18). Grieve the failure, pray for them, and if they wronged you, take it seriously. But hold on to what was true in what they gave you: the Christ you trusted is unchanged.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read on our behalf (ESV note): Epaphras then represented Paul among them. Either way, his faithfulness is the point.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras has told Paul about the love the Holy Spirit has produced in the Colossians.

Love in the Spirit. Love whose source and energy is the Holy Spirit himself, who pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5), the love seen when Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). Love is the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). This is the only explicit mention of the Spirit in Colossians, a letter focused on Christ, and that is fitting, because the Spirit’s work is to make Christ known.

The surest evidence. Natural love is real and good, but it prefers the lovable and dries up when not returned. Love in the Spirit can love the difficult and the enemy, because it draws on God’s love. Anyone can adopt new beliefs; not everyone comes to love people they would not naturally love. When Epaphras reported the Colossians’ love, Paul heard: the Spirit is at work here (1 John 4:7).

What if I do not feel much love for other believers? Then ask for it, because that is exactly what the Spirit gives; it is not manufactured by trying to feel warmer. Confess the coldness honestly, ask your Father to pour his love into your heart by the Spirit (Luke 11:13), and then act in love toward someone specific, even before you feel it. The feelings often follow the obedience. And look again at the cross. The Spirit’s way of producing love is to show us how much we have been loved (1 John 4:10–11).

May we pray to the Holy Spirit? The New Testament pattern is prayer to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18; Matthew 6:9; John 16:23); no New Testament prayer is addressed directly to the Spirit, and many Reformed Christians keep to that pattern, as this commentary does. But it is not wrong to address the Spirit. He is fully God: lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4), and we are baptised into the one name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Westminster Confession directs worship to God, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to him alone (21.2; 1689 22.2), and the Nicene Creed confesses the Spirit, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified. That is why the church has long sung prayers to the Spirit, such as Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire, and Breathe on me, breath of God. So pray ordinarily to the Father, in the Spirit’s strength; and if you say, Holy Spirit, fill me with love, you are speaking to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul never stops praying that God will fill the Colossians with a full, practical knowledge of his will, the wisdom the Spirit gives.

We have not ceased to pray. Paul prays rather than merely explains, because accurate teaching alone does not change a life; God must bring the truth home to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14). The most faithful teachers are the most persistent in prayer, as Epaphras was (4:12). And verses 9–14 are one long Greek sentence that climbs from knowing God’s will to thanks for the Father’s rescue, and the rescue brings Paul to the Son (vv. 15–20). The prayer is not a detour before the doctrine. It is the road into it.

Filled with the knowledge of his will. The false teachers seem to have promised special knowledge, as though the Colossians were half empty and needed topping up from their secrets. Paul prays for full knowledge of God’s will, a practical grasp of what God wants, filled from the source they already have, Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3).

All spiritual wisdom and understanding. Spiritual means given by the Spirit, not the human cleverness the false teachers were selling. Wisdom is chiefly the skill of living: the Old Testament word (ḥokmah) is used of craftsmen (Exodus 31:3–6), and in Proverbs it is choosing the right thing in a real situation; “By his good conduct let him show his works” (James 3:13). Understanding is closer to insight: seeing what a situation really is and how truths fit together (Proverbs 2:2–6; 1 Kings 3:9–12). Roughly, understanding sees and wisdom does. J. B. Lightfoot described understanding as the faculty that grasps how a truth bears on a particular case, which is why it is sometimes explained as applying truth; but the words overlap heavily, and in Scripture it is wisdom that is most clearly the skill of living.

The Spirit of wisdom and understanding. The pair comes from Isaiah’s promise that the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2). What Christ has fully, his people receive from his Spirit. And the purpose follows at once: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Knowledge of God’s will is meant to be lived.

In everyday life. Pray this by name for someone today: Lord, fill them with the knowledge of your will.

Does this mean God will show me which job to take or whom to marry? Paul means God’s revealed will: the wisdom to live a life worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Within it God gives his people freedom to choose wisely, praying, seeking counsel and weighing what is good; he guides by his word and providence, not usually by special messages. If two jobs are both honest and both open to you, you are not missing a secret answer. Ask which would let you serve God and love others best, take advice from mature believers, decide, and trust him with the result. Scripture does settle some questions for you: a believer is to marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39).

verseByVerse.quote: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing God’s will is meant to produce a life that fits the Lord and pleases him.

A manner worthy of the Lord. Walk in the Bible means the whole of daily life. “Worthy” first meant of equal weight, what balances the scales: a worthy life fits the one it belongs to (Philippians 1:27; Ephesians 4:1). And the order matters. Paul prays for knowledge so that they may walk worthily: prayer is not an extra but what drives the Christian life; and we please God because he loves us, not so that he will (1 John 4:19).

What does a worthy walk look like? Paul defines it in the same sentence with four marks: bearing fruit and increasing in the knowledge of God (v. 10), endurance and patience with joy (v. 11), and thanks to the Father (v. 12). Later he fills it in: compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiveness, and above all love (3:12–14), lived out at home and at work (3:18–4:1). And the measure is the Lord himself, the one Paul is about to describe, the image of the invisible God who made peace by the blood of his cross (vv. 15–20). He is gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). A life that fits him will look like him.

Fully pleasing to him. The aim of life is to please Christ (2 Corinthians 5:9). The Lord who needs nothing from us (Acts 17:25) delights in his children’s obedience, small and ordinary as it is (Hebrews 13:16).

Bearing fruit in every good work. The word used of the gospel (v. 6): the believer’s fruit is the gospel’s own, works God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10), in the whole texture of daily life: the honest word when a lie would be easier, the kindness to the person nobody notices.

Increasing in the knowledge of God. Not accumulating information but deepening a relationship, in which knowing and living feed each other. Knowing God better produces a worthy life: forgiving is easier once you have reckoned with how much you have been forgiven. And living worthily deepens the knowledge: if anyone wills to do God’s will, Jesus said, he will know whether the teaching is from God (John 7:17). The growth has no ceiling (2 Peter 3:18): you learn that he keeps his promises, and then you find him keeping them in a hospital corridor (Psalm 34:8).

What it does not mean. Not earning God’s approval: we are already accepted in Christ (1:22), and please him as children, not as servants anxious for wages. Nor is a worthy walk measured by human rules or a Christian look, a dress code, foods or special days: that is exactly the religion Paul rejects in this letter (2:16–23).

Not respectability, perfection or only the spectacular. The Lord himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19), and a life that fits him will sometimes look out of place to polite society, and even to religious people. The worthy walk is growing, not finished, and it includes failing, confessing and getting up again (1 John 1:9). Enduring a long illness with patience and joy is as worthy of the Lord as any public ministry. And it is not in our own strength: Paul prays for this walk, because it is God’s work in us (v. 11).

Can someone as ordinary and inconsistent as me really please God? Yes (2 Corinthians 5:9; Hebrews 13:16). Not because your obedience is flawless but because you are in his Son, so that your imperfect works are received through Christ, as a father treasures the crooked drawing his child brings him: believers’ good works, though imperfect, are accepted in Christ, God looking upon them in his Son (Westminster 16.6; 1689 16.6). So the smallest honest act done for his sake gives him pleasure. That is not a reason for pride. It is a reason to begin.

verseByVerse.quote: being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God’s own glorious power will keep strengthening them, not for spectacular feats but to endure hardship and bear patiently with people, and to do it with joy.

Being strengthened according to his glorious might. The Greek verb pictures an ongoing supply from outside: Paul does not pray that they try harder, but that they be strengthened. The measure is God’s own might, the same power that raised Christ from the dead (Ephesians 1:19–20), at work in believers through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16). Whoever thinks he needs only a little of God’s help has not understood what genuine love, sustained faithfulness and real forgiveness cost.

Endurance and patience. Endurance holds up under circumstances; patience bears with people, not retaliating but waiting for God to act. It takes nothing less than resurrection might to keep a tired believer gentle with a difficult neighbour for twenty years, and the might that flung out the galaxies is put to work in the quiet places of a believer’s life: a hospital bed, a hard marriage, a long wait. God is not too great to bother with our endurance. He counts it worth his glorious power.

With joy. Not grim endurance or forced cheerfulness, but the gladness of one who knows the inheritance is secure, so that no present suffering is the final word (James 1:2–4; Romans 5:3–5).

Endurance first seen in the Lord. Both graces were Christ’s before they were ours. He endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and he displayed his perfect patience in bearing long with Paul, the man hunting his church (1 Timothy 1:16). Endurance with joy is the shape of the Saviour’s own life, and the power that strengthens us is his risen life at work in us.

In everyday life. Name the trial you are enduring and the person who most tries your patience. Ask God for his glorious power, not to escape the trial, but to endure it with joy, and not to change that person first, but to make you patient with them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes trials, and joy does not mean pretending: the psalms of lament are in the Bible, and Jesus wept. Joy can sit alongside tears, because it rests on something deeper than the day.

How can I have joy when I am suffering? Not by denying the pain, but by looking past it to what it cannot touch. Your sins are forgiven (v. 14), your inheritance is kept in light (v. 12), you are in the kingdom of the Son the Father loves (v. 13), and the Lord who holds all things together is holding you (v. 17). Joy in suffering is often quiet, more like a steady floor under your feet than a feeling of happiness. If you cannot find it today, ask for it: Paul is praying for exactly that, and it is a gift, not an achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth mark of a life worthy of the Lord is thankfulness, because the Father has already made believers fit to share the inheritance of his people.

Who has qualified you. “Qualified” means made fit, and the choice is pointed. The false teachers suggested the believers still needed further experiences, angelic mediators or ascetic practices to be complete (2:18, 23). Paul cuts it off at the root: the Father has already qualified you, fully, not provisionally. This is the pastoral heart of the letter, a word for the anxious achiever as much as the rebel. Many church people quietly live as though they must still earn their place; the Father’s verdict ends that labour. He did not wait for us to become fit for his presence. He made us fit, at the cost of his Son.

The inheritance of the saints in light. This is the language of the promised land, Israel’s inheritance, where the LORD himself was the portion of his people (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 32:9). In Christ it becomes the new creation, the resurrection body, the face of God seen unveiled (1 Corinthians 2:9), coming as an inheritance comes to a child, a gift, not wages. It is in light because it is in the full presence of God, who is light, with nothing in between (1 John 1:5; Revelation 21:23), in contrast with the darkness of v. 13.

Heirs because of the Heir. Strangers inherit from God because the Father has appointed his Son heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and everyone joined to the Son shares his portion: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). Canaan was divided by lot among the tribes; this inheritance is not divided at all, because each of the saints receives it whole, in him.

What if I feel unworthy to stand before God? In yourself you are, and so is every believer. But the question is not whether you are worthy but whether God has qualified you, and if you trust Christ, he has. Your fitness for heaven rests not on your feelings, progress or record this week, but on what the Father has done in his Son. Feeling unworthy can be a healthy humility, but it must not become a doubt about God’s verdict. Bring the feeling to the cross and leave it there.

verseByVerse.quote: He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father has rescued believers from the rule of darkness and moved them, once for all, into the kingdom of his beloved Son.

Delivered. A rescue word, used of God snatching his people from Egypt. Without Christ we were dead and captive, not struggling toward the light but at home in the dark (Ephesians 2:1–5).

The domain of darkness. “Domain” is a word for rule: not merely a moral condition but a realm with a ruler, the one Jesus called the ruler of this world (John 12:31) and Paul the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4). It blinds minds while presenting itself as normal. Its people do not feel trapped; they cannot see that they cannot see, which is why rescue requires a power from outside.

Transferred. The word was used of deporting whole populations, and it is a completed action. The kingdom is not only future: every believer has already entered it, a citizen of another kingdom while his feet still stand on the old earth (Philippians 3:20). The voice with the last say over your life is no longer sin, fear or the crowd, but Christ, and his protection, his laws and his future are now yours (Romans 6:17–18).

The kingdom of his beloved Son. Literally the Son of his love, echoing the voice at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). You have been brought inside the Father’s own love for the Son, the atmosphere of the kingdom, and you are secure there, because nothing can remove the Father’s love for Christ, and you are in Christ (John 17:23). And he is the one who fills everything until v. 21: you cannot understand the kingdom until you see whose it is.

In everyday life. When a temptation comes dressed as normal life, call it by its name: that is the old country, and you do not live there any more. And when you pray for a friend who does not believe, pray as Paul would: not merely that they will improve, but that God will rescue them, because that is what it takes.

If I have been rescued, why do I still struggle with sin and temptation? Because the transfer is complete but the war is not over. You still live in enemy-occupied territory, with old habits that pull and an enemy who tempts, but sin is now a rebel in your life, not your rightful ruler (Romans 6:12–14). Every struggle against it is the struggle of a free citizen of Christ’s kingdom, not the hopeless effort of a captive. Fight it, confess it, and remember whose kingdom you belong to.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Son believers already have redemption: their freedom has been bought and their sins forgiven.

Redemption. The word comes from ransom: captives freed when someone paid the price. We could not pay our own way out; Christ paid, with his blood (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19), and we have this redemption now.

The forgiveness of sins. Forgiveness means release, the dropping of a charge. It does not pretend the offences did not happen; it declares the charge answered and the record cleared, finally and completely, nailed to the cross (2:13–14). And the One who cancelled the charge sheet is the Judge himself.

One event, two angles. Redemption says how we got free: a price was paid. Forgiveness says where we stand now: the record is clear (Romans 3:24–25). And “in whom” matters. Redemption is not a commodity Christ hands over and leaves us to manage; we have it because we have him.

In everyday life. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not argue with your feelings; answer with the fact: in Christ I have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. And because you are forgiven so much, forgive the person who has wronged you a little (3:13).

Does God forgive sins I commit after I become a Christian? Yes. Christ paid for all your sins on the cross, when every one of them was still future. That does not make sin small; it cost his blood. When you sin as a believer, you are not cast out of the family, but you grieve your Father, and should confess it honestly: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Confession does not buy the forgiveness again; it brings you back into the enjoyment of it.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add through his blood, borrowed from Ephesians 1:7; the earliest manuscripts do not have it here, but the truth is the same, as v. 20 will say.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ is first over everything, the old creation and the new, so nothing can be added to him. In what may be an early Christian hymn, Paul sets him over creation as the image of the invisible God, its maker, its purpose and the one who holds it together (vv. 15–17), and over the new creation as head of the church and firstborn from the dead (v. 18). The reason is that all God’s fullness was pleased to dwell in him, and through him God reconciles all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as Creator and Redeemer

The hymn holds Christ’s work in creation and redemption together: the one through whom all things were made is the one through whose blood all things are reconciled. So redemption is not rescue from a material world God has abandoned but the renewal of his creation. Abraham Kuyper’s famous claim, “there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’”, rests on passages like this one.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian error apparently involved a hierarchy of spiritual powers through whom one had to navigate to reach God. The hymn removes it: all these powers were created by Christ and are subject to him. Now: Whatever sets other mediators between the believer and God, whether saints, angels or spiritual powers, repeats the Colossian mistake. To see God, look at Christ. To reach God, come through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son makes the invisible God fully visible, and he holds first place over all creation as its heir and ruler. From here to v. 20 Paul answers the error not by matching its secrets but by showing the church more of Christ.

The Christ hymn. Verses 15–20 are often thought to be an early Christian hymn, written or quoted by Paul, in two stanzas: Christ and creation (vv. 15–17), and Christ and the new creation (vv. 18–20). They mirror each other: firstborn of all creation (v. 15), firstborn from the dead (v. 18); all things created through him (v. 16), all things reconciled through him (v. 20). The one who made the world is the one who remakes it.

The image of the invisible God. Image (eikōn) means the exact, living representation of the original. No one has ever seen God (John 1:18), yet he has made himself visible in a Person: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3).

Three echoes. An eikōn was the emperor’s head on a coin, carrying his authority (Mark 12:16). Humanity was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27): Christ is the true image Adam failed to be, in whom the broken likeness is restored (3:10). And Jewish wisdom writing had called Wisdom an image of God’s goodness (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). Paul lands all of it on one man, Jesus of Nazareth. The God no one has ever seen has stepped into view in his Son, with a human face and nail-scarred hands.

Firstborn of all creation. “Firstborn” speaks of rank, as the heir held first place in the family: not first created, but heir and ruler over creation. God made David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27), though David was the youngest son of Jesse. Christ is not the eldest member of creation’s family; he is the heir of the whole estate.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? By looking at Jesus. Read the Gospels and watch him touching lepers, weeping at a grave, forgiving the men who crucified him. That is what God is like.

How do I answer a Jehovah’s Witness at my door about this verse? Gently, and from the passage itself. Ask them to read on to verse 16: how can someone who made all things be one of the things made? Point out that David was called firstborn though he was the youngest, so firstborn can mean first in rank. Show them verse 19 and 2:9, where all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ. Their translation adds the word other (all other things), which is not in the Greek; ask them why. Above all, be kind. You are not winning an argument but pointing a person to the Christ who made them.

Where Christians differ: is Christ a created being? Ancient Arians (a fourth-century movement that denied Christ’s full deity) and modern Jehovah’s Witnesses take firstborn to mean that Christ was the first being God created, through whom he made everything else. This commentary’s view: Verse 16 gives the reason he is firstborn: “for by him all things were created.” If he created all things, he is not one of them. Firstborn here means supreme heir, not first created; Greek had a word for first created (prōtoktistos), and Paul did not use it. And verse 19 says all the fullness of God dwells in him. Christ is the eternal Son, uncreated, fully God, of one substance with the Father (John 1:1–3; Nicene Creed).
verseByVerse.note: “Firstborn” speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place, not that the Son was created.

parallels.desc: I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything that exists, including every unseen power, was made by Christ, through Christ and for Christ.

By him all things were created. Literally in him: creation took place in the Son, its centre and source (John 1:3; Hebrews 1:2). Creation is the work of the whole Trinity (1 Corinthians 8:6; Genesis 1:2), but Christ is in the spotlight because the false teachers were crowding him in among the spiritual powers (2:18). The One they would reduce to a creature made every creature.

Visible and invisible, thrones or dominions. The scope is exhaustive, shutting every door, and the unseen realm is where the Colossian error located its powers. Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers, angels good and evil, honoured or feared by the false teachers (2:15, 18), probably terms for angelic ranks. Paul is not teaching angelic grades; he sweeps the impressive vocabulary into one sentence: every rank, created by Christ.

Through him and for him. Through him: he is the agent of creation. For him: he is its goal, the one toward whom it all moves. In Romans 11:36 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 it is God the Father from whom and for whom all things exist; here Paul says it of Christ. Only God can be the purpose of creation, so this is a quiet but unmistakable claim to his full deity.

You do not tremble before what your Lord made. The Colossians were taught that these powers controlled the road to God and had to be appeased. Paul removes the fear with one fact: Christ made them. Even the fallen, hostile powers Christ disarmed at the cross (2:15) owe their existence to him: not an independent dark kingdom in even combat, but defeated creatures whose Maker is their Master.

What it means to be made for Christ. If all things were created for him, so were you: he is not only where you came from, but what you are for. Man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever (Shorter Catechism Q. 1), and this God is known in Christ. Three things follow.

Your life has a purpose that does not depend on success. Not only when you are useful, healthy or impressive: a bedridden grandmother who trusts him, or a child with severe disabilities, is as truly made for him as a missionary or a preacher.

You belong to someone, and nothing else will finally satisfy. You are not your own; you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Career, money or pleasure, good as they are, leave us restless when made the point of life. Augustine prayed: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Confessions 1.1).

Ordinary things are for him too. Work, food, marriage, music, a garden: everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4), to be lived for him, doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus (3:17), heartily, as for the Lord (3:23). You do your job well because he is the one you serve; you speak as you would be glad for him to hear; you decide by asking what pleases him (2 Corinthians 5:9). And when you fail, you come back to him, because he has already forgiven you (1:13–14).

Like a key in its lock. A key turns smoothly in the lock it was made for and jams in any other. The van you drive, the shelves you stack, the bill you pay honestly, the patience you keep with a difficult workmate: done consciously for Christ, the key slides into its lock, and the most ordinary Monday becomes the thing you were made for.

What it does not mean. Not that you must become a pastor or be doing something religious every minute. Not that God needs you (Acts 17:25): he made you for his glory and your joy, and those are not rivals. And not that your standing depends on how well you manage it: you are reconciled and presented holy through Christ’s death (1:22). Living for him is the response to that, not the price of it.

Should I be afraid of evil spirits? No, not if you belong to Christ. Scripture takes them seriously: they are real and deceive, and believers are to resist the devil and put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). But they are creatures, made by Christ, defeated at the cross (2:15), and unable to separate you from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39). You need no charms, rituals, formulas or anxious precautions, only to stay close to Christ: pray, trust his word, refuse sin, and leave the powers to their Master. The safest place in the universe is in the hands of the One who made them.

Is it not vain for God to make all things for himself? Only if he were less than the best thing there is. A person who demands all praise is vain, because no person deserves it; God is the one being who does, the source of every joy we know, and to point us to anything less would be unkind. And the goal of creation is the Son, who laid his glory aside to rescue runaways (Philippians 2:6–8): not a tyrant’s vanity but a giver’s glory, and to live for it is the joy we were made for.
verseByVerse.note: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ existed before everything and ranks above it, and he keeps the whole universe in being from moment to moment.

He is before all things. Before in time, and the present tense is startling: not he was, but he is, the timeless present Jesus used when he said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). And before in rank: to be before all things is to stand above them. The false teachers were fitting Christ into the created order, but there is no rung of the ladder higher than Christ, because Christ is not on the ladder. He made it.

In him all things hold together. To cohere, to be kept from flying apart, and the tense means has held and goes on holding (Hebrews 1:3). He is not a watchmaker who walked away. The atoms cohere, the planets keep their orbits, your next heartbeat comes, because Christ is actively holding it all.

The centre that holds. Just after the First World War, W. B. Yeats wrote one of the most quoted lines of the modern age: “Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.” Many feel it about their own lives: a work self, a family self, an online self and a private self, and nothing quite joins them. The modern answer is that you must be the centre and hold yourself together by force of will, a heavy load for a heart that cannot keep its resolutions until Friday. Paul offers something more radical than a technique for balance. The centre exists, and it is not an idea but a person, the one in whom the galaxies and your heartbeat cohere. A life is unified not by finding the right proportions among its parts but by putting him in the middle of them, where he already is; then work, family, rest and even failure take their place around him instead of tearing you between them.

In everyday life. On the day it feels as though everything is coming apart, say it to yourself: in him all things hold together, including this. Then do the next small thing in front of you, and leave the holding to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean scientific explanation is unimportant. The scientist who measures the laws of nature is measuring the faithfulness of the Son, whether he knows it or not.

If Christ holds everything together, why do things fall apart: illness, disasters, death? Because the world is held but also fallen, subjected to futility because of sin and groaning as it waits for renewal (Romans 8:20–22). He does not prevent every breaking, but nothing breaks outside his hand, and he works even the breaking for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The same Christ who holds the stars was himself broken on a cross. He knows what falling apart feels like, and he is bringing all things to a day when nothing will be broken again.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Creator is also head of the church and, by rising first from the dead, the beginning of the new creation, so that he holds first place in everything.

The head of the body, the church. The second stanza begins: Christ and the new creation. Scholars debate whether head means source, like the head of a river, or authority; here Paul seems to hold both together: Christ is the source of the church’s life and its ruler (2:19; Ephesians 1:22–23; 4:15–16). The church is not merely like a body; it is Christ’s body.

Why the church comes in here. To bring the hymn home: the Lord of galaxies and angels is Head of the little flock at Colossae. And to answer the false teachers, who were slipping angelic mediators between the believer and God: the church has one Head, and life and access to God flow from him alone. To go looking elsewhere is to let go of the Head (2:19).

The beginning. Origin, source, ruler: as he was firstborn over the old order (v. 15), so he begins the new order that dawned when he walked out of the tomb.

Firstborn from the dead. Lazarus was called back to the same mortal life, only to die again (John 11:43–44); Christ passed through death into deathless life, the first human ever to do so (1 Corinthians 15:20; Revelation 1:5). He is firstborn as an eldest brother is, the first of a great family who will follow him through the grave (Romans 8:29). Because the Head has risen, the body will rise too.

That in everything he might be preeminent. “Preeminent” means holding first place, and this purpose crowns the hymn: first in creation and in new creation, over angels and over death. The Colossian error was a quiet demotion of Christ, high but not highest, sharing the platform with angels and rules. But it is God’s settled purpose that his Son be first, with the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ needs the church to be complete; the church needs him. Nor does head mean that any human leader is head of the church. Pastors and elders are servants under the one Head, not substitutes for him.

What does it look like to give Christ first place? Think of a wedding ring. You may rightly love many things, your work, your friends, your hobbies, but the ring says one person comes first, and everything else takes its place around her. A life is put right not by adding Christ to the list of things you love but by moving him to the head of it, so that everything else, not thrown away but reordered, orbits him. In practice it shows in what you will not give up for anything else: time with him in his word and prayer, obedience when it costs, the worship of his people on the Lord’s Day. And it shows in how you decide: what does he want here?

verseByVerse.quote: For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ can be first in everything, and can reconcile all things, because God in all his fullness chose to live in him. The one who makes peace (v. 20) is God himself, not a go-between.

All the fullness. Fullness (plērōma) was perhaps the false teachers’ word for the totality of divine powers, spread among angels and spirits; later Gnostic teachers pictured it parcelled across a chain of intermediary beings, a ladder to climb. Paul turns the word: all the fullness, the entire divine nature and not a share, is in Christ alone. And if all of God is in Christ, the ladder of mediators is not merely unnecessary but an insult to the Son who holds it all.

To dwell. God dwelt in the tabernacle, and the Spirit dwells in believers by grace, but this is different: permanent residence, not resting on him as on a prophet. The whole divine fullness took up residence in him, bodily (2:9): not a copy or an outflow of God, but God himself dwelling in the man Christ Jesus (John 1:14).

Was pleased. The language of free, delighted good pleasure, the same root as the Father’s voice at the baptism, “with whom I am well pleased”. Picture a vast firm whose owner you knew only through messages passed down a chain of managers, until one Monday he walks onto the shop floor himself. God did not send fragments of himself down a chain of angels; he came himself, the whole of him, in a real man you could have stood beside (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the fullness came to dwell in him at some point, as if he were not God before. Nor does it mean that Christ’s humanity was swallowed up by his deity: he is one person, truly God and truly man.

If I have Christ, do I need anything more? Nothing more of God, no: no second blessing to complete what Christ began, no secret teaching, special experience or higher class of Christian. All the fullness is in him, and you are filled in him (2:10). You do need to grow, to know, obey and enjoy him more, but that growth goes deeper into Christ, not beyond him. Whatever claims to take you past Christ is taking you away from the only place God’s fullness is found.

Uncertain wording. The Greek does not name who was pleased, and has no word for “of God”. It may mean that all the fullness (God in his fullness) was pleased to dwell in Christ, as the ESV takes it, or that God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him. The ESV rightly supplies “of God” (compare 2:9). Either way, God himself, wholly and gladly, chose to dwell in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s death on the cross God brings everything in heaven and on earth back into peace with himself.

To reconcile. The strengthened Greek form means bringing the estranged all the way home, turning enemies into friends: through Christ God restores the harmony sin destroyed (2 Corinthians 5:18–19; Romans 5:10).

Through him. Through whom all things were created (v. 16), all things are reconciled. The hands that scattered the stars are the hands that were nailed to the beam. The Maker did not send the means; he became the means.

Whether on earth or in heaven. All things, not all people: the same sweeping phrase as for the created order in vv. 16–17, for the reach of the cross is as wide as creation. When Adam fell, the whole world was dragged down, subjected to futility and now groaning (Romans 8:20–22), so the rescue must be as large as the wreck: a renewed creation, the curse lifted, all things at peace.

Making peace by the blood of his cross. The means is not special knowledge but Christ’s death, and the peace is not a bare ceasefire but a relationship set right. There was real war: God’s holy wrath against sin, and our settled hostility. That wrath is no flash of irritation but the fixed resistance of a pure God to all that wrecks what he made, and a God without it would not be good (Habakkuk 1:13). God did not wave the conflict away; he satisfied his own justice and bore his own wrath in the body of his Son, so the peace is righteous, not cheap (Romans 3:25–26; 5:1). Paul lands the cosmic vision on a beam of wood outside a city wall: the reconciliation of the universe was achieved on one particular afternoon, by one particular death.

His throne is shaped like a cross. The rebels did not sue for terms; the King paid the price of the treaty himself and signed it in his wounds. That peace is wide enough to hold the stars and near enough to hold a single forgiven sinner, and the day is coming when nothing in heaven or on earth will be at war with God.

Two kinds of peace. For those who come to Christ and continue in the faith (v. 23), the restoration is the reconciliation of glad children welcomed home; for the hostile powers and all who refuse him to the end, it is the peace of a conquered enemy (2:15). Every knee will bow, some in joy and some in defeat (Philippians 2:10–11).

What does the blood of the cross have to do with my peace with God? Everything. Your peace with God is not a mood you work up or a truce you negotiate by behaving well. It was made, once, outside Jerusalem, when Christ bore the penalty your sins deserved (1 Peter 2:24; 3:18). So it is solid, resting on something finished, and free, with nothing to add by angelic ladders or man-made rules (2:13–15). When your conscience accuses you, do not look first at your feelings or your record. Look at the cross, where peace was made, and rest there.

Is it not primitive to say that peace was made by blood? Only if it meant an angry god bribed with a victim. Blood is Scripture’s shorthand for a life laid down in sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11), and here the life is God’s own, given in his Son: the Judge does not make someone else pay; he pays himself. The alternative is not a kinder God but one who shrugs at cruelty, betrayal and abuse, and calls it nothing. No one who has been badly wronged wants a God like that. At the cross God took evil with full seriousness, and took its cost on himself.

Where Christians differ: will all things, including all people and demons, be saved? Some read “reconcile to himself all things” as universal salvation. This commentary’s view: Paul means that Christ restores all creation to its proper order under God. Believers are reconciled as friends (vv. 21–22); hostile powers are pacified by being disarmed and defeated (2:15), not saved. The same Paul teaches eternal judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The whole universe will be brought back into peace with God, with evil judged and removed, and creation itself set free (Romans 8:19–21).

Uncertain wording. In “to reconcile to himself” the pronoun could point to God or to Christ (compare “for him”, v. 16). Most take it of God, as in 2 Corinthians 5:18–19; the sense is hardly affected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Reconciled and the Mystery Revealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Christ of the hymn is Christ for you and Christ in you. Paul turns to his readers: once enemies of God, they are now reconciled by Christ’s bodily death, to be presented holy on the last day, as long as they hold on to the gospel (vv. 21–23). Then he turns to himself, the servant of that gospel, who rejoices to suffer for the church and labours in Christ’s strength to make known the mystery now revealed to the Gentiles, Christ in you, the hope of glory, so that he may present everyone mature in Christ (vv. 24–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ in You: Union with Christ

“Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the New Testament’s shortest statement of union with Christ, the believer’s being joined to him. The mystery hidden for ages is not only that Gentiles would be included in God’s people, but that Christ himself would live in them by his Spirit. Union with Christ is the root of every benefit of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed further experiences and secret knowledge to be complete or mature. Paul says the mystery that makes for maturity is already in them. Now: To the believer seeking a higher experience: the one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you (see the note on v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God reconciled them, the Colossians were estranged from him and opposed to him in mind, and it showed in what they did.

And you. The camera turns from Christ’s glory to the readers: it is one thing to hear that Christ reconciled all things, another to hear that this includes you.

Once alienated. Estranged, shut out from a belonging that ought to be yours, alienated from the life of God (Ephesians 4:18). Once: for the believer, a country left for good; but it is the present address of every soul not yet in Christ (Isaiah 59:2).

Hostile in mind. Under the estrangement lies enmity in the seat of thinking and willing: not neutral, but opposed. Not every unbeliever consciously hates God; most never give him a thought. But the natural mind will not have him on the throne: “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot” (Romans 8:7). The polite indifference of the respectable man and the open scorn of the scoffer are two faces of one enmity.

Doing evil deeds. The deeds are the symptom, not the disease: we do not become alienated by doing wrong; we do wrong because we are alienated. And evil is measured by how a deed stands towards God, so even our righteous deeds can be like a polluted garment (Isaiah 64:6): not because kindness is worthless to a neighbour, but because it is offered by a heart still turned away.

The Son who was shut out for us. What we were, Christ took in our place. The Son who had lived in the Father’s love from eternity was numbered with the transgressors, and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). He bore the estrangement our hostility had earned, so that those who were far off might be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). That is why this dark verse is not a portrait of despair. It is the measure of what he carried.

But I was never a bad person. Paul is not saying the kind neighbour and the cruel criminal are equally wicked; many outside Christ are better company on a Monday than many a churchgoer. Think of the most decent man you knew growing up: paid every bill, lent out his ladder, not religious, he would say, he just did no harm. Not raging against heaven, simply running his own little kingdom, his Maker nowhere in his thoughts. Paul measures people not against each other but against God. The respectable man and the criminal are not equally far down the road, but they are on the same side of the one line that finally matters.

Why does Paul make me remember all this? Not to shame you, but to make you grateful: he paints the old life dark so that the grace of the next line blazes brighter (Ephesians 2:12–13; Titus 3:3–5). A believer who forgets what he was soon forgets what grace cost, and grows proud, cold or harsh toward those still outside. Remembering keeps you humble and gentle, because you were once exactly where they are, and only grace moved you.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has now made peace with them through Christ’s real bodily death, so that on the last day he may present them holy, without blemish and beyond accusation.

He has now reconciled. The subject is God, in Christ: the offended party makes the peace, and we brought nothing to the table but the hostility that needed reconciling. Not God meeting us halfway, but God crossing the whole distance to fetch his enemies home. And it is a completed act, peace accomplished at the cross (John 19:30), not a probation you must keep passing. You do not wake each morning to re-earn God’s welcome; you live the day from a settled peace, not toward one you are still trying to win.

In his body of flesh by his death. The false teachers prized mystical experience and may have despised the body; Paul nails reconciliation to flesh and blood. The One in whom all the fullness dwells became flesh to die for flesh. Our peace did not cost God a word; it cost him a body (Hebrews 10:10).

Holy and blameless and above reproach before him. The goal is the last day. Present is the language of a bride led to her husband, an offering set before God. Holy: belonging wholly to God. Blameless: without blemish, the word for a sacrificial lamb without defect. Above reproach: a courtroom word, a person against whom no charge can stick. All of it before him, through Christ’s work, not their own (Ephesians 5:27). Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, heard the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy, and cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:1–5). That this God should look at sinners and find nothing to charge them with is grace beyond telling, and it is true only because of the death Paul has just named.

But I never feel holy or blameless. How can this be me? Two truths set you free. First, this is your standing, not your feeling: not a description of how holy you have become but a verdict about how God sees you in Christ, whose flawless record was credited to your account while your sin was counted his and paid for (2 Corinthians 5:21). Above reproach is the literal truth of your case in heaven’s court right now: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33–34). Second, what God now counts you to be, you will one day be in full. A day is coming when Christ will set his people blameless before the throne with great joy (Jude 24; Ephesians 5:27), the feeling at last catching up with the fact.

The gap and who closes it. Your sense of falling short is the gap between your standing, perfect in Christ, and your experience, still being made holy. Its closing rests not on your grip on God but on his grip on you, for he does not begin a work he fails to finish (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This hope belongs to those who keep holding firmly to the gospel they first heard, the one gospel proclaimed throughout the world.

If indeed you continue in the faith. That little if can land on a tender conscience like a cold draught, but the condition is real. The faith means both their believing and the gospel believed, and those who will be presented holy are those who keep believing to the end.

Stable and steadfast, not shifting. Building words: founded, firmly seated, not budged. The false teachers were moving them off the simple gospel onto a deeper teaching dressed as progress. Stay put. The deepest thing in the universe is not beyond the gospel; it is the gospel.

Proclaimed in all creation, of which I, Paul, became a minister. Not that every person had heard, but a public announcement open to the whole world. Why trade a place in a worldwide, God-driven gospel for a little local secret society? And Paul is its servant, not its master or a self-styled expert: he did not invent the gospel; he serves it.

Kept by the prayers of Christ. On the night before Peter’s denial, Jesus told him, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), and Peter, though he fell, did not fall away. The same Lord always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The deepest reason true believers continue lies in their Saviour: the if of this verse is answered by the prayers of the One who died for them.

The climber and the rope. The continuing is not a weight laid on your own grip for fifty years but God’s gift: the saints persevere because God preserves them. A climber roped to a guide must keep climbing, but when his boot slips, the rope holds. So the if is not meant to torment you. It is a summons to keep going, and, for the one who keeps clinging to Christ through all his stumbles, the very proof that God is holding him.

How do I know my faith is the kind that continues? Not by looking for a feeling of certainty about the future, but by looking at Christ now. Are you still trusting him, however weakly, coming back to him when you fail, wanting to be his? Those are the marks of a faith God is keeping. Then use the means he uses to keep you: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. A believer who cuts himself off from these is not proving his security but endangering his steadiness.

What about someone I know who seemed to be a believer and has walked away? Do not pronounce the final verdict; that belongs to God, and the story is not over. Some who wander are true believers in serious backsliding, and God brings them back, as he brought back Peter. Others, if they never return, show that their faith was not the living kind (1 John 2:19). You cannot always tell which, and need not. Pray for them persistently, keep the door open, love them honestly, and tell them the truth about Christ when you can. The God who keeps his own is also the God who seeks the lost.

Where Christians differ: does this condition mean believers can lose salvation? Some read “if indeed you continue” as showing that true believers may fall away and be lost, and many earnest Christians hold this out of a proper respect for the warnings. This commentary’s view: Perseverance is the evidence of genuine faith, and the warning is one of God’s means of producing it. Those who are truly reconciled will continue, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). Those who finally abandon the faith show they never truly had it (1 John 2:19). The condition is real and must be heard; it is how God keeps his people steadfast (the Westminster Confession, chapter 17; the 1689 London Baptist Confession, chapter 17).

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is glad to suffer for the church, because his sufferings are his share of the afflictions Christ’s people must still bear as the gospel spreads, never an addition to the cross.

I rejoice in my sufferings. Paul writes in chains (4:18), after floggings, stonings and shipwreck (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), the cost of carrying the gospel to the Gentiles. He does not enjoy pain for its own sake, but he has three reasons for joy: it is for people he loves; it draws him into fellowship with Christ (Philippians 3:10; Acts 5:41); and it bears fruit, for through a prisoner’s chains the gospel runs free and a church is built.

What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions. Not a deficit in the cross, which the letter has just declared sufficient (1:20, 22).
