There is Christ’s atoning suffering, the once-for-all work of the cross, which we receive but never share. And there are his ongoing afflictions in his suffering people as the gospel advances in a hostile world. Christ is so joined to his church that to strike the church is to strike him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). There is an appointed measure of such affliction still to be borne before the end, and Paul takes up his share, not adding to the atonement but taking his portion of the cost of spreading it. Not one tear shed for Christ’s name is lost, and not one blow borne for his church is wasted.

For the sake of his body. His suffering builds up the church, and that is what turns hardship into joy. The place where Paul sat in chains was not a dead end; it was a pulpit (Philippians 1:12–14).

Does this apply to my sufferings, or only to Paul’s? In its measure, to yours. Loss or scorn borne for Christ’s sake is not meaningless misfortune but a share in his afflictions, counted into his great work and borne for the good of his people. Being passed over at work for refusing to lie, losing a friend because you follow Christ, the long labour of caring for a believer in need: none of it is wasted. Even illness or grief, borne trusting God, can serve the church, because others are strengthened by watching you. But do not go looking for suffering, and do not call the results of your own folly persecution (1 Peter 4:15–16).

Where Christians differ: the merits of the saints. Roman Catholic teaching has used this verse to support a treasury of merit: the sufferings of saints added to Christ’s, applied to others through indulgences. This commentary’s view: Christ’s atoning work was complete and finished (John 19:30; Hebrews 10:14). Nothing can be added to it. Paul’s sufferings did not atone for anyone; they were the cost of bringing the gospel to them. There is no treasury of merit and no need for indulgences.

Uncertain wording. “Filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions” is one of the hardest phrases Paul wrote. The word for afflictions (thlipseis) is never used in the New Testament of Christ’s atoning death, but exactly what idea stands behind it cannot be settled. Some think Paul draws on the Jewish expectation of an appointed measure of suffering for God’s people before the end; others stress Christ’s union with his people, so that their sufferings are his (Acts 9:4); others take him to mean that his sufferings complete in him the pattern of Christ’s. These overlap, and the likely meaning combines the first two, as explained above.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he shares in the afflictions that Christ’s people must still endure.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made Paul a steward of his word, to proclaim it in full: the secret God kept hidden for ages and has now opened to all his people.

The stewardship from God. A steward was the servant entrusted with the keys to give out the master’s provisions: he does not own what he handles, did not appoint himself, and must give account (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). The gospel, the mystery, the revealing and the stewardship are God’s, and even the strength to carry it out is his energy working in Paul (v. 29). From first to last everything descends from heaven; not one thread ascends from earth. The same grace that made a persecutor into a steward reached down for you (Ephesians 3:7–8).

To make the word of God fully known. The word of God here is the gospel (v. 5), and fully known has a double force: Paul preaches it completely, nothing edited out to please his hearers (Acts 20:27), and carries it to its full reach, out to the Gentiles. The false teachers wanted to add to the gospel as though it were lacking; Paul says it is already full, and his task is not to supplement it but to declare the whole of it.

The mystery. In the Bible a mystery is not a baffling puzzle but something once hidden in the mind of God and now revealed by him, a truth no one could have worked out (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26); its content comes in v. 27. The pagan mystery religions (cults with secret rites for members only), and very likely the false teachers too, traded in secret knowledge for an inner ring. Paul takes their favourite word and turns it inside out.

Hidden for ages and generations. Yet there in the Old Testament, veiled: the offspring who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15), the promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), the Servant given as a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6). Like a sealed letter lying on the table for generations, it waited to be opened, and Christ opened it (Luke 24:27).

Now revealed to his saints. Not unearthed by philosophers but unveiled from above, to all believers, not a spiritual elite (1 Corinthians 2:14). God drew back the curtain in his Son and put the secret of the universe into the hands of tradesmen, slaves and housewives in a small town.

In everyday life. You hold, in an ordinary Bible on an ordinary shelf, the secret that kings and prophets longed to see (Luke 10:24). Open it today as if that were true, because it is.

Are there still hidden truths God reveals today to special people? Not new truths of the gospel. The mystery has been revealed and written down by the apostles, the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God still opens eyes to see what is in his word (Ephesians 1:17–18), so that a passage read a hundred times suddenly shines; but that is illumination of what is written, not new revelation beside it. Christians who believe God still speaks through prophecy today generally agree that nothing said that way can add to Scripture or stand above it. Anyone who claims a secret truth that the ordinary believer with an open Bible cannot reach is offering exactly what Paul refused.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secret God chose to make known is astonishing in its reach and in its content: Christ himself living among and within Gentile believers, the guarantee of the glory to come.

God chose to make known. God owed the unveiling to no one, and could have kept his secret for ever. That he chose to tell it to outsiders and rebels is a wonder before it is a doctrine (Matthew 11:26).

Among the Gentiles. To a Jewish mind the Gentiles were outsiders, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). That God’s richest glory would be displayed among them was the part no one saw coming (Ephesians 3:6), and Paul piles up words to say it: the riches of the glory of this mystery. The Colossians are those Gentiles, and there is no room left for spiritual snobbery.

Christ in you. The greatest treasure God ever kept hidden turns out to be a Person (Galatians 2:20): not Christ far above you, reached through angels and rituals, as the false teachers sold him, but the living Lord himself, at home in the humblest believer. “In you” is plural: among you, and in each of you.

The hope of glory. Christ in you now guarantees glory to come: glorification, God’s final work of making his people perfectly holy and raising them in bodies like Christ’s own (Philippians 3:21). “When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (3:4; Romans 8:17–18). The present indwelling is the pledge and down payment of the coming splendour.

The King in the cottage. Imagine the King leaving his palace to live in a labourer’s cottage. Christ in you is the King in the cottage; the hope of glory is the palace that must follow. He did not move in to leave you there for ever: he means to take you home. Glory is not a maybe for those he indwells. It is as certain as he is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become divine. It means Christ dwells in them by the Spirit, uniting them to himself.

How can Christ be in me if he is in heaven at the Father’s right hand? Both are true, and the link is the Holy Spirit. In his human body Christ is in heaven, from where he will return (3:1; Acts 1:11); by his Spirit he dwells in every believer: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him, and if Christ is in you, your spirit is alive (Romans 8:9–10). This is not a feeling you must produce. It is a fact about every believer, whether you feel it or not, and it is why you are never alone, never beyond his help, and never without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s whole ministry is to proclaim Christ, warning and teaching every believer, so that each may stand mature in Christ on the last day.

Him we proclaim. The first word is emphatic: not a system or a ladder of disciplines, but a Person, to be known, trusted and loved. You do not get Christ by keeping the rules; you begin to keep his commands by having Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Warning everyone. True ministry warns as well as comforts, counselling people out of harm’s way, as Paul did at Ephesus night and day with tears (Acts 20:31); here chiefly away from anything that lures them from the all-sufficient Christ. To warn is love: a father shouts at the child wandering into the road precisely because he loves him.

Teaching everyone with all wisdom. Teaching builds up in the truth, with the wisdom found in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3), and the skill to fit it to each real life so that it takes root. And mark the drumbeat: everyone, three times. No elite here.

Present everyone mature in Christ. “Present” is the word of v. 22, with the great Day in view. “Mature” means full-grown, a word some mystery cults used for their initiates. But maturity is not head knowledge or a higher tier for an elite, the very thing the false teachers dangled. It is growing up into Christ: rooted, steady, discerning, Christlike in character, no longer blown about by every new teaching, able to stand and feed yourself from God’s word (Ephesians 4:13–15; Hebrews 5:13–14). A sapling and an oak share the same life: maturity is the new convert’s Christ-life grown up.

Is warning only the pastor’s job? No. Paul uses the same word when he tells the whole church to teach and admonish one another in all wisdom (3:16). But how you do it matters. Warn someone you actually love, in private first (Matthew 18:15), humbly, aware of your own weakness (Galatians 6:1), with the aim of their good and not your relief. Begin with Christ, not with a list of their faults. And be willing to be warned yourself. A church where no one ever lovingly says, I am worried about this, is not gentle; it is neglectful.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul labours to exhaustion for this goal, yet the power at work in his labour is Christ’s own.

I toil, struggling. The shift to “I” shows what the goal costs Paul. “Toil” means to labour to the point of exhaustion, the bone-weariness of a field hand at harvest; “struggling” is the word for the athlete straining every sinew in the games, from which we get agony.

With all his energy. Yet the power he strains with is not his own. “Energy” and “works” share a root, doubled for emphasis: Christ’s power energising him from inside, by the Spirit who dwells in every believer (Romans 8:11). Here is the balance the whole Bible keeps: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). Maximum effort and total dependence held together in one breath: not fifty-fifty, but fully Paul’s striving and fully God’s working (1 Corinthians 15:10).

His own power moving through weak hands. The risen Christ does not stand at a distance watching his servants strain; he works in them, powerfully. Every sermon faithfully preached, every prayer that struggles for a church, every tired act of love for his people is his own power moving through weak hands. The labour is ours; the might, and the glory, are his.

Neither passive nor self-driven. Two ditches. One is “let go and let God”, as if effort were unspiritual; but Paul toiled to the point of agony, and this ditch breeds a stalled faith that blames God for its barrenness. The other is “it is all up to me”: white-knuckled willpower that breeds pride when it works and burnout when it does not.

Set the sails. Work hard, and lean hard. A crew hoists and trims the sails, but it is the wind that drives the boat home. So set the sails: pray, fight sin, feed on the word, serve the church, keep going. And let the wind of God’s own power carry you on.

I am exhausted. Does this verse mean I should work even harder? Not necessarily. Paul’s toil was aimed at one thing, Christ’s people growing mature, and powered by Christ’s strength, not by guilt or the fear of letting people down. If you are worn out, ask whether you are carrying things God never gave you, or the right things in your own strength. The Lord who works powerfully in his servants also gave the Sabbath and told his tired disciples to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31). Rest is not a failure of devotion; sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is sleep, and trust him to hold what you put down. And be honest about what drives you: weariness sometimes comes not from Christ’s call but from a hunger to be needed, praised or in control, a master never satisfied. Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30); a burden that never lightens may not be his.

Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,<sup>6</sup>which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,<sup>7</sup>just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf<sup>8</sup>and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.<sup>9</sup>And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,<sup>10</sup>so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;<sup>11</sup>being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;<sup>12</sup>giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.<sup>13</sup>He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,<sup>14</sup>in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.<sup>15</sup>He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.<sup>16</sup>For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.<sup>17</sup>And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.<sup>18</sup>And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.<sup>19</sup>For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,<sup>20</sup>and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.<sup>21</sup>And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,<sup>22</sup>he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,<sup>23</sup>if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.<sup>24</sup>Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,<sup>25</sup>of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known,<sup>26</sup>the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.<sup>27</sup>To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.<sup>28</sup>Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.<sup>29</sup>For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.

keyVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
keyVerse.note: Here the two halves of the great passage on Christ meet, and its last clause states God’s purpose in creation and redemption alike: that his Son should have first place in everything. Every part of the chapter serves it, from Paul’s prayer to his labour, and it answers the Colossian error, which kept Christ high but not highest.

1.reflection:
Paul thanks God that the gospel is bearing fruit among the Colossians and across the world (vv. 3–8). What evidence of the gospel’s work can you thank God for in your own church, including in people you find difficult?

Paul says the Father has already qualified believers, rescued them and forgiven them (vv. 12–14). Where are you tempted to live as though you still had to earn your place with God, and how does this passage answer it?

Verses 15–20 say that all things were created by Christ and for Christ, and that in him all things hold together. How would it change an ordinary week to believe that you, your work and your worries were made for him and are held by him?

The false teachers offered something more than Christ. What forms does Christ plus take today, in the church or in your own heart, and why does Christ in you, the hope of glory (v. 27), leave nothing to add?

2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 showed the Colossians the Christ they already have; chapter 2 names the danger that threatens them and answers it with that same Christ, closing the teaching half of the letter before the turn to Christian living in 3:1.

The message. Christ is enough, and you already have him. All that God is lives in Christ, bodily, and you have been filled in him: your old self cut away, your debt cancelled at the cross, the powers you feared disarmed. So let no one talk you into adding to him, or rule you out for lacking their extras. Keep walking in Christ the way you began.

Why it was said. Teachers were offering a “philosophy” that sounded deeper than the gospel the Colossians had first received: food laws and holy days, harsh self-denial, devotion to angels and visions (see the introduction). They asked the believers not to give up Christ but to add to him, and looked down on those who would not, leaving plain believers to wonder whether faith in Christ alone was second-class.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul labours in prayer that they may be fully sure of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, and gives the command on which the chapter turns, “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (vv. 1–7). Then he warns against any philosophy “not according to Christ”, because God’s fullness dwells in Christ, believers are filled in him, and in him God has already given new birth, forgiveness and victory over the powers (vv. 8–15). So no one may judge or disqualify them (vv. 16–23): food laws and holy days were shadows of Christ, the false teachers’ severity and visions are pride that has let go of the Head, and man-made rules have no power against sin.

Where it leads. At the centre stands the cross, seen from two sides. Towards God, the record of our debt was nailed there and wiped out (v. 14). Towards the powers, it was a Roman triumph, with the rulers of darkness led in chains behind the conqueror (v. 15): what looked like his defeat stripped every accuser of its weapon. And the one who did it is no lesser mediator but God himself, dwelling bodily in a man (v. 9), the substance every shadow outlined (v. 17) and the Head from whom the whole church draws its life (v. 19).

For us. Christ plus is always on offer: plus a rule, a diet, a calendar, an experience, an elite to tell you whether you measure up. This chapter answers every version: you are complete in him. Go deeper into Christ, never beyond him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep going with Christ the way you began, because all of God’s wisdom is in him. Paul labours in prayer for churches he has never seen, that their hearts may be strengthened, knit together in love and brought to full assurance of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (vv. 1–3). He says this to guard them from persuasive talk, and he rejoices that their faith is holding firm (vv. 4–5). Then he gives the command on which the whole chapter turns: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted, built up and thankful (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 has shaped how Reformed Christians think about learning. Writers such as Abraham Kuyper drew on the conviction that all true wisdom and knowledge come from Christ and hold together in him. This does not mean that only Christians can know things. It means that whatever is truly known is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” knowingly or not, in a world that Christ made and holds together. So the Christian can study anything without fear, knowing that every true path leads back to the One in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered a secret wisdom that seemed to go beyond the gospel (on Paul’s answer, see the note on v. 3). Now: A believer who turns to a therapy, a spirituality or a philosophy for what Christ supposedly cannot give has accepted the false teachers’ premise. He may learn from every honest source, while treating Christ as the source and the test of all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul labours hard in prayer for believers he has never met, simply because they belong to Christ. His struggle has a goal, which the next verse names.

How great a struggle. “Struggle” (agōn) gives us our word agony: the all-out exertion of the wrestler, the word Paul used of his ministry in 1:29. He writes in chains (4:18), so how does he struggle for a church he cannot reach? Chiefly on his knees, as Epaphras was always struggling on their behalf in his prayers (4:12). Pastoral love is hard, hidden work.

And for those at Laodicea. Laodicea lay about ten miles away, a wealthy banking and textile city whose church was later rebuked as lukewarm (Revelation 3:14–22). Paul wrote to them too, and wanted the two churches to exchange letters (4:16). The same danger threatened the whole valley.

All who have not seen me face to face. These would include Hierapolis (4:13). Paul would not have known these people in the street, yet he agonises for them because they belong to Christ. A hired hand cares only for what the flock does for him; the true shepherd cares for the flock itself (John 10:12–13).

Hidden hands and pierced hands. The church is held up by hidden hands folded in prayer, and above them all by the pierced hands of the great Shepherd, who knows his sheep by name in every valley of the earth, and who prayed for us before we were born (John 17:20).

In everyday life. Choose a church you have never visited, a persecuted church, a struggling plant, a missionary’s congregation, and keep praying for it. Learn one name from it and pray for that person by name.

How do I struggle in prayer for someone? Not by straining to feel intense or praying for hours, but by praying with persistence and purpose: coming back to the same people again and again, asking for what matters most (as Paul does in v. 2 and 1:9–12), and not giving up when nothing seems to change, even when you are tired. Struggling prayer is ordinary prayer that keeps going, because you care what happens to that person’s soul.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that their hearts will be strengthened and knit together in love, and that they will grow rich in a sure grasp of Christ, who is God’s mystery. He does not ask for wealth, comfort or success, nor even larger numbers.

Encouraged. “Encouraged” (parakaleō) means braced, given courage to stand, because the false teachers press in with plausible arguments (v. 4). It is the strengthening the Spirit gives, the Helper Jesus sent (John 14:16), whose name comes from the same root.

Knit together in love. “Knit together” (symbibazō) is used of the joints of a body (v. 19), and what binds them is love (Romans 5:5). The lone sheep is picked off; the flock knit together stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body into one, and is the soil in which true understanding grows.

Full assurance of understanding. “Full assurance” (plērophoria) is faith brought all the way to certainty, resting not on a leap in the dark but on actually grasping the truth. God’s desire for you is not that you be clever or initiated but that you be sure: rich in the settled, glad certainty of knowing the Lord Jesus (2 Timothy 1:12).

God’s mystery, which is Christ. The mystery is not a secret doctrine for initiates but a person (1:26–27). The false teachers dangled mystery as a prize beyond Christ; Paul says the mystery is Christ, and to know him is to know it.

Is it proud to be sure I am saved? Not if your assurance rests on Christ rather than your own goodness. John wrote so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13), and Paul prays here for the riches of full assurance. Doubts come to many believers and do not prove you are not his. The remedy is to know Christ better, his promises, his finished work, his faithfulness: the more clearly you see him, the surer you will be.

Textual note. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has a longer reading at the end of this verse; on either reading the mystery is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything worth knowing about God and about life is stored up in Christ, so there is no true wisdom to be found beyond him.

All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Knowledge is the understanding of God and reality; wisdom, the skill of living rightly in its light. “Hidden” (apokryphos) means not out of reach but treasured up, as gold is kept in a vault, ready to be found by those who seek him.

The sharp edge. The false teachers peddled hidden wisdom for the initiated few. Paul turns their prized word back on them: all the hidden treasures are in Christ. There is no wisdom worth having outside him, and no lack of it inside him. The Christian does not graduate from Christ to something higher; he goes ever deeper into Christ, who is himself the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). God did not scatter his wisdom across the universe in fragments for the clever to collect. He stored it all in his Son, and gave his Son to us.

Two freeing things. You need not look anywhere else: the real riches do not belong to scholars and mystics, and you have Christ. And the treasure has no bottom. Imagine a man chasing one get-rich scheme after another, who is told that the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago, and the mine runs so deep a thousand lifetimes could never empty it. That is you and Christ (Matthew 13:44).

Does this mean non-Christians can know nothing true? No. By God’s common grace unbelievers discover much that is true, and Christians may learn from them. The doctor who sets your broken arm may not believe, and his skill is still a gift of God. But only in Christ do you learn who made the arm, why you are here, and how a sinner can stand before God.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has pressed Christ’s sufficiency so hard to guard them against persuasive talk that would lead them away from him.

That no one may delude you. “Delude” (paralogizomai) means to deceive by false reasoning, the way a swindler reasons a man out of his money. The teaching at Colossae (see the introduction) did not deny Christ outright; it added to him: Christ plus these rules, these mediators, this deeper experience.

With plausible arguments. “Plausible arguments” (pithanologia) are fine-sounding words. Error does not arrive looking false; it comes dressed as wisdom (v. 23): “Faith in Christ is a fine beginning, but for real fullness you must also keep these days and honour these powers.” The packaging changes; the giveaway is always the little word “plus”. Know Christ fully, and you will not be talked out of him (2 Corinthians 11:3).

What it does not mean. Argument is not wrong; Paul himself reasoned and persuaded (Acts 17:2–4; 18:4). The question is whether an argument leads to Christ or away from him.

What if I cannot answer an argument against my faith? You do not have to win every debate to be right; many false teachings sound convincing because their teachers are skilled speakers. Do not panic and do not pretend. Say honestly that you will think about it, then take it to Scripture and to a wise believer or a good book; Christians have faced most arguments before. Meanwhile hold on to what you know: Christ died, Christ rose, and his word has not failed you. A question you cannot yet answer is no reason to let go of him.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though Paul is far away, his heart is with them, and he rejoices that their faith in Christ is holding firm. Before he warns them, he names the good he sees.

With you in spirit. Present in thought, prayer and care (1 Corinthians 5:3), for believers are bound together in Christ by one Spirit, and miles cannot sever that bond. A man in chains rejoices, not over his release but over the health of a congregation he has never seen (3 John 4).

Your good order and the firmness of your faith. “Good order” (taxis) was often used of soldiers drawn up in ranks, and “firmness” (stereōma) is solidity; many hear in them a battle line that does not give way. Under the plausible arguments of v. 4, the church is still holding the line. And its firmness is not self-made grit but rests on its object, faith in Christ: a line that holds because the One it leans on cannot be moved (1 Corinthians 15:58; 16:13).

Why does Paul praise them before warning them? Because that is how love corrects. He is not flattering them but telling the truth about what God has done in them. A church that hears only warnings grows discouraged; one that hears only praise grows careless. Paul gives both, in that order, so that they hear the warning from a friend on their side. When you must correct a fellow believer, a child or a colleague, begin by honestly naming the good you see.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go on with Christ the way you began: receiving him as Lord, resting on him alone, and growing in him with a thankful heart. This is the command on which the whole chapter turns.

Therefore. The hinge of the letter: because Christ is supreme and all-sufficient, here is what to do.

As you received Christ Jesus the Lord. “Received” (paralambanō) is the word for receiving a tradition handed down. But what they received was not only teaching about Christ but Christ himself, as Lord: Master, not an optional extra bolted onto the old life.

So walk in him. Walk is the whole daily conduct of life, and the way you began is the way you go on. You came to Christ with empty hands, resting on him alone; keep walking the same way. That cuts the heresy at the root: you do not move on from Christ to higher teachings; you go on in him. “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

Rooted and built up in him. Two pictures, cheerfully mixed (Ephesians 3:17): a tree sunk deep into the soil, a house rising on its foundation. Even the tenses differ. Rooted (errizōmenoi) is done once with lasting effect; built up (epoikodomoumenoi) goes on day by day. Anchored and rising. “In him” means joined to Christ by faith, so that his life flows into yours as sap flows from the vine into the branch (John 15:4–5).

Established in the faith, just as you were taught. “Established” (bebaioumenoi) means made firm, in the faith as Epaphras taught it (1:7). The mark of truth is not novelty but faithfulness to what the apostles handed down. When a teaching promises more than the plain gospel you were first taught, that is the moment to be on guard (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 1:13–14).

Abounding in thanksgiving. A heart overflowing with thanks for all it already has in Christ has no appetite for the false teacher’s offer of something more. Ingratitude is the crack through which discontent creeps in, and discontent is the foothold the heretic needs; gratitude bolts the door. But thanks does not come naturally: Israel was fed with bread from heaven every morning and spent the journey murmuring, and we do the same.

The same Christ to the end. The Christ we received with empty hands at the beginning is the Christ who carries us to the end: the soil we are rooted in and the bedrock we are built on, who never runs dry and never gives way.

In everyday life. Cultivate thanks deliberately, against the grain of a forgetful heart. Stop and name the mercies, a Saviour, sins forgiven, Christ living within you, the sure hope of glory, until the grumble shrinks. It is nearly impossible to grumble and give thanks in the same breath (1 Thessalonians 5:18; Colossians 3:15–17).

How do I go deeper without going beyond Christ? By going further into the same things, not into new things. Read the Gospels again and again and get to know him. Learn what his death and resurrection accomplished, and what union with him means. Keep the means of grace he has given: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of his people. Obey him in the next thing he asks, because obedience opens understanding. Deep Christians are not people who found a secret; they are people who kept looking at Christ for a long time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be carried off by a philosophy that adds to Christ, because in Christ you already have everything. Paul names the danger: teaching rooted in human tradition and the elemental spirits, not in Christ (v. 8). The reason it is empty is that the whole fullness of God dwells bodily in Christ, and believers are filled in him (vv. 9–10). Then he lists what God has done for them in Christ: the old self cut away, buried and raised (vv. 11–12), dead sinners made alive and every debt cancelled at the cross (vv. 13–14), and the evil powers disarmed and led in triumph (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Verses 13–15 give two vivid pictures of what the cross achieved: one from the law court, the record of debt cancelled and nailed to the cross (see the note on vv. 13–14), and one from the battlefield, the powers disarmed and led in triumph (see the note on v. 15). Together: freedom from guilt and from spiritual bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers treated the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as threats to be kept happy by ritual. Paul says those powers are disarmed and paraded in defeat (see the note on v. 15). Now: A Christian who lives in dread of spiritual attack or dark forces needs to hear the same thing (on why a beaten devil is still active, see v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let any teaching carry you off whose source is human ideas and spiritual powers rather than Christ. Christ himself is the test of every system.

Takes you captive. “Takes captive” (sylagōgeō) means to carry off as booty, to kidnap. When a teaching carries off a mind, almost no one notices, least of all the captive, who feels enlightened. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress, which is why Paul shouts rather than whispers.

By philosophy and empty deceit. “Philosophy” means love of wisdom. Paul does not condemn careful thinking (he reasoned with the philosophers at Athens) but this particular philosophy, and in the Greek the words form one phrase: a philosophy that is empty deceit. It promises fullness and delivers a void, while in Christ you have been filled (v. 10).

According to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world. Its source is human, the charge Jesus brought against the Pharisees: leaving the commandment of God to hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8). And behind it lie the elemental spirits, the basic principles of religion or the powers people believed ruled the world (see the box below). To crawl back under them is to return to the slavery Christ broke (Galatians 4:3, 9).

Not according to Christ. The decisive test, and a freeing one: you need not master every false system, only know Christ surpassingly well. A bank teller spots forged notes not by memorising every counterfeit but by handling the genuine so constantly that anything false feels wrong at once. Know Christ deeply, and a teaching that diminishes him or adds to him will feel wrong, however clever it sounds (1 John 4:1).

What does captivity to human philosophy look like today? Rarely a robed philosopher; more often the quiet assumptions of the age, absorbed without noticing: that you are what you feel, that truth is whatever works for you, that the physical world is all there is, that God exists to make you happy, that freedom means having no master. Some come dressed in Christian words. Ask of each idea: what does this say about Christ, about sin, about how a person is made right with God? If it pushes Christ to the edge, it is not according to Christ.

Where Christians differ: should Christians study philosophy? Some take this verse to forbid all philosophy. This commentary’s view: Paul condemns philosophy that is empty deceit, rooted in human tradition and not according to Christ. Christians may study philosophy, as many great Christian thinkers have, but must take every thought captive to obey Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5) and judge all systems by Scripture. Philosophy is a good servant and a bad master.

Uncertain wording. “Elemental spirits” translates stoicheia, literally things set in a row: letters of the alphabet, the physical elements, first principles. Whether Paul means the ABCs of religion, the rules of the old order, or the spirit powers thought to rule the world, perhaps through the stars and the calendar, is uncertain, as in Galatians 4:3, 9. The ESV’s choice fits the letter’s concern with powers (v. 15) and calendars (v. 16), and the two ideas may have run together: rules and the powers behind them.
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that God is lives in Christ, and lives in him in a human body, so there is nothing of God to look for anywhere else.

The whole fullness of deity. “For” gives the reason for the warning of v. 8. The whole fullness (pan to plērōma) leaves nothing over. “Deity” (theotēs) is the strongest word available: the divine nature itself, not just divine qualities. Christ is not a creature filled with divine attributes but the One in whom the complete divine nature resides.

Dwells bodily. “Dwells” (katoikeō) means to take up residence, and it is present tense: God is at home in Christ still, risen and reigning. And “bodily”: all of God, in a body you could have stood beside. Few verses state the full deity of the incarnate Christ more plainly.

Three blows against the error. If all the fullness of deity is in Christ, angels and elemental spirits have no fullness to offer, so why seek lesser mediators? The fullness is not spread thin across a chain of powers but concentrated, entire and undivided, in Christ alone. And the one word bodily rebukes every teaching that seeks God by escaping the physical, for God himself dwells bodily in Christ.

Is Jesus still a man now, in heaven? Yes. He rose bodily, ascended bodily and dwells bodily, and he will return in the same way he went (Acts 1:11). So there is a human being at the Father’s right hand who knows what it is to be tired, tempted, grieved and in pain (Hebrews 4:15). The God you pray to has a human face and human scars, and he wears your nature still.

How can the infinite God live in a human body? Not by being squeezed into it. The Son did not stop upholding the universe when he lay in the manger (1:17; Hebrews 1:3); he added a human nature to the divine nature he always had, without either being changed into the other. We cannot picture how: a God we could fully explain would not be God. Scripture gives us not a puzzle to solve but a Person to bow before: the infinite God has come near enough to be touched (1 John 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ, you share his fullness: you already have everything you need to know God and be right with him, under the Lord of every power.

You have been filled in him. The fullness (plērōma) dwells in Christ, and you have been filled (peplērōmenoi) in him: the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members. The tense describes a finished act with lasting results; the verb is passive, for God filled you; and it is in him, yours by union with Christ, not by attainment. The heresy said they were lacking; Paul says they are complete. Christ’s righteousness counts as yours (2 Corinthians 5:21), his Spirit lives in you (Romans 8:9), and his Father is your Father (Galatians 4:6).

Who is the head of all rule and authority. Christ rules the very powers the false teachers urged the church to revere. He created them (1:16), he disarmed them at the cross (2:15), and he is their head. Why seek help from angels or spirits, when you are joined to their Lord?

In everyday life. If you carry a vague dread of fate, of dark forces, of whatever pulls the strings behind life, say it plainly: the One I belong to is the head over every power that exists.

What it does not mean. Not that believers have nothing more to grow into: they grow in experiencing what they already have. Nor that you are sinlessly perfect or divine. You lack nothing for salvation or access to God.

If I am complete, why do I feel so incomplete? Because there is a difference between what you have and what you have yet to enjoy. A man with a fortune in his account who frets that he is poor does not need to earn more; he needs to wake up to what is his. Some of your sense of lack is the right longing for the glory still to come (Romans 8:23). But much of the heart’s restless hunger, for more approval, more success, more spiritual experience, is a search for a fullness you already have in Christ. The answer is not a new technique but a deeper grasp of what is yours in him, and patient trust that he will finish what he started.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ God has already done what the false teachers’ rites promised and could not do: cut away the old self, buried it with Christ, and raised believers to new life through faith. You cannot improve on death and resurrection.

A circumcision made without hands. The false teachers were pressing physical circumcision. In Christ you have already received the circumcision of the heart the Old Testament promised (Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:28–29), done not by a knife but by God: the new birth, God giving a dead heart new life and new desires (Ezekiel 36:26; John 3:3–8).

By putting off the body of the flesh. What is cut away is not a scrap of flesh but the whole old sinful self, stripped off like a garment (3:9). Not that a believer no longer feels sinful desires, but that the person you were in Adam, ruled by sin, died with Christ, so sin is no longer your master, even when it still tempts you (Romans 6:6–7).

By the circumcision of Christ. Union with Christ achieves what circumcision pointed to, and no human knife can add to it (on the two readings of the phrase, see the box below).

Buried with him in baptism. Paul sets baptism beside circumcision as a sign of the same reality: union with Christ in his death and burial (Romans 6:3–4). The old life is not improved but put in the grave alongside Christ’s buried body.

Raised with him through faith. Rising in baptism pictures resurrection with Christ, the fact on which 3:1 builds. And it happens through faith: not the water by itself, but God’s power laid hold of by faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives; God’s power actually raises.

The powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead. Paul says God raised Jesus; elsewhere the Spirit raised him (Romans 8:11), and the Son has authority to take up his life again (John 10:18). The resurrection is the one act of the triune God, and the greatest display of power in history is the power that raised you with him and is at work in you now (Ephesians 1:19–20).

Why all this, in the middle of a warning? The false teachers said: you need more; be circumcised, keep our rules, climb higher. Paul answers by showing what has already happened to you in Christ: the old self cut away by God, buried with Christ, raised by the power that raised Jesus. What could anyone add?

In everyday life. When an old sin pulls at you today, say: that person was buried with Christ. Then live as the raised person you already are (Romans 6:4–5).

I trust Christ but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s own command (Matthew 28:19), and in the New Testament those who believed were baptised, usually very soon (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; 16:33). It does not make you a Christian, but it is Christ’s way for you to confess publicly that you are joined to him in his death and resurrection. If you are unsure or afraid, talk to the pastor or elders of your church. And if you were baptised as an infant and now trust Christ, ask them to help you think it through from Scripture, with patience and charity toward the church that baptised you.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Paedobaptists (who baptise the infant children of believers) argue from this verse that baptism replaces circumcision and so belongs to infants. This commentary’s view: the circumcision Paul links with baptism is the heart’s, made without hands, and the raising happens “through faith,” so the sign belongs to believers, while we warmly respect brothers who read it differently.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Some churches hold that God gives new birth through baptism. This commentary’s view: Paul ties the raising to faith, not to the water; baptism is God’s appointed sign of union with Christ, not working apart from faith.

Uncertain wording. “The circumcision of Christ” can mean the circumcision Christ performs, cutting away the old self, or the circumcision Christ underwent, here his death, when his body was cut off, a death the believer shares. Both fit, and both end in the same place: what circumcision pointed to is done in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has raised dead sinners to life together with Christ and forgiven every one of their sins, by cancelling the debt they owed and nailing it to the cross.

Dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. Not sick or struggling, but dead: unable to respond to God or contribute one thing to our rescue (Ephesians 2:1, 5). And the Colossians were Gentiles, outside the covenant, the unrenewed heart shut out as strangers.

God made alive together with him. All one Greek word (synezōopoieō): God did for us what he did for Christ in the tomb. You do not improve a corpse, you raise it (Ephesians 2:5). Not God helping those who help themselves, but God giving life to those who had none.

Having forgiven us all our trespasses. “Forgiven” (charizomai) is built on the word for grace: forgiven freely. Paul shifts to us, including himself. Then the word to stop the heart: all. The sin that haunts you at three in the morning, the besetting sin you keep stumbling back into. God did not pardon most and keep a private reserve of charges. And it is no cheap amnesty; it is possible only because Christ bore every one of those sins himself (Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19).

The record of debt that stood against us. A handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor himself, an IOU (cheirographon): our guilt before God’s law, a debt beyond paying. The word for cancelling (exaleiphō) means to wipe out, as writing was washed off papyrus: not deferred or reduced but erased (Isaiah 43:25).

Nailing it to the cross. When the Romans crucified a man, they nailed his charge above his head; over Jesus it read, King of the Jews (John 19:19). But Paul says our certificate of debt was nailed up at Calvary. How? Because our debt was laid on him. This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty we deserved, in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13). The charge sheet with your name on it was fastened to the cross in the flesh of the Son of God and carried into the grave, and it never came back out. The empty tomb is the receipt stamped paid in full.

In everyday life. When guilt accuses you today, name the sin that haunts you most, and say over it: forgiven, all of it, nailed to the cross. Then go and forgive someone who owes you far less.

If all my sins are forgiven, why must I still confess them? Because forgiveness has two sides. As our Judge, God has forgiven us once for all; there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). As our Father, he still wants us to confess the sins that spoil our fellowship with him, and Jesus teaches us to pray daily, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12; 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children. A son who has broken his father’s window is not disowned, but he does not pretend nothing happened either.

Is it fair for an innocent person to pay someone else’s debt? It would be unjust to force a stranger to pay. But Christ came willingly (John 10:18), he is the Head who joins his people to himself, and he is God himself bearing the cost of God’s own pardon. A holy Judge cannot tear up a just account as if it did not matter (Exodus 34:7); that would make sin small. At the cross the debt was neither ignored nor dumped on an unwilling victim. It was paid in full by the One who loved us and gave himself for us (Galatians 2:20).

Uncertain wording. What the record of debt stands for is debated. Some take it as the law of Moses itself, which condemned. The more likely reading is our own signed guilt before God’s law, which Christ cancelled by paying it. Either way, the law can no longer condemn those in Christ. That does not abolish God’s moral will: the ceremonial law is fulfilled, but love still keeps the commandments (Romans 13:8–10).
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the cross Christ stripped the evil powers of their weapon and paraded them as his defeated captives, so his people need never fear them again.

The rulers and authorities. Not human kings but the spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), whom Christ created (1:16) and rules (2:10), and whom the false teachers urged the church to fear and appease. They are real, personal and malevolent, and they held humanity in a threefold grip: as the powers behind our sin, as accusers wielding the law’s condemnation (the record of debt of v. 14), and through the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

He disarmed. “Disarmed” (apekdyomai) means stripped, as defeated soldiers were stripped of their weapons. And the powers’ great weapon was not brute force but our sin and its just condemnation. The devil is the accuser of our brothers (Revelation 12:10), and his whole case rested on our unpaid debt. So v. 15 is welded to v. 14: once the record is wiped out, the accuser has nothing left to accuse with, the jailer has lost his keys, and death has lost its sting.

Put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him. At Calvary it looked as though darkness had won: the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), and it was the hour of the power of darkness (Luke 22:53). But in that very act they were undone, made a public spectacle before the unseen world, and through the church wider still (Ephesians 3:10). “Triumphing” (thriambeuō) is the word for a Roman triumph, when a general paraded through the city with conquered kings in chains behind his chariot. What looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumph, and the instrument of death became the chariot of victory.

The point for Colossae. The cross did not only forgive your sins (v. 14); it defeated the very powers the Colossians were told to appease. Why bow to, bargain with, or tremble before an enemy your Lord has already led in chains?

If Satan is defeated, why does he still seem so active? He is defeated but not yet removed, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and fights on in the hills. He still tempts, deceives and accuses, and believers must be watchful and resist him (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11). But he cannot condemn you, because your debt is paid; he cannot own you, because you belong to Christ; and he cannot win, because his end is fixed. A fierce guard dog on a short chain still barks and lunges, but it cannot drag down the one who belongs to its Master. Stand in Christ’s victory, and the devil will flee from you (James 4:7).

Uncertain wording. “In him” may also be translated “in it”, that is, in the cross; either way the victory was won by Christ on the cross. The verb rendered “disarmed” can also mean to strip off from oneself, and some since early times have pictured Christ throwing off the powers like a garment. Most modern translations take it as stripping the powers of their arms, which fits the triumph that follows.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Christ has done everything, no one may judge you or rule you out for lacking their extras. Food laws and holy days were shadows, and the substance is Christ (vv. 16–17). The severity, angel worship and visions of the false teachers are pride that has let go of the Head, from whom alone the church grows (vv. 18–19). Believers have died with Christ to that whole order of human rules, which look wise but have no power against the flesh (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance

Verse 17 gives a key for reading the Old Testament, and Reformed interpreters have leaned on it heavily: the ceremonial law was truly given by God, but it was a shadow, and the substance is Christ (this is treated fully in the note on v. 17).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers made Jewish days and food laws part of their system. Paul says these were shadows, and Christ has come. Now: The same answer meets any movement that makes Old Testament ceremonies the mark of true spirituality. What those ceremonies taught about holiness and love is fulfilled in Christ and worked out in us by the Spirit; the ceremonies themselves have reached their goal in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Christ has done everything, no one may judge you as a lesser Christian over food laws or holy days. Your standing is in Christ, not in menus and calendars.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you. “Therefore” draws the conclusion: filled in Christ (v. 10), forgiven at the cross (v. 14), with the powers disarmed (v. 15), believers are free. The false teachers were condemning the Colossians for not keeping their rules and making them feel second-class. Paul forbids it flatly.

In questions of food and drink. The food laws of Moses, and perhaps ascetic rules besides (v. 21). Why would Jewish rules press on a largely Gentile church? Phrygia had a sizeable Jewish population, descended in part from the two thousand Jewish families Antiochus III settled in Lydia and Phrygia around 200 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 12.147–153), and Cicero mentions Jewish temple-tax gold collected at Laodicea, ten miles away (Pro Flacco 28.68). Food laws and holy days were familiar and respected in the neighbourhood, and easy to present as the next step for serious believers.

A festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. Israel’s annual festivals, monthly new moons and weekly Sabbaths (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11). The next verse gives the reason they can no longer be made binding: they were shadows pointing to Christ. The rest the Sabbath pictured is found in him (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the feasts are fulfilled in his death, resurrection and gift of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 5:7; 15:20). To make them a condition of acceptance is to deny that Christ is enough.

Does this include the weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that Paul means only the ceremonial sabbaths of Israel’s festivals, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (a pattern God gave at creation for all people, Genesis 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day. But festival, new moon and Sabbath is the Old Testament’s standard way of naming the yearly, monthly and weekly holy days together (1 Chronicles 23:31), so the weekly Sabbath is more likely included (see the box at the end of this note).

The same error in modern clothes. It returns whenever a secondary or man-made practice is made the measure of true spirituality. “A real Christian would never touch a drink.” “You must follow this diet or this fast to be holy.” “You must keep, or must not keep, Christmas or Lent.” “You must use only this translation, sing only these songs, school your children in this one way.” Wherever someone turns a matter Christ has left free into a test of acceptance with God, and looks down on you for failing it, that is the Colossian error in a Sunday suit.

So may I judge a brother who keeps these things? No. The rebuke cuts both ways. Do not let anyone make you feel second-rate over such things, and do not sit in judgment on a brother who differs from you (Romans 14:1–4). The one who keeps Sunday strictly and the one who keeps it more freely, the one who abstains and the one who drinks with thanksgiving, are accepted by the same Christ. Nor is this licence to despise discipline; the gospel frees us from sin, never to it. It is liberty of conscience: Christ alone is the ground of our acceptance, and no one may add a rule to him (Galatians 5:1).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath. Some say Christians must keep the seventh-day Sabbath; others, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, that the fourth commandment carries over to the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath. This commentary’s view: Paul includes the Sabbath among the shadows fulfilled in Christ (v. 17). Christians are not bound by the Mosaic Sabbath law, and no one may judge them or bind their conscience over it (Romans 14:5). Christ is our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is the day the church gathers (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a binding law with rules about work. The Westminster and 1689 view (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8) is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Old Testament food laws and holy days were shadows thrown ahead by Christ; now that he has come, hold on to him, not to them.

A shadow of the things to come. A shadow (skia) has the shape of a thing but none of its substance; you cannot shake a shadow’s hand. The ceremonial law was a God-given shadow cast ahead of Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1). The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God, the Day of Atonement his once-for-all sacrifice, the Sabbath the rest he gives, the tabernacle God come to dwell with his people. A shadow is real and useful, for it tells you something is on its way, but it was never meant to be clung to as the thing itself.

But the substance belongs to Christ. The word for substance is literally body (sōma), echoing v. 9, where the fullness of deity dwells bodily. The body that cast this whole shadow play of feasts and foods and sacred days is Christ himself. When your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall. To return to the ceremonies now is to prefer the outline to the person. You have lost nothing by leaving the shadows behind; you have gained the One they all pointed to.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless: studying its shadows helps us see Christ. Nor that God’s moral law, summed up in love for God and neighbour, was a shadow; it is the ceremonial signposts that have reached their destination.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? Ask what each one was pointing to: the sacrifices to Christ’s death, the food laws to the clean heart he gives (Mark 7:19), while the moral commands still show God’s will (Luke 24:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let anyone who boasts of severe self-denial, angels and visions rule you out of the prize Christ has already won for you. Beneath the show is plain pride.

Let no one disqualify you. “Disqualify” (katabrabeuō) comes from the games: an umpire ruling against a competitor. The false teachers set themselves up as umpires, pronouncing the Colossians out of the running unless they took up their programme. But the Father has already qualified them (1:12). The programme had three strands.

Insisting on asceticism. The word (tapeinophrosynē) is literally humility, but here it is false humility: harsh self-denial, probably including rigorous fasting, used as a technique for higher spirituality (v. 23). It looked humble, even impressive, but it was a performance of lowliness.

And worship of angels. Religious devotion to angels as mediators and channels to God (on the exact sense, see the box below). It dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5) and bows to powers Christ is head over (2:10). Angels themselves refuse it: when John fell down to worship one, he was told to worship God (Revelation 19:10). Christ needs no angel to bring us to God, because he is God come to bring us home.

Going on in detail about visions. The teacher paraded mystical experiences won through his disciplines and built his authority on them: “I have seen what you have not; follow me and you can too.” It was spiritual one-upmanship, making private revelations rather than Christ and his word the measure of who is advanced.

Puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind. Literally the mind of his flesh. For all the display, the man is simply inflated, with nothing inside. And here is the irony: the man who beats his body to escape the flesh, and scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is driven the whole time by the flesh, by the fallen nature’s craving for status. His humility is vanity in disguise.

Still with us. All three strands remain: holiness equated with severity; fascination with angels, spirit guides and other mediators slipped between the believer and Christ; and experience-chasing that rates Christians by their dramatic encounters. Beneath them runs the same thing, an elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified, and the same fleshly pride (1 Corinthians 8:1). The safeguard in every age is the next verse: hold fast to the Head.

What if a Christian friend tells me about a dramatic vision or experience? Listen kindly, and do not mock; God is free to move his people deeply. But test it by Scripture, and ask where it points: to Christ and his word, or to the person and their experience? Be wary of any experience used to claim a higher rank, to add teaching beyond the Bible, or to make others feel second-class. The closed canon of Scripture (the complete, finished collection of God’s written word) is sufficient for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). You do not need someone else’s vision to know Christ fully; you have his word, and his Spirit to open it.

Where Christians differ: praying to angels and saints. Some traditions encourage prayer to angels or departed saints for help and intercession, distinguishing such requests from worship, and many sincere believers practise them. This commentary’s view: Paul warns against worship of angels, and Scripture forbids worshipping any creature (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). There is one mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Believers pray to God through Christ alone.

Uncertain wording. This is one of the hardest verses in the letter. “Worship of angels” can mean worshipping angels, or joining in the worship angels offer in heaven, which the visionaries may have claimed to see. “Going on in detail” (embateuō) means entering into; some ancient inscriptions seem to use it of initiates entering a sanctuary, so it may mean entering into, or taking his stand on, what he has seen. The details are uncertain; the shape is clear: a teacher who claimed special experiences and used them to rank himself above ordinary believers.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add not (things he has not seen); the earliest lack it, so most modern Bibles read what he has seen.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers have let go of Christ, the Head, from whom alone the whole church receives its life and growth.

And not holding fast to the Head. “Holding fast” means to grip tightly, and the Head is Christ (1:18; 2:10). Here in one phrase is Paul’s diagnosis: for all the visions and disciplines and angel talk, they had let go of Christ, shifting their grip to rules, experiences and spiritual beings. That is fatal, because everything depends on the Head. It is the opposite of being rooted and built up in him (2:7), and it implies our part: do not loosen your grip when something newer and more impressive comes along.

The whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments. The body is the church (1:18). The joints and ligaments are the tissues that both link the parts and carry the supply from the head to every limb. So life flows from Christ through all the connections into every member, and the body is fed, held together, and grows. Believers grow through their relationships with one another (Ephesians 4:15–16).

A growth that is from God. The increase is God’s doing, through Christ, not something the body manufactures by rules, visions or technique (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Cut a branch from the vine and it withers, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5); no exercise will make a severed hand grow. Drawing people off Christ onto their rules, the false teachers offered a fancier life while cutting the branch from its only source.

The Head who was crowned with thorns. Every ounce of life in the church flows down from her risen Lord. He feeds the smallest member through the plainest joint: a word from a friend, a prayer in a kitchen, a sermon in a small hall. The Head who was crowned with thorns now crowns his body with a growth that is God’s own, and no member joined to him has ever been starved.

In everyday life. Your growth is not a technique to master but the fruit of staying joined to Jesus, in faith, his word and prayer, while God supplies the increase. Think of one believer through whom God has fed you, and tell them.

Can I grow as a Christian without belonging to a church? Not as God intends. The body grows through its joints and ligaments, and a Christian was never meant to be a severed limb. Other believers teach you, correct you, pray for you, need your gifts, and show you Christ in ways you would never see alone. In seasons when illness, persecution or distance cut you off, God is not limited. But if you are able, join a faithful local church, and be known there. Holding fast to the Head and staying joined to the body go together.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You died with Christ to the whole order of man-made religious rules, so do not take them up again: they look wise, but they have no power against sin. Only Christ does.

If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world. The “if” is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died. The elemental spirits (as in v. 8) are the principles and powers of the old order: the whole system of religious rules and the forces behind it. United to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were released from that regime, for death dissolves every old bond (Romans 7:1–6). Its rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died.

In the flow. This last paragraph of the chapter opens, “If with Christ you died”; Colossians 3:1 will open with its partner, “If then you have been raised with Christ”. Here Paul shows what your death with Christ frees you from, man-made rules; there, what your resurrection frees you for, a life set on Christ above.

Why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations? “Submit to regulations” (dogmatizō) means to be subjected to decrees. To take them up again is to act as if the death had never happened: a freed slave walking back into the slave quarters and picking up his old chains.

“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch.” The false teachers’ slogans: every one a prohibition, rules piled on rules, each stricter than the last. Touch is lighter than handle, so even the faintest contact is banned.

Things that all perish as they are used. Then Paul lets the air out of it. Food and drink are used up and gone, and cannot touch the soul: what goes into the stomach does not defile the heart (Mark 7:18–19).

According to human precepts and teachings. The words echo Isaiah 29:13, quoted by Jesus against the Pharisees, who taught as doctrines the commandments of men (Mark 7:7). Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

An appearance of wisdom. The fasting looks like devotion, the strict rules like holiness, the severity like depth: a convincing surface with no reality beneath. And rules appeal to the heart because they can be measured. I can tick them off, compare myself with others and feel I have earned my place, which is religion used to save myself. But no one keeps even God’s own commands perfectly; the only obedience that ever earned a place is Christ’s, and God counts it to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). The irreligious person who sees through that pride is right about the pride, and he needs the same Christ, who alone can make the proud and the careless clean.

Self-made religion. “Self-made religion” (ethelothrēskia) is will-worship: worship a man chooses for himself rather than worship God commands. The word is not found in any earlier Greek writing we have, and Paul may have coined it; either way it exposes the root: self-will dressed up as devotion.

Of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh. The system fails at the one thing it claims to do. Rules may restrain behaviour outwardly, but they cannot change the heart; they feed pride, leave sinful desires untouched, and may even inflame the sin they forbid (Romans 7:5–8). Starve the body, and the flesh (the sinful nature) does not die; it grows fat on pride in its own discipline. Such rules are like cutting weeds at ground level: tidy for a day, while the roots live. Only Christ digs out the root. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule book but a living Saviour: you have died and been raised with him, so hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, where he is seated (3:1–5; Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16).

Does this make fasting and self-discipline pointless? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), Paul disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance with God. Discipline as a means of growth, done in faith, is good.

So how do I actually fight a sin I keep falling into? Not by rules alone, though wise boundaries help: if you know you are weak, do not walk into temptation (Romans 13:14). The heart of the fight is Christ. You died and were raised with him, so sin is no longer your master (Romans 6:11–14). Set your mind on things above, where he is (3:1–2). Put sin to death by the Spirit, not by willpower alone (Romans 8:13): pray, confess it honestly, bring it into the light with a trusted believer (James 5:16), fill your mind with his word, and feed on his love. The flesh is starved most effectively when the soul is feasting on Christ. And if you have fallen again, do not conclude that you are lost: hating the sin and still fighting it is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17), so go straight back to Christ, for your standing rests on him, not on your record.

Where Christians differ: rules for holiness. Many churches add rules beyond Scripture, such as no alcohol, no dancing or strict dress codes, as tests of holiness. This commentary’s view: Christians may make wise personal choices and churches may give wise counsel, but when human rules are made a test of spirituality or bound on others’ consciences, they become self-made religion. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and nothing is to be required beyond his word (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). The power to defeat sin is found in Christ, not in rules.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of v. 23 is among the most difficult in Paul’s letters. The ESV takes the last clause to say these rules are of no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence; others read it as saying they are of no real value and serve only to gratify the flesh. Either way the verdict is the same: man-made severity cannot conquer sin, and may feed it.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,<sup>2</sup>that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,<sup>3</sup>in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.<sup>4</sup>I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.<sup>5</sup>For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him,<sup>7</sup>rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.<sup>8</sup>See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.<sup>9</sup>For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,<sup>10</sup>and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.<sup>11</sup>In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ,<sup>12</sup>having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.<sup>13</sup>And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,<sup>14</sup>by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands.
