This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.<sup>15</sup>He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.<sup>16</sup>Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.<sup>18</sup>Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,<sup>19</sup>and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.<sup>20</sup>If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—<sup>21</sup>“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”<sup>22</sup>(referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings?<sup>23</sup>These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

keyVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
keyVerse.note: These two verses are the answer to the whole false teaching. If all of God dwells in Christ, there is nothing to seek outside him; if believers are filled in him, there is nothing to add; and if he is head over every power, there is no one else to fear or appease. Everything else in the chapter, from the cross of v. 14 to the warnings of vv. 16–23, unfolds what it means to be filled in him.

2.reflection:
Paul tells the Colossians to walk in Christ the same way they first received him (vv. 6–7). How did you first come to Christ, and where are you tempted to try to go on with him in a different way, by effort, rules or experiences?

Verse 14 pictures our record of debt cancelled and nailed to the cross, and v. 15 the powers disarmed and led in triumph. Which of these do you most need to believe this week, and what difference would it make to your guilt or your fears?

Verses 16–23 describe people who judged and disqualified others by food, holy days, severity and spiritual experiences. What versions of Christ plus do you meet today, in the church or in your own heart, and how can we resist them without judging those who keep such things freely?

Paul says man-made rules “are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (v. 23). If rules cannot conquer sin, what does this chapter offer instead, and how does holding fast to the Head (v. 19) help in a real struggle you face?

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 and 2 showed the Colossians who Christ is and that in him they are already full; chapter 3 turns, with its first word, to how such people live. It answers the question chapter 2 left open: if rules have no power against sin (2:23), what does? The household teaching it begins runs on to 4:1.

The message. You have been raised with Christ, so live where your life now is. Your life is hidden with him in God and will appear with him in glory; so kill what belongs to the old life, take off its clothes and put on his: compassion, humility, forgiveness and love, with his peace ruling, his word dwelling richly and his name over everything you do, right down to how you treat your husband or wife, your children and those you work for or over. Holiness does not come by climbing up to Christ through rules, but by living out the union he has already made.

Why it was said. The false teachers offered a holiness of rules, severity and visions, and their rules looked wise but could not touch the flesh (2:23; see the introduction). Believers who had laid those rules aside would naturally ask whether they now had any way to fight sin at all, and how faith in Christ alone reaches the kitchen, the workshop and the marriage. Paul’s answer is not lower standards but a deeper root.

How the chapter makes its case. First the foundation (vv. 1–4): raised with Christ, believers set their minds where he is seated, for their real life is hidden with him and will be revealed with him. Then the stripping off (vv. 5–11): put to death the sins of the appetites, on which God’s wrath is coming, and take off the sins of the temper and the tongue, because the old self has already been put off and the new self put on, in a people where race and class no longer rank anyone. Then the putting on (vv. 12–17): as God’s chosen and beloved, wear Christ’s own character, with love over all, his peace as umpire, his word richly at home in the church, and every word and deed done in his name with thanks. Last, the household (3:18–4:1): wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters each answer to the Lord, and those who hold power receive the restraining command.

Where it leads. Christ fills the chapter. He is seated at God’s right hand, he is our life, he will appear, he is all and in all, his peace rules, his word dwells, his name covers everything, and he is the Master even of masters. The holiness it describes is not a ladder up to him but the life of people joined to him, and the new self it describes wears his own likeness: the compassionate, meek and forgiving Son who bore with slow disciples, washed their feet and prayed for those who crucified him. The one who will appear in glory first took the form of a slave, and by that service made slaves his heirs.

For us. When you face a stubborn sin or a hard relationship, do not start with a new rule; start with where your life is. Then ask which old clothes you are still wearing, and what of Christ you need to put on in their place, beginning at home today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because you have been raised with Christ, your life is now where he is, so set your heart and mind there. Everything else in the chapter rests on these verses. Believers seek and think about the things above, where Christ reigns at God’s right hand (vv. 1–2). They have died, and their true life is kept safe with him, out of sight for now (v. 3), until he appears and they appear with him in glory (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer

Colossians 3:3 is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament of the believer’s security (see the note on v. 3). Reformed teaching therefore grounds assurance not in the believer’s performance but in where he is: in Christ, kept by God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were told their spiritual safety depended on handling the angels rightly, keeping the festivals and food laws, and reaching special spiritual states. Paul says their life is hidden with Christ in God, where none of that can touch it. Now: A Christian whose sense of security rises on good days of prayer and falls on days of failure needs the same word (see the note on v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because believers have already been raised with Christ, they are to make the risen, reigning Christ the aim of their whole life. This is the true way to holiness that the false teachers missed: not climbing up by rules, but living from a union already made.

If then. The “if” turns the argument, and it means since, as in 2:20: Paul is not asking whether they belong to Christ but building on the fact that they do. Chapter 2 ended with the verdict that the false teachers’ rules have no power to stop our sinful desires (2:23). Now comes the second half of one truth: died with Christ, you are free from the world’s rules (2:20); raised with him, you seek what is above. The cure for a failed religion of rules is not more severity to the body but a new direction, up towards the risen Christ.

Raised already. “Raised with Christ” is not a distant promise but a finished fact. United to Christ (2:12), you share his resurrection now: God counts his death and rising as yours (Romans 6:4–5), and the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you, giving a new heart that wants what is above (Romans 8:11; Ezekiel 36:26). The false teachers urged the Colossians to climb to heaven through fasting, visions and angels. They need not climb a single rung, for in Christ they are already raised and seated there (Ephesians 2:5–6). Every other way is a ladder. The gospel is the news that someone came down the ladder, took hold of you, and carried you up.

Seek the things above. The verb (zēteō) is present tense: keep seeking, keep making Christ’s kingdom your aim and treasure, turning a whole life’s desires and ambitions towards him, because “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Seated at the right hand. The things above are not a vague spiritual atmosphere but wherever Christ is, seated at God’s right hand, the place of supreme honour and authority promised in the psalm the New Testament quotes more than any other (Psalm 110:1). And he is seated. The old priests stood day after day because their work was never finished; this priest sat down because his was (Hebrews 10:11–12). The powers the false teachers feared are disarmed beneath his feet (2:15). The Jesus who hung on the cross bearing your debt now sits on heaven’s throne as your head, your brother and your high priest, with your name on his heart (Romans 8:34). Our head is there, so our hearts belong there.

In everyday life. When the pressure is highest this afternoon, stop for ten seconds and remember where he is: not anxious, not hurried, not wondering how it will turn out, but seated. Your work today is real and it matters. It is not, however, holding up the universe. Someone else is doing that, and he has sat down.

How do I actually seek the things above in an ordinary day? Begin with a few minutes of Scripture and prayer in the morning, before the day’s demands start talking. Carry one question into the day: what does the risen Lord want done here? When you decide about money, time or ambition, ask which choice treats his kingdom as the treasure. Gather with his people on the Lord’s Day, where heaven’s realities are preached and sung. And when you notice your heart has drifted to anxiety or getting, do not berate yourself; simply turn it back. Seeking is a direction you keep returning to, not a feeling you must sustain.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to keep their whole way of thinking fixed on Christ and his kingdom, not on the passing things of earth. Verse 1 engaged the will; verse 2 engages the mind.

Set your minds. The verb (phroneō) means the settled bent of the mind, the whole direction of a person’s thinking and valuing, the word Paul uses in “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). There is nothing above to set the mind on but Christ, and Christ is enough to fill a mind for ever. We are invited to think about the most glorious being there is, and to find that he has been thinking about us first.

Not on earthly things. Earthly things here are not the earth itself, which God made and called good, but passing things treated as if they mattered most: the food rules and regulations of 2:21–22, and the sinful desires Paul is about to name in v. 5. The man of strict rules and the man of pleasure look like opposites, but one is preoccupied with what he must not touch, the other with what he must have, and neither is looking at Christ.

The expatriate. A man working abroad does his job well and is kind to his neighbours, but his heart is set on home: he is not crushed when the local currency falls, and he does not mistake the posting for his life. So it is with the Christian, whose citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

If my thoughts drift constantly, am I failing at this? No; the command assumes drift, which is why it is in the present tense: keep setting. A mind is set the way a compass needle is set, not by never moving but by always swinging back to north. You do not fix your thoughts by grim concentration; you feed them. What you read, watch and scroll shapes where an idle mind goes, so give it things worth returning to: Scripture memorised, a psalm sung, a truth about Christ turned over on the commute. Every believer’s mind wanders this side of glory. The question is where it comes back to.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seek the things above, because your old life ended when Christ died, and your real life is now kept safe with him, out of sight. “For” gives the ground beneath the command: your life is where Christ is.

For you have died. The verb is past and finished. In union with Christ’s death, the old you, who belonged to the world and lived for its things, died and was buried with him (2:20; Romans 6:2–7). Not that you feel dead to sin, but that God counts you as having died with Christ. Sin’s right to rule you and the law’s sentence against you were dealt with there, once for all. The old master can still shout, but he no longer owns you.

Hidden with Christ in God. Hidden and staying hidden (the perfect tense of kryptō). Hidden means safe: stored in the most secure place in the universe, and double-wrapped, your life in Christ and Christ in God. Jesus says, “no one will snatch them out of my hand”, and “no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:28–29). Hidden also means concealed: your true life and glory are not yet on display, and for now look ordinary and often weak. But hidden is not lost; it waits to be unveiled (v. 4).

Hidden where no darkness can reach. The God who hid Moses in the cleft of the rock while his glory passed by has hidden us in his Son, and the Son in himself. Our Saviour went into the darkness of the tomb so that our lives might be hidden where no darkness can reach. His keeping is stronger than our weakness, and he has never lost one whom he hid.

Treasure in a strongroom. Your real life is not held in your own trembling hands. On your worst day, when you feel like a failure and a fraud, it is still safe, because it hangs on Christ, not on your performance. You may look ordinary and weary, like an acorn in winter ground, but the glory is real and coming: “we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared” (1 John 3:2). You do not have to achieve your life, guard it or prove it.

What it does not mean. “You have died” does not mean you can no longer sin or feel temptation. The rest of the chapter commands believers to put sin to death precisely because it is still active in them. What died was your old identity and its claim on you, not every trace of its habits.

If my life is hidden and safe, why does it so often feel fragile? Because you are looking at the part that is not hidden: your moods, health, circumstances and recent failures, which do fluctuate. But Paul is describing not how your life feels but where it is kept. A deposit in a bank vault does not become less safe because the depositor has a bad week. When you feel fragile, do not try to feel stronger; look to where your life is kept, and who is holding it. Assurance grows by attending to Christ, not by taking your own temperature.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ appears, the life now hidden will be revealed, and believers will share his glory. The pattern is hidden now, revealed then.

Christ who is your life. Christ does not merely give us life, as a gift we hold apart from him; he is our life: its source, its substance and its centre. Your pardon is his death, your righteousness his obedience, your new heart his Spirit’s work, your future his glory: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). This is the final answer to a teaching that offered Christ plus something. Christ is not part of the package; he is the whole of it.

Appears. To appear (phaneroō) is to be brought out of hiding into open view. Now the world does not see him, but a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory before the whole creation. Mark the word: “when”, not “if”. It will be one appearing, public and visible to all (Matthew 24:27, 30–31). This commentary does not expect a secret rapture before it, since the New Testament describes Christ’s coming for his people and his coming in glory as one open event; but believers who do expect one long for the same appearing, and that shared hope is Paul’s point.

Appear with him in glory. Your destiny is bound to Christ’s. You, who look like nothing much now, will share his glory: “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2; Romans 8:17–19). He will not be ashamed of us on that day. He who is our life will show us to the universe as his own, robed in a glory he won and gives away.

The bucket list and the hidden life. If this life is the only one, every unseen country and road not taken is lost for ever, and the sensible response is to cram in as much as possible. That is the quiet logic behind the bucket list and the fear of missing out: dread that time is running out on the only chance we have. It leaves us half-present even on holiday. Paul’s word cuts the root of it. Your real life is not the sum of your experiences; it is a person, and it has not yet been shown. The best is not behind you, or on someone else’s screen; it is ahead, and certain. So a Christian can enjoy a sunset without needing it to be the last one, because he is not trying to squeeze eternity into eighty years. The world says you only live once. The gospel says the life you have in Christ has hardly begun to appear.

The hinge of the chapter. Having settled who you are and who you will be, Paul draws the conclusion: “Put to death therefore” (v. 5). Future glory is the great motive for present holiness: “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). People who know where they are going start dressing for it.

What it does not mean. Believers will not become divine or be absorbed into God; they will share his glory as human beings, body and soul, still creatures and still themselves, made perfectly like their Lord. Nor does glory wait until the end with nothing before it. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); the soul does not sleep. But the full public unveiling, with resurrected bodies, comes when he appears.

What will glory actually be like? Scripture tells us more than we notice: a body raised imperishable, never again sick, ageing or dying (1 Corinthians 15:42–44); a character free from sin, loving without the drag you feel now; Christ seen face to face, which is the heart of it; and all of it shared with his people in a renewed creation (Romans 8:21). Glory is not becoming a spotlight but being made fully what God meant you to be, reflecting his light without distortion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since you have died and been raised with Christ, get rid of everything that belongs to the old life. Believers put to death the sins of the appetites, with greed unmasked as idolatry (v. 5), because God’s wrath is coming on them and this was the road they once walked (vv. 6–7). They strip off the sins of the temper and the tongue, lying among them (vv. 8–9), for they have already put off the old self and put on the new, which God is renewing in his image (vv. 9–10). In that new humanity the old divisions no longer rank anyone, because Christ is all, and in all (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the classic Reformed treatment of Colossians 3:5 (see the note on v. 5). Mortification (putting sin to death) is applying the cross, by the Spirit, to particular sinful desires: these belong to the old self that died with Christ, and by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were offered a programme of outward self-denial to deal with their sinful desires, and Paul says it has no value against them (2:23; on how true mortification differs, see the note on v. 5). Now: A Christian fighting sin by willpower alone is using the wrong weapons. The fight is real, and it is fought in prayer, by the Spirit, among God’s people, with the cross as its ground.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they have died and been raised with Christ, believers are to kill, not manage, the sins of the appetites that still cling to them, and greed above all, which is idolatry. “Therefore” reaches back to vv. 1–4: live out what you already are.

Put to death therefore. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v. 3); now you put to death its lingering expressions, daily. The word (nekroō) is violent: kill, execute; not manage, not tame. Sin is an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. Yet this is not the harsh self-denial of 2:23, rules imposed from outside that cannot touch desire. The killing is done from the inside, by people already raised with Christ, through the Spirit: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13). John Owen, the great Puritan, put it in a sentence his readers never forgot: “be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”

From the act to the root. The four words dig from act to root. Sexual immorality (porneia) is every sexual act outside marriage, the outward deed; impurity (akatharsia), the defiled imagination. Passion (pathos) goes deeper, to the ungoverned lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the bottom: the wrong craving of the heart itself. Sin runs all the way down into what the heart wants, which is why rules alone can never cure it: they trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

Covetousness, which is idolatry. Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed, the restless craving for more: looking to created things for the security and worth only God can give. Whatever a man treasures above God is in practice his god, and the greedy man bows at an altar he would never admit was there (Ephesians 5:5; Matthew 6:24). It comes last because it exposes the idolatry beneath all these sins, and because it is the sin that looks respectable. “Take care,” said Jesus, “and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

A sentence already passed. A believer fights sin with hope, because the enemy he must execute is already condemned. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, God condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3), and our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). At the cross sin lost its right to rule us; in the daily fight it loses its grip. The believer is carrying out a sentence already passed and paid for, by the power of Christ’s risen life within him.

Covetousness grasps; the Son of God let go. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Offered all the kingdoms of the world, he would not bow to get them; he carried our idolatries to the cross, and his Spirit finishes in us what he finished there. When Christ himself is our life, the idols lose their grip, because we have found the one treasure they were all pretending to be.

How do I actually put a sin to death? Name it plainly as an enemy, not a weakness or a phase. Refuse it at the first stirring, not after an hour of entertaining it. Starve it: remove what feeds it, whether a device in the bedroom, a route home past the shop, a friendship that always ends the same way, or the shopping app on your phone. Flee the situations where you know you fall (2 Timothy 2:22). Bring it into the light with a trusted believer. And do all of it leaning on the Spirit’s power and Christ’s finished work, not gritting your teeth to earn God’s favour. The fight is from acceptance, never for it.

What if I have been fighting the same sin for years and keep losing? Then you are in a real war, which is itself a sign of life; the dead do not fight. Long struggle does not prove you are not a Christian; making peace with the sin would. But look at how you are fighting. Have you been fighting alone and in secret? Tell someone. Have you fought the act and ignored the desire? Ask what the sin promises you, and seek that in Christ. Have you been fighting from guilt instead of grace? Go back to the cross every time you fall, at once, not after a period of self-punishment. The Spirit is patient, and he finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6).

Is this not simply a repressive view of sex? No, it is a high one. The world treats sex as an appetite like hunger, and then wonders why so many end up used and lonely. Scripture treats it as a gift so precious that God fences it within the lifelong promise of marriage, where two people give themselves wholly and are not discarded (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). The command is not God frowning at pleasure but the Maker guarding a gift from misuse, and people from being treated as things.

Uncertain wording. Paul literally says put to death the members that are on the earth, then lists sins, not parts of the body. “Members” may be the limbs through which sin acts, or the sinful practices themselves, pictured as the old self’s limbs. Either way the ESV’s “what is earthly in you” gives the sense: the desires and habits of the old life that still cling to the believer. Paul is not calling the body evil.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These sins must be killed because God’s wrath is coming on them. Set between the two lists of sins (vv. 5 and 8), the warning makes the fight urgent: the day of judgment is fixed (Romans 1:18; Ephesians 5:6).

What God’s wrath is. Not a bad temper or God flying off the handle, but the settled, holy opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil: the response of a just judge to sin. Far from being a flaw, it flows from his holiness: he is “of purer eyes than to see evil” (Habakkuk 1:13). A God indifferent to the abuse of children or the betrayal of a marriage would be no good God, as those badly wronged often see most quickly.

One appearing, two outcomes. The day Christ appears (v. 4) and the coming wrath are one event. God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed”, and he has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The appearing that is glory for those hidden in Christ will be judgment for those who refused him (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). For some his face will be the face of the one who is their life; for others, the face of their Judge.

Not one drop remains. Believers will not face God’s wrath. Christ bore it in their place, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and we wait for Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). There was a day when the wrath of God against these very sins came down, and it did not fall on the guilty. It fell on the Lamb of God, who drank the cup to the bottom, so that for everyone who trusts in him not one drop remains. He was forsaken so that we would never be. The verse is meant not to frighten Christians about their standing but to show how serious sin is.

If Christ has taken the wrath for me, why should this warning move me? Because it shows you what your sin really is and what it cost. A man pulled from a burning house does not wander back in to collect a souvenir. The warning keeps you from treating as harmless the very things that brought the cross on your Saviour. It is also a test: one who carries on in these sins with no fight and no grief, while claiming to be safe, should ask whether he has ever been rescued at all. For the believer who is fighting, it drives him not into fear but back to the shelter, where the wrath has already fallen on someone else.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add the words “upon the sons of disobedience”, which appear in the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. Whether or not Paul wrote them here, the meaning is the same: God’s wrath falls on those who persist in these sins without repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These sins were the road the Colossians themselves once walked, before grace turned them round. Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile.

Once walked. Many people apart from Christ are outwardly decent, because God’s common grace, his kindness to all, holds back the full flood of sin. Paul’s point is that this was the Colossians’ own former road, the direction a heart turned from God naturally runs, whether or not every sin shows in every person.

You too. There is tenderness in those two words. They keep the believer humble, for he was once where others are still trapped, and grateful, for grace lifted him out. “And such were some of you,” Paul tells the Corinthians. “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:3–5).

Once, but now. “Once” sets up the turn of the next verse: “But now”. The letter has already said what stands between the two: “you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him” (1:21–22). The way out of the old country was not a better effort but a body nailed to a cross. You have emigrated, and he paid for your papers. Do not move back.

If I was a Christian from childhood, does “once” apply to me? Yes, though it may look different. If you never walked in open sexual sin or drunkenness, that is a mercy to thank God for, not a credential. But the heart apart from grace is turned from God at the root, and that was true of you too. The pride, self-will and quiet idolatries of a well-behaved child are the same country with tidier streets. Grace lifted you out as surely as it lifted the man with the dramatic story, only earlier, and that is more grace, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that they belong to Christ, believers must strip off the sins of the temper and the tongue as well as the sins of the appetites. These are the sins respectable church members can commit for decades without anyone calling them sin.

Put them all away. Where v. 5 said kill, v. 8 says take off (apotithēmi), like stripping off filthy clothes and throwing them aside. “All” sweeps up both lists: the first (v. 5) was sexual and greedy, the sins of the appetites; this one is relational and verbal, the sins of the temper and the tongue.

Anger, wrath, malice. Two words for temper, often read as two kinds. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind: the grudge nursed, the banked fire of resentment that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind: the flare-up that explodes and subsides. Beneath both lies malice (kakia): ill will itself, the meanness of spirit that wishes another harm, or is quietly pleased when harm comes.

Slander and obscene talk. Slander (blasphēmia) is speech that runs a person down. It is the same word as blasphemy against God, and the overlap is no accident: to tear down someone made in God’s image is to speak against his Maker (James 3:9). Obscene talk (aischrologia) is foul, shameful, abusive speech. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).

Reviled, he did not revile. Every sin on this list was once aimed at one man. False witnesses slandered him, the high priest called his words blasphemy, and passers-by hurled abuse at the cross (Mark 14:55–65; 15:29–32). And “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), the sins of our mouths among them, and his silence under them is the pattern of the new self.

In everyday life. Pick the one sin on this list your family would name if asked about you, and next time it rises, replace it with its opposite. If the words have already come out, go back and apologise without explanation. A sentence that begins “I’m sorry, but” is not an apology.

Is all anger sinful? No. Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul says, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at cruelty, injustice and the abuse of the weak can be righteous. Paul means selfish anger, about my rights, comfort and pride, which wants to hurt. A useful test: righteous anger is about God’s honour and others’ good, is slow to arise, and moves towards putting things right. Sinful anger is about me, is quick, and moves towards getting even.

How do I tell slander from a legitimate warning? Scripture names real dangers and sometimes real names (2 Timothy 4:14). Ask three questions. Is it true? Slander trades in falsehood and exaggeration; a warning is accurate. Is it necessary, for a good end? A warning protects someone from harm; slander only wounds, entertains, or makes the speaker look better. And why are you saying it, and to whom? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, usually to the person who can do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen.

How do I put these off when I have tried to “just stop” so many times? Not by white-knuckle willpower, the harsh self-denial of chapter 2. Putting off always comes paired with putting on (vv. 10, 12), and a sin is driven out not by an empty space but by a stronger love: take off anger and put on compassion; take off slander and speak well of people behind their backs. And it flows from who you already are, for you have already put off the old self (v. 9). The old clothes feel familiar, so you keep taking them off, day after day, while the Spirit keeps remaking you. Progress, not yet perfection (Ephesians 4:22–24).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not deceive one another, because they have taken off the old self that lied and put on the new self, which God is remaking in his own image. Truthfulness is not a rule laid on from outside; it is the likeness of the new person they already are.

Do not lie to one another. One more sin of speech, and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, exaggeration and the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together (Ephesians 4:25). The devil is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44); to deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness.

Put off the old self. The old self, literally the old man, is not merely a bundle of bad habits but the whole person you used to be as a child of Adam: your old identity under the reign of sin, together with its practices. It was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6) and taken off once for all at conversion; the daily putting away of its leftover habits (vv. 5, 8) lives out a change already made. The believer is like a discharged soldier: he may still reach for the old uniform, but his old officers can no longer give him orders (Romans 6:14).

Put on the new self. Your settled identity in union with the risen Lord, the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). It is shared as well as personal, which is why v. 11 says the old divisions of race and class now fall away. Christ is forming not only new individuals but a new humanity.

Being renewed in knowledge. The new self is not static: God is renewing it day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 12:2). The decisive change is done; the transformation goes on. And it is renewal in knowledge (epignōsis): not the secret knowledge the false teachers offered, but the personal knowledge of God as he really is in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3). Knowing God rightly is itself transforming.

After the image of its creator. Man was made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27), defaced though not erased by the fall, and now being restored in Christ, who is himself “the image of the invisible God” (1:15). To be renewed after the Creator’s image is to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29; Ephesians 4:24). Salvation is not self-improvement; it is new creation, God stamping his own likeness on the soul again. The Creator did not discard the ruined portrait, but sent his Son to bear its ruin and make it new, and one day every one of his people will bear his likeness without a blemish.

What counts as lying in everyday life? The excuse that is not quite the reason. The figure rounded up on the claim form. Saying you are fine to avoid a conversation that needs to happen. Letting a false impression stand because it flatters you. The CV that implies more than it says. Agreeing to do something you have no intention of doing. Truthfulness does not require you to say everything you think; silence and tact are not lies. But whatever you do say should be true, and you should not set out to make anyone believe what is false.

Where Christians differ: is it ever right to lie, for example to protect life? The Hebrew midwives deceived Pharaoh, and Rahab hid the spies. Some Christians hold that deceiving people set on murder is not the lying Scripture forbids, since God dealt well with the midwives (Exodus 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that every lie is a sin, though God may honour the faith and courage behind it. This commentary’s view: the first reading is more likely. The ninth commandment forbids false witness against a neighbour, and those bent on murder have no right to the truth they would use to kill; Rahab, and those who hid Jews from the Gestapo, stood in the same place. But such cases are rare and extreme, godly believers have differed on them, and they are not the subject of this verse. The command here is about trust among believers: Christians should be people whose word can always be relied on, in small things as in large.

Uncertain wording. “You have put off” and “have put on” are participles. The ESV, with most interpreters, reads them as completed facts giving the reason for the command; some read them as further commands (put off, put on), as some take Ephesians 4:22–24. The past tense and the argument favour the ESV, and either way the change is both done and still to be lived out.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new humanity Christ is making, the old divisions of race, religion, culture and class no longer rank anyone, because Christ is everything and lives in every believer. Paul names the great dividing lines of his world, and sets Christ over them all.

Not Greek and Jew. In the new humanity of vv. 9–10 the old divisions disappear. Race: Greek and Jew, the deepest divide of all. Religion: circumcised and uncircumcised, the mark that had separated the covenant people from everyone else.

Barbarian, Scythian. Culture. A barbarian was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, the ancient way of calling someone uncivilised. The Scythians, nomads from north of the Black Sea, were the Greek byword for savagery. Paul reaches for the most extreme example he can: even they are welcome as equals in Christ.

Slave, free. Class. A slave was legally property, and slave and free seldom ate as equals. In the church they did. Philemon, a slave owner in this very congregation, was about to welcome back his slave Onesimus as a beloved brother (4:9; Philemon 16). Onesimus had probably run away, and now came home with Tychicus, the bearer of this letter.

Christ is all, and in all. Christ is all: the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts. And Christ is in all: he lives by his Spirit in every one of his people, the Scythian and the Pharisee alike, and his living in them makes them one (Romans 8:9–10). The Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary believers: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27; Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

The Jew and the Scythian at one table. Christ broke down the dividing wall in his own flesh, making one people of every kind of person without flattening them into sameness. Now the Jew and the Scythian kneel at the same table, the slave and the master call on the same Father, and none of them has anything to boast in but him. Heaven will be full of every tribe and language and people and nation, every voice singing one name.

What it does not mean. Cultural, ethnic and social differences do not simply disappear. A Jew remained a Jew and a slave remained a slave, and men and women remain men and women. Paul goes straight on to give different instructions to wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (3:18–4:1). The differences are not erased but dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family.

What does this look like in a church today? The businessman and the unemployed man share the bread and the cup as equals, and elders are chosen for godliness, not for wealth, education or ethnicity. The congregation does not drift into tables of people who look alike, and a believer from another culture who worships differently is a brother, not a curiosity. And it means looking honestly at your own instincts: who do you naturally assume will be the most mature Christian in the room, and why? The world ranks; the church must not, because Christ does not.
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As people God has chosen and loves, dress in the character of Christ and let him govern your life together. Believers put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness and patience, bear with one another and forgive as the Lord forgave them, with love binding it all together (vv. 12–14). Christ’s peace is to rule as umpire in the one body (v. 15), his word is to dwell richly as they teach and sing (v. 16), and his name is to cover every word and deed, with thanks to the Father through him (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The virtues of 3:12–15 are a portrait of Christ himself. Sanctification is growing to be like him (Romans 8:29), and these are the features of that likeness. They are not produced by moral effort alone; they are the fruit of the Spirit in those united to Christ (Galatians 5:22–23).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian church mixed Jew and Greek, slave and free, people with very different habits of living together and quarrelling. In a world built on honour and revenge, humility and forgiveness looked strange. Now: They still do, and a church that truly puts on compassion, humility and forbearance will look unlike other communities, because these are the features of the One who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has already chosen them and loves them, believers are to clothe themselves in Christ’s own character, forgive as he forgave them, and wear love over everything. Having stripped off the old sins (vv. 8–9), they get dressed in the new, daily and in the Spirit’s strength.

Put on then. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad but clothing yourself with the good, acting in compassion even before the feeling arrives. And Paul names who you are before he names a single virtue, with three titles that once belonged to Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).

Chosen, holy, beloved. Chosen (eklektoi): God set his love on you before the foundation of the world, before you had done anything (Ephesians 1:4). Holy: set apart as his treasured possession. Beloved: dearly loved, with the love God has for his beloved Son, into whose kingdom he has transferred you (1:13). You do not put on these graces to become chosen and loved; you put them on because you already are, and those who know they are loved are free to love.

Compassionate hearts, kindness. The first garments are tender ones. Compassionate hearts is literally bowels of mercy, the ancient way of naming the deep, gut-level feeling that moves when someone else is in pain. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is that compassion turned into action. Compassion feels; kindness acts.

Humility. The very word the false teachers had twisted into a show of self-denial (2:18, 23), but here the real thing: a right estimate of yourself as a sinner saved by sheer grace and therefore above no one, counting others more significant than yourself (Philippians 2:3). It is not self-hatred, which is self-absorption with a long face. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less.

Meekness, and patience. Meekness is not weakness. The Greeks could use the word of a gentle horse or a tame animal. It is the gentleness of someone who could retaliate and chooses not to. Jesus was “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and he overturned the temple tables (John 2:15). Patience (makrothumia) is literally long-tempered: slow to anger, the patience God shows to us, now worn towards others.

Bearing with one another. Putting up with each other’s rough edges: the brother who talks too long, the sister who is always late. Most church life is small frictions, not great wrongs, and love absorbs them without keeping a tally.

As the Lord has forgiven you. Then come the real wrongs: “if one has a complaint against another”. To forgive (charizomai, the verb built on the word for grace) is to release the debt, refusing the grudge and the revenge, just as God cancelled the record of debt that stood against you (2:14). The measure is the Lord’s forgiveness of you: freely, fully, at great cost, and while you were still his enemy (Romans 5:8–10). The forgiven man cannot easily hold a small debt over his brother (Matthew 18:21–35).

Above all, love. Love is the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe. Not mainly a warm feeling, for you can love a person you do not naturally like, but a settled decision to seek another’s good, whatever it costs and whether or not he deserves it. It is the bond (syndesmos, a ligament, the word used of the body’s ligaments in 2:19) that ties all the other graces, and the whole body, together. Without love the rest fall apart and ring hollow (1 Corinthians 13:1–3): humility becomes a pose, patience cold endurance, forgiveness a transaction. And “by this,” Jesus said, “all people will know that you are my disciples” (John 13:35).

Every garment is his. Each of these virtues is a portrait of Christ, who had compassion on the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). He was kind to the outcast, humble enough to wash feet, meek before Pilate, and patient with disciples who never seemed to understand. He bore with us when we were unbearable, and he forgave us while we were driving in the nails. To put on these clothes is to put on him (Romans 13:14).

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not pretend a serious wrong did not happen. It names the wrong and then releases it; it does not always remove the consequences or immediately restore trust. Nor does bearing with one another mean tolerating anything at all: serious, persistent sin in the church is to be dealt with (Matthew 18:15–17), gently and with the aim of restoration.

Must I forgive only when the other person apologises, or at once? Both, in different senses. The forgiving heart, released from bitterness, you must have at once, whether or not the other ever asks: “whenever you stand praying, forgive” (Mark 11:25). But full reconciliation, forgiveness spoken and received and the relationship restored, is completed when the other repents (Luke 17:3); restoration takes two. So forgive from the heart at once, and stand ready, even eager, to welcome him back the moment he turns.

Must I seek reconciliation with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of resuming closeness or trust. Forgiving from the heart means letting go of revenge and handing the wrong over to God, who judges justly. It does not mean trusting a dangerous or unrepentant person, resuming contact, keeping the abuse secret, or giving up church discipline or the protection of the law; the governing authority is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). Reporting a crime is not a failure to forgive. Reconciliation needs genuine repentance and changed behaviour shown over time, and safety comes first. A church that pressures a victim to reconcile has misunderstood both forgiveness and love.

How do I forgive when I still feel the hurt? Forgiveness is first a decision and then a process. You decide before God not to pursue revenge, not to bring the matter up as a weapon, not to dwell on it, and not to speak of it to damage the person. When the memory returns with fresh pain, as it will, you make the same decision again and hand the wrong back to God. Feelings usually follow slowly. Pray for the person by name; it is hard to keep hating someone you pray for. And look again at the cross, where your own debt was paid.

Uncertain wording. Paul literally calls love the bond of perfection. It may be the bond that holds the other virtues together in a complete whole, as the ESV takes it, or the bond that brings the church to maturity, the goal of 1:28. The two meet: love both unites the graces and makes the body whole.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the peace Christ won settle the inner struggles and the quarrels of his people, and be thankful. Christ’s peace is to be the umpire in every heart and in the one body.

The peace of Christ. The peace he made by the blood of his cross (1:20): first peace with God (Romans 5:1), and out of that the settled calm he leaves with his people, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27), and the peace that should reign between them.

Rule. Rule (brabeuō) is the umpire’s word: the referee who makes the call and settles the contest, the official at the games who awarded the prize. When you are torn, or relationships are strained, let his peace make the call, not anger, fear or self-will. Much of our turmoil comes from wanting to control what only God controls: how others see us, how things turn out. Christ’s peace gives us not that control but the One who has it.

Called in one body. You were called to this peace (1 Corinthians 7:15) as members of the one body of Christ, the one new humanity of v. 11. So it is not merely a private calm but the bond meant to keep the whole church one. Coming straight after vv. 12–14, the call the umpire most often has to make is between holding a grievance and forgiving.

Be thankful. The first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses (vv. 15, 16, 17), in a letter full of thanks (1:3, 12; 2:7; 4:2). It belongs beside peace, because the person counting his mercies has no room left to nurse complaints (Philippians 4:6–7). It is more than good manners or a technique for feeling better: it is the heart’s honest recognition that what it has was given, not earned: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). That is why it comes hard. Under our grumbling lies a quiet sense of entitlement: I worked for this, I deserve better, life owes me. Paul traces humanity’s whole drift from God to a refusal to give thanks (Romans 1:21).

Thanks for an inexpressible gift. The cure is not trying to feel grateful; it is looking at Christ. We were owed judgment, and instead the Son was given for us: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15). Timothy Keller often pointed out that religion obeys God out of fear, to get something from him, while the gospel obeys out of grateful joy, because everything has already been given. That changes the motive behind every command in this chapter. See also Thanksgiving in the Theological Dictionary.

In everyday life. This week, when you catch yourself complaining, stop and name one gift you did not earn, and thank the Father for it through his Son.

What it does not mean. A feeling of peace is not always a sign of God’s will, nor a feeling of unease always a no. A person can feel very peaceful about a sinful decision already made; Christ’s peace is not a mood to consult like an oracle. It governs decisions as we ask what would honour him and keep peace with God and with his people, tested always by Scripture.

So how do I let Christ’s peace decide something? First ask what Scripture says; Christ’s peace never contradicts his word. Then ask which course keeps a clear conscience before God, and which serves peace in the body rather than division. Ask whether a choice is being driven by fear, pride or the wish to win, and rule those out as referees. Pray, seek wise counsel from mature believers, and then act in faith. If two good options remain, you are free to choose, and your peace with God does not depend on choosing perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message about Christ is to make its home richly in the church, so that believers teach, correct and sing it to one another with grateful hearts. This is how the putting off and putting on actually happens.

The word of Christ. Rare in Paul (elsewhere only Romans 10:17), the phrase means the message of which he is the heart, “the word of the truth, the gospel” (1:5): not only the words of Jesus in red, but all of Scripture that proclaims him. Let Christ’s word fill you, not the philosophy and empty deceit of the false teachers (2:8).

Dwell in you richly. To dwell (enoikeō) is to take up residence: the word is to be a resident, not an occasional guest, furnishing every room of the heart. And “in you” is plural: among you, as a church. Paul pictures a congregation saturated with Scripture, its mind renewed (v. 10) as the word takes up rich residence within.

Teaching and admonishing. Teaching passes on truth; admonishing (noutheteō) warns a brother away from wrong. Paul used the same pair of his own ministry (1:28). And it is “one another”: not the task of official teachers alone but of every member, ordinary believers ministering the word to each other (Romans 15:14). It is done in all wisdom, knowing what word the moment needs. A verse thrown at a grieving friend can wound; the same verse given gently, at the right time, can heal.

Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. The third overflow is song. Psalms are the inspired Old Testament songbook; hymns are songs of praise, perhaps like the great hymn to Christ in 1:15–20; spiritual songs are songs prompted by the Spirit and full of his truth. Together they cover the full range of sung worship, and singing is itself a way of teaching one another (Ephesians 5:19).

With thankfulness in your hearts to God. From the heart, not just the lips, and aimed at God, not at the audience.

In the flow. In Ephesians the same teaching, singing and thanks flow from being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18–20); here, from Christ’s word dwelling richly. The two are not rivals, for the Spirit fills a church by means of Christ’s word. To teachers who promised fullness through visions and rules (2:8, 18), this is Paul’s reply: you have been filled in Christ (2:10), and you go on being filled as his word makes its home among you.

The Word who dwelt among us. The Word who was with God in the beginning became flesh and dwelt among us, and now he sends his word to dwell in us. He sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:30), very likely walking out to Gethsemane with the Passover psalms on his lips. He is the theme of every true song the church has ever sung, and he has put his own word in our mouths.

How do I let the word of Christ dwell in me richly? Think of a guest you love coming to stay, not a lodger you put up with. Open the door daily. Read some Scripture most days, slowly, asking what it shows you of Christ; a little read well settles deeper than a lot skimmed. Keep it with you. Carry one verse through the day and learn some by heart, so it is there in the queue, the car and the sleepless hour. Let it answer back. Turn what you read into prayer, and let it question your plans, fears and grudges. Do it together. Sit under preaching, talk about the sermon afterwards, and be ready both to give a word to a friend and to receive one. None of this earns his favour. Through his word the living Lord speaks to his sheep (John 10:27), and he and his Father make their home with those who keep it (John 14:23); letting it dwell richly is simply living in the home he has made.

How do I know if a song is good to sing? Ask whether the word of Christ dwells in it richly. Is it true to Scripture about God, Christ, sin and grace? Is it about God more than my feelings, though feelings are welcome? Does it plant truth in the heart? Can a congregation sing it together, or is it a performance to watch? Does it lead to thankfulness? Old or new, simple or complex, what matters is whether it carries Christ’s word to the heart.

Where Christians differ: what should churches sing? Some Reformed churches hold to exclusive psalmody, singing only the inspired Psalms in worship. They note that all three words, psalms, hymns and songs, appear in the titles of the Greek Psalter, and that only inspired songs are fit for God’s worship. Others sing a wide range of songs. This commentary’s view: the Psalms should have a central place in Christian worship, and many churches would be richer for singing far more of them. But the three terms most naturally describe a variety of songs, and the New Testament itself contains early Christian songs about Christ (1:15–20; Philippians 2:6–11; 1 Timothy 3:16). Churches may sing new songs that are faithful to Scripture and centred on Christ; the test is whether the word of Christ dwells richly in what is sung. Those who hold to exclusive psalmody do so out of reverence for God’s word, and they deserve to be honoured as brothers.

Uncertain wording. No one can now draw a sharp line between psalms, hymns and spiritual songs; the words overlap, and Paul probably piles them up to cover every kind of song. “With thankfulness” is literally in grace: with gratitude, as the ESV takes it, or by God’s grace at work in the heart. And “in all wisdom” may belong with the word dwelling rather than with the teaching. None of these choices changes the sense of the verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word and every deed of a believer’s life is to be done as Christ’s representative, with thanks to the Father through him. This sums up the whole section, and there is no secular corner walled off from Christ.

Whatever you do. Word and deed are the two halves that cover the whole of life: not merely the religious parts, but the entire ordinary round of work, family, meals and rest.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. To act in someone’s name is to act as his representative: under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him. So you drive the van, pay the bill and speak the word as Christ’s representative, by his help and in a manner that would not shame his name. This makes ordinary tasks holy and rules out sinful ones, for you cannot do in his name what dishonours it: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Not a fence but a lordship. The false teachers wanted a fence of external rules: “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (2:21). Paul gives instead the lordship of Christ, reaching into every word and deed from the inside. Rules cover the situations someone thought of in advance; his name covers the rest. Yet the heart prefers the fence, because a list can be ticked off, leaving us safe, in control and with God in our debt. A Lord cannot be completed like a list. He asks not for a list kept but for a life given, and the only way to give it gladly is to know that he gave his life first.

Giving thanks through him. The third call to thanksgiving closes the paragraph. Our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator: the quiet final answer to the angel mediators of chapter 2. No other channel is needed, and none is allowed (1 Timothy 2:5). He did everything in his Father’s name, in the carpenter’s shop, at sinners’ tables, asleep in a boat and dying on a cross, and all of it was worship. Now he takes our clumsy words and ordinary deeds, cleanses them, and carries them to the Father as offerings.

In everyday life. Take the most ordinary task you have today, and before you start it, say quietly: “Lord Jesus, I do this as yours.” Then do it well, and thank the Father for it when it is done. You may find that the task has not changed, but you have.

What about the parts of my life that seem to have nothing to do with Jesus? There are none that he has excused himself from. A spreadsheet, a nappy, the lawn, a football match: all can be done in his name, honestly and gratefully. Ask two questions: could I thank God for this, and could I do it with Christ beside me? If yes, do it heartily and enjoy it as his gift. If no, the verse has just answered the question for you. And if there is a part of your life you would rather he did not see, that is the part this verse is most kindly aimed at.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s lordship reaches into the home, and everyone in it answers to him. Paul addresses each member directly, as a person who stands before Christ: wives and husbands (vv. 18–19), children and fathers (vv. 20–21), slaves and masters (3:22–4:1). Those under authority serve as to the Lord; those who hold power receive the harder, restraining command, to love and not be harsh, not to provoke, to treat justly, knowing that they too have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household

The household code shows that there is no corner of life outside Christ’s rule. The Lord praised in the hymn of chapter 1 is Lord of marriage, parenting and daily work; Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is what 3:17 means in practice. A faithful spouse, a patient parent and an honest worker are living out their theology in its most concrete form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In the Roman household the father held near-absolute legal power over children and slaves. Paul does not abolish the structure, but he fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. Now: The same witness shows wherever a Christian works honestly when no one is checking, treats employees fairly, or encourages a child instead of crushing him.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives are to place themselves willingly under their own husbands’ loving leadership, as an act of devotion to Christ. With this verse Paul carries the lordship of v. 17 into the home.

The household code. Greek writers had household codes too, telling the head of a household how to manage his dependants. Paul’s (3:18–4:1, as in Ephesians 5:21–6:9) speaks directly to wives, children and slaves as persons who stand before Christ for themselves, and lays real duties on husbands, fathers and masters, who are themselves under a Master. “In the Lord”, or a phrase like it, appears in almost every line. The household is not a little kingdom under the husband but an outpost of Christ’s kingdom, and everyone in it answers to him. On leadership and submission in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Wives, submit to your husbands. Submit (hypotassō) means to arrange oneself under, and the form is voluntary: the wife does it freely. Nowhere in the New Testament are husbands told to make their wives submit. It is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership, the headship of Ephesians 5:23. And it is to her own husband: one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is respect, support and trust: strengthening his leadership rather than competing with it, and trusting his lead when a real decision must be made and they still differ. Paul frames it as the reflection of something beautiful, the church’s glad submission to Christ (Ephesians 5:24).

As is fitting in the Lord: “do it for my sake”. A friend going abroad asks you to look after his elderly father: “Do it for me.” You really help the father, but for your friend’s sake. “In the Lord” works the same way (see on Ephesians 5:22). A wife really does follow her husband’s lead, but she does it for Christ’s sake. So it is devotion to Christ, not a concession to a husband’s superiority, and it rests on Christ, not shifting custom. And because it is for the Lord, it can never require what the Lord forbids: to sin, to lie, to hide abuse or to give up her faith (Acts 5:29). The same phrase that asks for her submission also guards her. See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

What it does not mean. The wife is not inferior: she is fully equal before God, a fellow heir of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7; Galatians 3:28). Submission is a matter of role, never of value, as the Son is equal to the Father and yet gladly does his will. It is not slavish obedience: tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to obey (vv. 20, 22) but wives to submit, the gentler word. It is not silence or having no voice: she is a strong helper and counterpart (Genesis 2:18) who speaks, advises and may freely disagree, as godly women in Scripture did (Abigail in 1 Samuel 25). And it is never obeying into sin: if a husband demands what God forbids, “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Never a cover for abuse. Submission is not a licence for harshness or abuse, and the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh. A wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger. Abuse, whether physical, sexual, emotional or financial, is a grave sin, and often a crime. A wife who is being abused should seek safety at once, and help from the church and the civil authorities; she is not failing to submit by doing so. Where there is abuse, the church must protect the victim and call the abuser to account, never preach submission to the one being harmed.

In everyday life. Wives, find one way today to honour your husband’s leadership, as to the Lord: a word of thanks, backing a decision you were not sure of. Husbands reading this verse: it was not written to you, and the moment you start quoting it at your wife you have already stopped obeying the next one.

What does it look like in an ordinary marriage? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, and headship and submission rarely come into play. But picture the genuine deadlock over a move or a major purchase: they have prayed and talked it through, they still disagree, and a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it afterwards. Day to day it looks like speaking well of him, not undercutting him in front of the children, and treating him with genuine respect (Ephesians 5:33). The model is Sarah (1 Peter 3:5–6): a woman of strength who freely honoured her husband, not a doormat who had lost her voice.

What if my husband is not a Christian, or does not lead at all? Peter addresses the first case directly: a believing wife may win an unbelieving husband without a word, by her conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2). Her submission is still in the Lord: she never follows him into sin, and keeps her own walk with Christ, her church and her conscience. Where a husband is passive, submission does not mean pretending he leads when he does not. She may lovingly ask him to take responsibility, encourage every step he takes, and pray for him, without either seizing the role in contempt or abandoning the family to drift. And she should not carry it alone: wise counsel from the church can help them both.

Where Christians differ: is a wife’s submission still God’s will? Egalitarian Christians (those who believe husband and wife share leadership equally, without distinct roles) read this in the light of the call to mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21) and Paul’s statement that in Christ there is no male and female (Galatians 3:28). They see the household instructions as a cultural accommodation tied to the ancient world, now outdated, or as mutual only. This commentary’s view: Paul grounds the wife’s submission in the Lord, and elsewhere in creation and in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:3, 8–9). That makes it permanent, not merely cultural. And Paul gives husbands a different command, to love, not to submit. But the wife’s submission is her willing response to her husband’s loving, sacrificial leadership, not a licence for him to dominate. It never requires a wife to sin or to endure abuse. Husband and wife are equal heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), with different callings in the one marriage. Egalitarian believers who hold their view from Scripture are brothers and sisters, and the debate should be carried on with charity.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands are to love their wives with Christ’s self-giving love, and never let their position sour into harshness. The husband leads by giving himself away.

Husbands, love your wives. Love here (agapaō) is the same love as in v. 14. What makes it self-giving is not the word itself but its measure, which Ephesians, sent alongside this letter, spells out: “love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). So the husband’s leadership is defined by sacrifice, not domination. He nourishes and cherishes her as his own body (Ephesians 5:28–29), puts her good ahead of his preferences, provides and listens, and serves in small unglamorous ways, as the Lord himself knelt to wash feet (John 13:5), and keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a promise, not a mood.

Do not be harsh. Do not be embittered (pikrainō, from pikros, bitter): do not grow sharp or sour with your wife. Paul names love’s opposite at once because it is the husband’s characteristic temptation: the strength of his position can curdle into domination, and small resentments can harden into a cold, critical spirit towards the one he should cherish most. Peter adds a sobering reason: a husband who does not live with his wife in an understanding way finds his prayers hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

The familiar clothes of harshness. Harshness wears many disguises: the cutting tone, sarcasm, criticism never satisfied, contempt, silence used as a weapon, winning every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the sin of the man who is pleasant with everyone else and saves his harshness for his wife. The cure is the character of vv. 12–13: compassion, kindness, meekness, patience and a readiness to forgive. A wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves.

A bride who was nothing to look at. The love that defines a husband’s duty was first poured out on a bride who was nothing to look at. Christ loved the church when she was unfaithful, unlovely and in rags, and gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, cleanse her and present her to himself in splendour. Every Christian husband is a small, flawed picture of the greatest Husband there is, and every Christian marriage points to the wedding supper of the Lamb.

What do I do if I have been harsh with my wife? Confess it to God and then to her, plainly and without excuses: not “I’m sorry you felt hurt”, but “I was harsh with you, and it was wrong.” Ask her to tell you, honestly and without punishment, when it happens again, and receive it when she does. Look for the root: usually an expectation she has failed to meet, or a pressure elsewhere you are taking out on her. Bring that to Christ. And if the harshness has become a pattern of control or intimidation, seek help from your pastor and a biblical counsellor at once. That is no longer a bad habit; it is a danger to her.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children are to obey their parents gladly in everything that is not sin, because this pleases the Lord. Paul speaks to the children directly, as real members of the church who were present when the letter was read aloud.

Children, obey. Obey (hypakouō) is built on the verb to hear, and means to heed and do: not merely to feel respect but to act on what is said. For a young child it is glad, prompt obedience, the nursery where a little one first learns to submit to God; for a teenager, keeping the household’s rules and receiving correction without rebellion.

In everything. The sweep is wide, but not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s. The parallel reads, “obey your parents in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1), and a child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare: for nearly every child on nearly every day it means obey, gladly, even when you do not see the reason.

Obedience and honour. For the grown child with his own household, the duty changes. The duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires; it is the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2; Exodus 20:12). The adult child no longer takes orders, but he never stops respecting his parents and providing for them as they age (1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

For this pleases the Lord. Literally, this is well pleasing in the Lord. Above all, an obedient child walks in the footsteps of the great obedient Son, who said, “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), and who became “obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8). He was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51), so an obedient child bears the family likeness of the Son. And underneath, obedience to parents is obedience to God, who set them over the child.

The Lord of glory once had a bedtime. He learned his letters, carried water, swept the workshop and did what he was told, and every hidden hour of it pleased his Father. He obeyed perfectly where we have not, and that obedience is counted to every child of God who trusts him, so that the smallest believer in the house is clothed in the obedience of the eternal Son. He became a child so that children might become the sons and daughters of God.

In everyday life. Children, obey cheerfully today, the first time you are asked. And if you are grown, ring your parents this week, or visit, and ask what you can do for them. Honour does not retire.

What it does not mean. Children are not to obey parents who abuse them; a child who is being harmed should tell a trusted adult. And adult children make their own decisions before God, especially within their own marriages (Genesis 2:24).

What about a child whose parents are not Christians? The command still holds, and may shine brighter there. A Christian child or teenager in an unbelieving home is to obey and honour his parents in everything that is not sin, and his cheerful obedience can be one of the most powerful testimonies they ever see. Where a parent forbids something God commands, such as faith in Christ itself, the child must follow Christ, but respectfully and humbly, without contempt, looking for every lawful way to honour his parents at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers must not exasperate their children with harshness or unfairness, because a child who is constantly provoked loses heart. As with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is given the restraining word.

Fathers, do not provoke your children. To provoke (erethizō) means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment. The parallel puts it sharply: “do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). It is addressed to fathers because they bear the chief responsibility for the home, but it applies to mothers as well. The ways to provoke are many: harshness, unfairness, favouritism, punishing in temper, hypocrisy, cold neglect.

Lest they become discouraged. To become discouraged (athymeō) is to lose heart, to have the spirit go out of you. It shows in a little child’s tears and timidity, in a school child who gives up (“I will never be good enough for him”), in a teenager’s rebellion or joyless compliance. Fathers are responsible for the spirit they create in the home.

The Father who sets the pattern. The earthly father is to father as God fathers his own: “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). God disciplines but never crushes, firm and tender (Ephesians 3:14–15; Hebrews 12:7–11), and the Christian father parents as a dearly loved child of that Father, passing on the grace he has received.

Arms that blessed children. The Father’s heart towards children has been shown in the face of his Son (John 14:9). When the disciples tried to send children away, Jesus was indignant and said, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them.” Then he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them (Mark 10:14, 16). He never treated a child as an interruption, and kept some of his sternest words for anyone who causes a little one to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
