A father who wants to know how not to provoke his children has only to watch the Son with them.

Across the years. A young child is provoked by a sharp tongue over the spilled cup and rules that change with his father’s mood; he needs gentleness, clear boundaries held with warmth, and expectations that fit his age. A school-age child is provoked by constant criticism, comparison with a sibling and praise that never comes; he needs his honest effort noticed, and fair discipline with reasons. A teenager is provoked by control that will not loosen, endless lecturing, and “because I said so” where a reason was owed; he needs trust and responsibility to grow together, a father who listens, and above all to be pointed to Christ, not merely to a rulebook. Even a grown child can be provoked by a father who still dictates; now the good way is to advise when asked, and to bless rather than control.

What it does not mean. Fathers are not to give up discipline. They must discipline; a father who never corrects his child does not love him (Hebrews 12:7–11; Proverbs 13:24). But discipline must be loving, fair, controlled, and aimed at the child’s good, never at venting the father’s anger. And it never means violence that injures, terrifies or humiliates a child; that is abuse, not discipline.

Is it too late if I have provoked my children? No. One of the most powerful things a father can do is go to his child, whether six or forty-six, and say: “I was wrong, I was too harsh, I am sorry, will you forgive me?” Many grown children have waited their whole lives to hear it. It does not undo the past, but it often opens a door that has been shut for years, and it shows the child the gospel in a way no lecture could. Then change the pattern, with God’s help and counsel if needed. The Father in heaven delights to redeem what earthly fathers have damaged.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slaves are to serve their masters wholeheartedly, as working for Christ, who sees everything, will give them the inheritance, and judges every wrong without favouritism. Paul addresses them as full members of the church, responsible before Christ for themselves.

Bondservants, obey. Bondservant means slave (doulos). Slaves were a large share of the empire and probably of the early church; Onesimus, returning to Philemon with this letter, was one (4:7–9). “Obey in everything” means doing what the master lawfully directs, and doing it thoroughly. It never means obeying into sin, for the Lord outranks every master. And earthly masters, literally masters according to the flesh, are masters only on the passing, earthly level. On authority and submission at work and elsewhere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Not by way of eye-service. Eye-service (ophthalmodoulia, a word Paul may have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you: busy when watched and idle when his back is turned. It has not aged a day: looking busy when the manager passes, gaming the figures, skimping the task nobody sees. The gospel has no room for “as long as nobody is looking”, because Someone always is.

Sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. An undivided heart, the same whether watched or not, because the Lord is now the audience of your work. We tend to think of fear and love as opposites, but the Bible holds them together. To fear the Lord is to be so gripped by how great, holy and real he is that his verdict on you matters more than anyone else’s. Everyone lives before some audience they fear, and whatever you fear most will run your life. Paul does not tell this slave to fear his master but to fear the Lord, and that sets him free, because if Christ’s verdict is the one that counts, no master’s verdict can own you.

Not a criminal’s dread. Not a criminal’s dread of sentence, for the sentence has fallen on Christ (see on v. 6). “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). The more you see what your forgiveness cost him, the more you tremble, not for fear of being thrown out, but because you are so loved. Before the corner is cut or the sharp email is sent, the question is not “Will anyone notice?” but “Will this please the Lord who is with me and who died for me?” See also Fear of God in the Theological Dictionary.

Work heartily. Work from the soul, as the Greek puts it, not skipping the menial or unseen task. Drudgery becomes worship, because you are working not for the man who signs your orders but for the Lord, and a mean master cannot rob a floor swept for Jesus of its glory (Ephesians 6:7). The Reformers drew from this the dignity of every lawful calling: the maid sweeping a room serves God as truly as the minister in the pulpit. In plain words, “as for the Lord and not for men” means do it for my sake (see the note on v. 18, and As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary).

The inheritance as your reward. Under Roman law a slave owned nothing in his own right and could inherit nothing; inheritances went to sons. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance, the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). The man who can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God; the Lord sees and will repay. Yet it is not wages earned: you receive it as a son, by grace, God crowning the very service his own grace enabled.

You are serving the Lord Christ. The lowliest labour, done in faith, is service to Christ (Matthew 25:40). There is no higher title in the universe than servant of the Lord Christ, and Paul hands it to the people at the very bottom of Roman society.

No partiality. The warning cuts both ways: the slave’s low place does not excuse lazy or spiteful work, and the master (4:1) who wrongs his servant will not escape. God plays no favourites (Romans 2:11). He weighs the deed, not the rank, and the powerful cannot buy their way out of judgment.

Roman slavery and ours. Roman slavery was harsh, and nothing here excuses it. But it was not the race-based slavery of the later Atlantic trade. People became slaves by capture, by birth or through debt, and many were educated, held some money, and could in time be freed. Paul is not blessing the system; elsewhere he quietly undermines it: “if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity” (1 Corinthians 7:21); he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10); and he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). He teaches believers to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve. What these verses say about how to work carries straight across to any modern job; the conditions of slavery do not.

The price of a slave. The Lord Christ himself took the form of a slave. He who flung the stars into space knelt with a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then was sold for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). He served without eye-service, for no audience but his Father, and he was paid with a cross. Because he did, the servant who owns nothing and is invisible to the great of this world is the heir of all things.

What it does not mean. Slavery is not good, and the Bible does not endorse the trade that later carried millions from Africa in chains. Scripture condemns man-stealing as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10), and Christians who used these verses to defend that trade twisted them. Nor must a worker accept abuse, fraud or unsafe conditions without seeking redress. The verses mean that within whatever situation God has placed him, the believer serves Christ with an undivided heart.

How does this apply to my job today? Directly: your employer has lawful authority over your work. So work as well when the manager is on holiday as when he is in the room. Do not pad your hours, take credit for others’ work, or skimp on what nobody checks. If your boss is unfair, you may seek a fairer job, raise concerns properly, or use lawful means of redress; Paul encouraged slaves to gain their freedom where they could. But while you are there, your work is for the Lord, and he is the one keeping the record.

What if my work feels meaningless? Then this passage was written for you, to people who did the most repetitive, unseen and unrewarded work in the empire. Meaning in work does not come only from the task; it comes from the One you are doing it for. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch, the parent changing the same nappy for the fifth time today: when it is done for the Lord, it is laid into the hands of the King. Your foreman may never say thank you. The Lord is keeping account, and he forgets nothing.
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.

keyVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter rests on this verse. Its “if” means since: believers are already raised with Christ, so their seeking flows from a union already made, not from an effort to reach him. The putting off, the putting on and the life of the household all come from minds set where Christ is seated.

3.reflection:
Paul’s cure for sin is not more rules (2:23) but union with the risen Christ (vv. 1–4). Why are rules alone powerless against sin, and what difference does it make to fight a sin knowing your life is already hidden with Christ in God?

Verse 5 names sins of the appetites; verse 8 names sins of the temper and the tongue, which respectable church members can commit for years without anyone calling them sin. Which list do you tend to take more seriously, and why?

Verses 12–14 describe Christ’s own character as clothes to put on, and call us to forgive “as the Lord has forgiven you”. Which of these garments is hardest for you to wear at home or in church just now, and how does remembering his forgiveness of you help?

In 3:18–4:1 every member of the household answers to the Lord, and those who hold power are given the restraining command. How would doing everything “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (v. 17) change one ordinary relationship or task in your week?

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter of the letter. Verse 1 completes the household code begun at 3:18; then Paul turns from the home to prayer and to the watching world, and closes with news, greetings and his own signature.

The message. The Christ who fills all things rules the ordinary places too. Those with power answer to a Master in heaven. A church that knows Christ is enough shows it by depending on him in prayer and by commending him to outsiders with wise lives and gracious words. And the gospel this letter has preached is not an idea but a family: real people, a runaway slave, a restored deserter, a praying pastor, a woman who opens her home, bound together in Christ and kept by grace.

Why it was said. The Colossians were being offered a religion for an inner circle, of visions, rules and secret wisdom (see the introduction). Paul’s closing words point outward instead: to God in plain, persistent prayer, to unbelievers in everyday conduct, and to the wider church, whose members they are to greet and welcome. And the man writing is in chains.

How the chapter makes its case. First, masters are told to treat slaves justly and fairly, because they too have a Master (v. 1). Then two closing commands: keep praying, watchful and thankful, and pray for Paul’s preaching, that God will open a door and give him clarity (vv. 2–4); and walk wisely toward outsiders, buying up every opportunity, with speech gracious and seasoned with salt (vv. 5–6). Last comes a page of names that shows the gospel in human form, from the runaway now called a beloved brother to the restored deserter and the friend who would later leave; one man is charged to finish his ministry, and Paul signs with his chained hand, his last word grace (vv. 7–18).

Where it leads. Every name on the page is a small picture of what Christ has done. A runaway is welcomed home because someone said, charge it to my account. A deserter is restored and writes the Gospel of the Servant who never deserted. The letter that began with Christ over all creation ends with Christ over a few house churches in a small valley, and grace has the first word and the last.

For us. Pray as if everything depends on God, because it does. Treat everyone under your authority as someone whose Master is also yours. Speak to unbelievers with grace and salt. And look around your own church: people you would never otherwise have met, given to you as family. Welcome the ones who have failed, finish what you were given, and live inside grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters must treat those under them with justice and fairness, because they too answer to a Master in heaven. The household code (3:18–4:1) ends by reminding the one with the most power that he too is under authority.

Masters. Masters (kyrioi) is the very same word as Lord. In the Roman world a master could command, punish and sell his slaves, and in law even kill them; Aristotle had called a slave a living tool (on the background, see slavery in the ancient world). Household duties ran one way, from slave up to master; Paul quietly overturns the order by laying an obligation on the masters.

Justly and fairly. Justly (dikaios) means giving what is due: honest dealing, fair provision, discipline that is not arbitrary. Fairly (isotēs) is literally equality, or equity: even-handed treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is your equal and your brother. This went far beyond anything Roman law asked: the slave is a person to whom justice is owed. Think of Philemon, a master in this very church, about to be told to welcome Onesimus back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

A Master in heaven. Here is the whole motive: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man at the top of the earthly ladder is himself a servant. Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up: you will answer to the Lord above you, with whom there is no partiality, for how you treat those beneath you (3:25; Ephesians 6:9). The law of Moses had said it of a fellow Israelite who had become a servant: “You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43).

Side by side at one throne. Master and slave kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made them both and the Saviour who bought them both. The Christian who holds authority wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder.

What does this look like for an employer or manager today? The old temptation survives: to see workers as replaceable parts valued only for their output. Justice and fairness look like a fair wage paid on time, honest contracts kept, safe conditions, no favouritism, and no treating people as disposable when it is convenient. They look like discipline by principle rather than mood, the same dignity for the night cleaner as for the senior partner, honesty about people’s position and a hearing for their grievances. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town, because he knows whose servant he is.

What if I have power over others but not as an employer? Teachers over pupils, officers over soldiers, landlords over tenants, carers over the vulnerable, church leaders over congregations: wherever you hold power over someone, you hold it on loan from the Master in heaven. Ask of every use of it whether you would be glad to explain it to him. Power is not sinful; it is a stewardship, and the Lord pays particular attention to how the strong treat the weak.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pray steadily for the gospel’s advance, and live and speak so that outsiders meet Christ in you. Paul’s closing commands face two ways. Toward God: keep praying, awake and thankful (v. 2), and pray for Paul, that God will open doors for the word and give him clarity to make Christ plain, though he is in chains (vv. 3–4). Toward outsiders: walk wisely among them, buying up every opportunity (v. 5), with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt, ready to give each person a fitting answer (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steady Devotion, Not Occasional Request

The verb Paul uses for continuing in prayer is the one Acts uses of the first church (see the note on v. 2). Prayer is not an emergency measure but the ordinary stance of creatures who depend on their Creator. A church that keeps at it shows that it knows its need.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In prison, Paul could not open doors for the gospel himself. He could pray, and ask the Colossians to pray with him, leaving the gospel’s advance in the hands of the One who controls it. Now: A church that wants to reach the lost but neglects praying together has forgotten where open doors come from.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep on praying, alert and thankful, because everything you need must come from God. A letter about the sufficiency of Christ fittingly ends on prayer, the plain confession of that dependence.

Continue steadfastly in prayer. To continue steadfastly (proskartereō) is to keep at something doggedly. It is the word used of the first church, who devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:42). That Paul must command it tells us steadfast prayer is hard. It is hidden labour, answers seem slow, we tire easily, and an enemy would rather we did anything else. It was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, to show “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). The Spirit who taught you to call God Father keeps you at it (Galatians 4:6).

Being watchful in it. To watch (grēgoreō) is to stay awake, like a sentry who dare not doze. It carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said, “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). To be watchful is to pray awake: alert to what needs praying for, expectant for God’s answer, and on guard against temptation. Prayer’s great enemy is less hostility than drowsiness.

With thanksgiving. Thankfulness sounds yet again in this short letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15–17), now woven right into prayer. It keeps prayer from collapsing into demands or complaint. We do not come to wring favours from a reluctant stranger, but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son (Philippians 4:6; Romans 8:32).

Jesus kept watch alone. In the garden the disciples slept, and Jesus kept watch alone. He watched and prayed so that his drowsy people might be kept, and the one who keeps his people neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). We have a Saviour who stayed awake for us, and a door into the Father’s presence that no drowsiness of ours can close.

In everyday life. Pray today for one thing you have stopped praying for because the answer seemed slow, and begin with thanks before you ask.

What can I do when my mind wanders every time I pray? Many believers find this; it does not make you unfit to pray. Try praying aloud, quietly, or writing your prayers down. Pray with an open Bible, turning a psalm into prayer phrase by phrase, and keep a short list of people and needs. When your mind drifts, do not scold yourself; turn the distraction into a prayer and come back. And the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding for us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

Does persistent prayer change God’s mind? God is not reluctant or uninformed. But he has decided that many of his purposes will be carried out through the prayers of his people, so prayer really does bring things about in his world, though it never forces his hand. Persistence is not wearing him down but depending on him, and in the waiting he often changes us. Keep asking, and trust him to answer as a wise Father: sometimes yes, sometimes wait, and sometimes with something better than you asked.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray that God will give Paul openings for the gospel and the clarity to make Christ plain. A man in chains asks not for an open prison door but for an open door for the word.

Pray also for us. The apostle once caught up into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2–4) leans on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers (Romans 15:30). No Christian outgrows his need of others’ prayers, and the humblest believer’s prayers truly count. Your prayers for your pastor are no formality.

A door for the word. The open door is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Corinthians 16:9; Acts 14:27). It is God who opens it, not our cleverness. Paul’s freedom is not his first concern; the gospel’s is. He could write elsewhere that he was “bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!” (2 Timothy 2:9).

The mystery of Christ. A mystery in Paul is not a puzzle but a secret long hidden in the heart of God and now thrown open: “Christ in you, the hope of glory”, for Gentiles as well as Jews (1:26–27). The gospel is not a secret technique for an inner circle, as the false teachers offered, but a Person: God’s mystery, which is Christ (2:2).

On account of which I am in prison. Paul names the reason for his chains without self-pity or complaint. He looks past the magistrates to the sovereign hand behind them, calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1), and from a cell could write, “what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12). That is what believing in God’s sovereignty looks like: peace where there might have been bitterness.

That I may make it clear. An open door needs a clear word. The verb (phaneroō) means to reveal, to make plain. Even this gifted preacher does not rely on his own skill; he asks for prayer that he will be clear, as he ought to speak.

Doors that no one can shut. The word Paul longed to declare is the Word himself, made flesh, whom no chain could bind. They bound Jesus, nailed him down and sealed his tomb, and on the third day he walked out. The Lord who holds the keys of death and Hades opens doors that no one can shut (Revelation 3:8), and his gospel cannot be imprisoned.

What about my own prisons? Most of us have our own confinements: unjust treatment, a shut door, an illness, a hardship that will not lift. Do we grumble, or trust the sovereign hand and ask how Christ might be made known even here? The hospital ward or the job you cannot leave may be where God has opened a door for the word. Pray for release if you wish, and pray first for the door.

How do I pray for missionaries and pastors? Use these verses as your outline. Pray for open doors: real opportunities, people ready to listen, freedom to speak. Pray for clarity in explaining Christ, for boldness, as Paul asked in the parallel (Ephesians 6:19–20), and for contentment in hardship. Then ask them what they need, and pray specifically. A missionary’s newsletter is a prayer list in disguise.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live wisely among unbelievers, and seize every opening God gives you to commend Christ. Paul has asked them to pray for his witness (vv. 3–4); now he turns to theirs.

Walk in wisdom toward outsiders. Outsiders are the non-Christians around them, and the world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it (1 Thessalonians 4:12; 1 Peter 2:12). “Walk” is the whole conduct of life, and “in wisdom” means with the skill and tact that come from Christ, in whom all wisdom is hidden (2:3). It looks like integrity, kindness, a life that disarms criticism, and the tact to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. It avoids two ditches: compromise, blending in until no one can tell the difference, and the sour, judgmental superiority the world rightly recoils from.

Making the best use of the time. Literally, buying up the opportunity (exagorazomai ton kairon). The word for time is not the ticking clock (chronos) but the opportune moment (kairos), the open window. The picture is a merchant snapping up a bargain: seizing every God-given opening before it passes, because the days are evil (Ephesians 5:16). The window with this neighbour may not come again.

The only offence. Christ crucified is a stumbling block to some and folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Paul would not remove that offence for anyone (Galatians 5:11). But he took great care that nothing else, no rudeness, hypocrisy or foolishness of ours, should stand in its way. If outsiders stumble, let it be over Christ and not over us. The opposite danger is real too: often what keeps us quiet is not wisdom but the wish to be liked. The cure is to care more about Christ’s approval than theirs (Galatians 1:10), and the believer who already has it, by grace, is free to speak. Your daily conduct before unbelieving colleagues is itself an argument, for Christ or against him.

He never wasted a moment. Christ walked in perfect wisdom among outsiders. He ate with tax collectors, spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well, touched lepers and welcomed children. He never wasted a moment, and he never forced one, and every opportunity we are given to speak of him was bought by the life he spent for us.

In everyday life. Name one unbeliever you see regularly. Pray for them by name, ask God for one opportunity this week, and when it comes, buy it up.

How do I spot an opportunity without forcing one? Listen more than you speak. Opportunities usually arrive as questions, griefs or crises: a death in the family, a question about how you stay calm, a confessed fear. The window is often a single sentence, and the wise response a single sentence back, honest, gentle and brief, leaving a door open: “Can I tell you what has helped me?” Pray that God would put such moments in your path and make you notice them; then take them, and leave the result to him.

If I am shy, am I failing at this? No. Walking in wisdom is first a matter of how you live, and an honest, kind, faithful shy believer is already speaking loudly. A card to a grieving neighbour, an invitation to a carol service, a book given with a short note, a quiet answer when asked why you believe: these are open to anyone, and God has used quiet people in countless conversions no one outside heaven has heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let all your speech be kind and full of flavour, so that you can give each person the answer that fits. Gracious, salted speech is the soil; a fitting answer is the fruit.

Always gracious. All your talk, not only religious talk. Gracious, literally with grace, means kind and winsome, not harsh, sarcastic or preachy, speech that gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29), as the gracious words of Jesus drew the crowds (Luke 4:22).

Seasoned with salt. Salt gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling, and Greek writers used salt as a picture of wit. So salted speech has savour and substance, worth listening to, and it is wholesome, not corrupt or coarse. This is not the modern “salty” speech, which is crude.

Grace and salt together. Grace without salt is kind but bland; salt without grace is clever but cruel. The Christian’s tongue is to be both: answering a hostile remark with unexpected kindness, seasoning a hard truth so it can be heard, and trading the coarse joke and the sour complaint for words that build people up.

How you ought to answer each person. Not a canned formula fired at everyone, but an answer suited to this person’s question, objection and need. Peter says the same: always be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Winsome everyday words draw people to ask; harsh or dull talk shuts the conversation down. You need no sermon by heart, only a gracious, salted tongue and a heart ready with a fitting word (Proverbs 15:23). Wisdom listens before it speaks.

No one ever spoke like this man! Grace was poured upon his lips; he silenced his accusers and comforted sinners in the same afternoon. He answered the rich young ruler, the woman at the well and the thief on the cross each in the way that fitted, and every word was true and every word was kind. The Word made flesh is full of grace and truth, and he is teaching our clumsy tongues to speak with his accent.

What if someone asks a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly. “I don’t know, but I would like to find out” is a gracious answer, and it often opens a second conversation. You need not win every argument, only give a reason for your hope, and the simplest is often the strongest: what Christ has done for you. Then find out, ask your pastor, and come back. Humble honesty usually moves people more than a quick reply for everything.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel Paul has preached comes home in real people, bound together as one family in Christ. Paul sends Tychicus with news and encouragement, and with him Onesimus, a runaway slave now called a faithful and beloved brother (vv. 7–9). He passes on greetings from his companions: Aristarchus his fellow prisoner, Mark the restored deserter, Epaphras wrestling in prayer, Luke who stayed and Demas who would leave (vv. 10–14). He greets Laodicea and the church in Nympha’s house, asks for his letters to be shared, and gives one charge, to Archippus (vv. 15–17). Then he signs with his chained hand: remember my chains; grace be with you (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ in Named People

The list of names puts flesh on 1:18, where Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstraction; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. That is why Reformed teaching has stressed the visible local church: not an ideal church somewhere, but these people, in this place.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The runaway slave Onesimus is commended to the church as a “faithful and beloved brother” (on how the teaching of 3:11 walks through the door, see the note on v. 9). Now: The church is still a gathering of people who would never otherwise share a room, brought to the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends Tychicus, a trusted brother, to bring the Colossians his news and to strengthen their hearts. The roll call of names that begins here is not filler but a photograph of the gospel at work.

Tychicus will tell you. Tychicus was a native of Asia (Acts 20:4) who carried these pages to Colossae with Onesimus beside him, and the letter we call Ephesians on the same journey (Ephesians 6:21–22). Listen to Paul’s words in this list: beloved brother, faithful minister, fellow servant, fellow prisoner, a comfort to me. Not colleagues but family.

Beloved, faithful, fellow servant. Beloved brother: family. Faithful minister: dependable service, the word from which we get deacon. Fellow servant: partnership, literally fellow slave, standing beside Paul under the same Master.

For this very purpose. Tychicus has two jobs, and the second is the larger: news of Paul for a church anxious about him, and then to encourage their hearts, the longing Paul expressed for them in 2:2. Scripture reaches most people through somebody, and the messenger’s character is not incidental to the message. Paul could have sent a courier. He sent a brother.

As the Father has sent me. Behind Paul’s sending of Tychicus stands a greater sending. The Father sent the Son into the world not to condemn it but to save it (John 3:17), and the risen Jesus said, “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). A messenger who travels a long road to encourage hearts does in small what Christ did in full: coming in person, at cost, to people who needed more than a letter. The Lord of glory did not send instructions from a distance; he came himself, the message and the messenger one and the same.

In everyday life. Think of the Tychicus in your own church, the person who sets up chairs, drives the elderly, sends the news, and thank them this week.

Why does sharing news matter in the church? Because the church is a family. Paul thought it worth a long, dangerous journey for the Colossians to hear how he was. News is the raw material of prayer and love: you cannot pray for someone whose circumstances you never hear about, or rejoice with someone whose joys are never shared. Prayer letters, news after the service, a visit to someone housebound: these knit the body together and encourage hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A runaway slave comes home to Colossae as a faithful and beloved brother, a full member of the church. The teaching of 3:11 walks through the door on two legs.

Onesimus. Onesimus was a slave in the household of Philemon, a member of the Colossian church. He had almost certainly run away (the usual reading of Philemon), and in Roman law a runaway could be branded, flogged, or worse. In his flight he had met Paul in prison and been converted (Philemon 10). Now he walks back into the town he fled, carrying a letter to his master.

Our faithful and beloved brother. The congregation knew him as somebody’s runaway property. Paul says not a word about his legal position, but gives him almost the very words he has just used of Tychicus (v. 7), very likely a free man and Paul’s own delegate. His standing in the church has changed long before his standing in law.

Who is one of you. He is not an outsider being tolerated but a member of that church, with the same standing as the man who owns him, and Paul states it in a public letter that would be read aloud in the room where Philemon was sitting.

The doctrine walking through the door. Set this beside 3:11: “Here there is not Greek and Jew … slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.” Paul stages no revolt against Rome’s slave system; he does something slower and more corrosive to it, giving a runaway and a delegate the same titles. And there is a gentle play on the name, which Paul makes openly in Philemon 11: Onesimus means useful. Formerly he was useless, Paul says, but now he is indeed useful.

Charge that to my account. Onesimus walked home with a letter that said charge it to my account, and in that sentence the whole gospel was written small. We were runaways from our Master, and the Son of God said to the Father: if he owes you anything, charge it to me. He paid what we had stolen and more, and sent us home with a new name, the useless made useful, outcasts made family.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul excused Onesimus’s wrong. The letter to Philemon shows that he sought reconciliation and offered to make restitution himself: “If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (Philemon 18). Grace did not pretend the wrong had not happened.

What should a church do with a new believer who has a criminal past? Receive him as Paul received Onesimus: a faithful and beloved brother, not a project or a risk to be managed in whispers. That does not mean ignoring wisdom. Where there is a real danger to others, especially to children, safeguards are a form of love, and a genuinely repentant person will understand them. Where restitution is owed, it should be made, as Paul arranged. But the man’s name in the church is no longer his record. Do not remind him of his past, introduce him by it, or hold him at arm’s length. Christ has not.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the church at Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three Jewish fellow workers send greetings, among them Mark, once a deserter and now restored, whom the church is to welcome.

Aristarchus my fellow prisoner. Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4). He had been seized by the mob in the theatre at Ephesus (Acts 19:29) and had sailed with Paul on the voyage that ended in shipwreck (Acts 27:2). Now he shares Paul’s custody. The word Paul uses (synaichmalōtos) is literally fellow prisoner of war, a man captured alongside him in the same campaign. (In Philemon 23 the title goes to Epaphras, so perhaps they took turns.) We would never have known him but for a greeting, a man who followed the apostle into a riot, a shipwreck and a cell.

Mark the cousin of Barnabas. This phrase is the sound of a wound healing: this is the John Mark who abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through the first missionary journey and went home (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas wanted to take him again, Paul refused, and the disagreement was sharp enough to end the two men’s partnership (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul writes ahead to make sure Mark gets a warm reception.

Welcome him. A church that had heard the story might be wary. Near the very end Paul will send for him: “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). Grace does not discard those who have failed. It restores them, and it restores the people they failed too, for Paul’s own heart had to change toward Mark.

Jesus who is called Justus. Jesus was a common Jewish name, the Greek form of Joshua, and this man also used the Roman name Justus. He is otherwise unknown, remembered for ever because he stood by Paul.

The only men of the circumcision. Only three Jewish believers in Paul’s circle, and the word only carries a quiet ache from the man who could wish himself accursed for the sake of his kinsmen (Romans 9:3). Some Jewish believers opposed his mission to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:4), and many of his own people worked against him (Acts 21:27–28).

Fellow workers for the kingdom of God. Some conclude the kingdom is not the church’s present business, that it belongs to Israel or waits wholly in the future. Its full visible glory is indeed still to come. But these men are, right now, fellow workers for it, and God has already transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (1:13). So the kingdom is already here, wherever Christ is acknowledged as King, and not yet complete: its fullness waits for his return. We live in it now and labour for its advance (Romans 14:17; Acts 28:31).

A comfort to me. Comfort here is a medical term (parēgoria, found only here in the New Testament), the root behind paregoric, a soothing medicine. These men were medicine to Paul’s soul. He was no self-sufficient hero; he needed friends, and said so.

The Gospel a restored man wrote. The early church held that this Mark wrote the second Gospel, and it bears the marks of a man who knew both failure and grace. It does not spare the disciples (when Jesus was arrested, “they all left him and fled”, Mark 14:50), yet it records the angel’s message at the empty tomb: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). The Lord chose a deserter to write the Gospel of the Servant who never deserted, and the welcome Paul asks for him is simply the risen Christ’s way with those who have failed him, passed on.

He went into the dark without a comforter. When Jesus was bound, no Aristarchus stood beside him. He went into the dark without a comforter, so that none of his servants would ever be without one. Now the King makes the failures, the fearful and the forgotten his fellow workers, and as his sufferings overflow to his people, so through him their comfort overflows too (2 Corinthians 1:5).

In everyday life. Is there a Mark in your life, someone who let you down and whom you have quietly written off? Ask whether God is asking you to welcome him back.

If I have failed in serving God, can I be used again? Yes. Mark deserted in the middle of a mission and became the man Paul asked for at the end of his life. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored by the lakeside to feed his sheep. God’s grace is not only for the start of the Christian life but for its failures along the way. Be honest about what happened, put right what you can, accept that trust may take time to rebuild, and take up whatever service is put in front of you, however small. The question is not whether you have failed but whether you will let him restore you.

Uncertain wording. We do not know what the “instructions” about Mark were, who sent them, or when they arrived; Paul assumes the Colossians already have them. Most likely they were an earlier message, from Paul or another leader, commending Mark in case he came their way, and the words in brackets sum them up: if he comes to you, welcome him.
verseByVerse.note: Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras, the church’s own founder, wrestles in prayer for them, that they may stand firm, grown up and fully sure in all God’s will. His prayer is the whole letter distilled into one petition.

Epaphras, who is one of you. Without Epaphras there would be no church at Colossae: he first brought them the gospel. Paul called him “a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf” (1:7), and his report prompted this letter. Here Paul calls him a servant of Christ Jesus, literally slave (doulos), a title Paul uses of himself (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1) and in this letter gives to no other individual.

Always struggling. Struggling (agōnizomai) is the athlete’s straining word, the root of our word “agony”, used of a wrestler in the contest; Paul used it of his own labour (1:29; 2:1). We think of intercession as the least strenuous thing a Christian does. Epaphras, far from home and able to do nothing else for these people, is in combat. The person who says “all I can do is pray” has misunderstood which activity is the strenuous one.

Mature and fully assured. Stand: firm, not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). Mature (teleioi): full-grown, the goal Paul named in 1:28. The false teachers offered an advanced inner circle, but Paul’s maturity is not a grade above ordinary Christians; it is the growing up of people already filled in Christ (2:10). Fully assured (peplērophorēmenoi) means carried all the way to settled conviction, not swayed by every new teacher. And all of it in all the will of God: not in secrets for the few, but in the whole will of God made known in his Son.

Laodicea and Hierapolis. Epaphras had evidently cared for the whole Lycus valley, and Paul, who had never been there, vouches for him. Such a word steadies a church’s confidence in its teacher when others are trying to undermine him.

A greater Intercessor. Behind Epaphras on his knees stands a greater Intercessor. In Gethsemane Jesus wrestled in prayer until his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44, verses missing from some early manuscripts though found in many others), and in the upper room he prayed for his disciples and for all who would believe through their word. He still prays at the Father’s right hand that we may stand. The church at Colossae was held up by the prayers of a faithful pastor and by the prayers of the Son of God, and so are we.

What do I actually pray for the people I love? Most of our praying is for circumstances to improve: health, jobs, exams, journeys. God invites such prayers. But Epaphras wrestles for their maturity and assurance. It is a larger ambition than comfort, and it survives whatever happens. Pray it for your children, your friends and your church, using the prayers of 1:9–12 as your words.
verseByVerse.note: Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two companions send greetings: Luke, who would stay to the end, and Demas, who would later desert. Nobody in Colossae could yet have told them apart.

Luke the beloved physician. Luke is, by early and consistent tradition, the author of the third Gospel and Acts, and this is the only place in the New Testament that tells us his trade. It fits his careful research (Luke 1:3) and his warm interest in illness and healing. He is not listed among the men of the circumcision (v. 11), so he was most probably a Gentile, perhaps the only Gentile writer in the New Testament. Where “they” becomes “we” in Acts (from Acts 16:10), he quietly writes himself into the story.

Beloved. Paul had a physical affliction he could not shake (Galatians 4:13–14), and had been flogged, beaten, stoned and shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). Travelling with him for years was a doctor. At the very end, when everyone else had gone, Paul wrote: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). The apostle who healed others by God’s power still travelled with a physician: using doctors and medicine is no lack of faith.

As does Demas. Every other name gets a title; Demas gets his name and nothing else, though here he is still a fellow worker (Philemon 24). The sequel is on record: “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10). Not scandal or heresy, but the ordinary, respectable pull of comfort, safety and a quieter life, stronger than his attachment to a chained old man in Rome. That is how most people leave: not by renouncing the faith but by drifting.

Two loves. A few lines before he writes that Demas loved this present world, Paul speaks of the crown laid up for all who have loved the Lord’s appearing (2 Timothy 4:8, 10). The same verb stands in both places. Demas found something he loved more than the coming of Christ. That is the root of every drift, answered not by trying harder to love the world less, but by seeing more of the one who is coming. Christ who is your life will appear (3:4), and a heart that longs for that day has less room for the pull of this one.

One friend who never deserts. Side by side stand the man who stayed and the man who did not. Let it make us watchful rather than smug, and make us pray that we may stand. And there is one friend who never deserts. When all forsook Paul, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17), and he has promised never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Demas was certainly lost, or that every Christian who goes through a cold or weary season is a Demas. Tiredness and grief are not the love of the world, which rarely announces itself and usually looks perfectly reasonable.

Was Demas a true believer who lost his salvation? Scripture does not tell us his final state, and he may have returned; we should not pronounce on him. If he never returned, the Reformed reading is that he showed he had never truly belonged, for “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). What we do know is that those whom God has truly called and justified, he keeps to the end (Romans 8:30; John 10:28–29). That is the perseverance of the saints: the truly saved continue in faith to the end, and it is his keeping, not the strength of our grip, that guarantees it (Philippians 1:6). The doctrine does not make warnings like this unnecessary, for they are one of the means by which God keeps his people: he warns them, and they take heed.

How do I know if I am drifting like Demas? Watch for the quiet signs rather than the dramatic ones. Prayer becoming rare, then optional. Church slipping from weekly to occasional, always for a good reason. Scripture squeezed out by screens. Decisions about jobs, homes and money made without reference to Christ’s kingdom. A growing irritation with Christians who seem too serious. None alone proves anything; together they are a direction. That you are asking is a sign you have not let go. Do not despair: turn back now, tell a trusted friend, and return to the means of grace, God’s word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the gathering of his people. The Shepherd goes after drifting sheep.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor. Demas later deserted Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets the neighbouring church at Laodicea and Nympha, who opens her home to a congregation. Here is what a first-century church looked like: a room, not a hall.

The brothers at Laodicea. Laodicea keeps appearing in this letter (2:1; 4:13, 16) as Paul knits the valley congregations together: greet them, swap letters with them, pray for them. Brothers here, as often in Paul, includes the sisters.

Nympha. A woman is named, and a congregation meets in her home. For two centuries Christians met in houses, whose owners filled them every week with people who might attract official attention. Nympha had means, and used them. The New Testament names several such women: Lydia at Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40), Priscilla with Aquila (1 Corinthians 16:19), and Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12). The early church would have been homeless without them.

The church in her house. Not an audience but a group small enough to eat together. Bearing with one another and forgiving each other (3:13) meant people who sat in the same room every week and could not avoid one another’s faults. Our arrangements differ; the demand does not. And the Son of Man, who had nowhere to lay his head, has made his home in his people: where two or three gather in his name, he is among them, in every crowded room in Laodicea and every kitchen where believers meet today.

A shadow over Laodicea. A generation later the risen Christ dictates a letter to this same church, rebuking it because it says it is rich, has prospered and needs nothing, not realising that it is wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked (Revelation 3:17). Churches greeted warmly by an apostle can still drift. Yet the risen Lord does not give up: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). The Lord who rebukes them still wants a place at their table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Nympha was the pastor or elder of the church. Hosting a church was a valuable and costly ministry of hospitality, and the New Testament honours it by name; the oversight of the church was given to qualified elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). Christians who read the New Testament as opening church oversight to women see such hosts differently, and they are brothers and sisters; this verse itself tells us nothing about how her church was led.

Could my home be used for the church? Very likely. A kitchen table is enough for a Bible study, a meal for a lonely student, a prayer meeting, or a welcome for a new family. Hospitality is commanded of all believers (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), not only of the gifted. It will cost time and tidiness, and it will sometimes be inconvenient. That is what made Nympha’s gift a gift.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read a man’s name, Nymphas, and “his house”. The feminine reading is better supported, and it is the one most modern translations follow.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s letters were meant to be read aloud to the gathered church and shared between churches. From the beginning they were public words for the whole people of God, not private mail.

Read among you. Read among you means read aloud to the gathered congregation (1 Thessalonians 5:27). For most Christians in history Scripture came in through the ears, in a room full of people, and its public reading is still central to worship (1 Timothy 4:13).

Also in the church of the Laodiceans. Paul expects congregations to swap his letters, copy them and read one another’s. That habit is one of the first stirrings of what became the collected New Testament.

The word of Christ, passed hand to hand. A prisoner’s letter carried such weight because the apostles did not speak on their own authority: Jesus promised that the Spirit would teach them all things and bring to their remembrance all that he had said (John 14:26), and Paul received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12). What the Colossians sent on to Laodicea was the word of Christ (3:16), and in the apostles’ letters the risen Lord still speaks to his churches.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church created Scripture, or gave the books their authority by voting on them. The church recognised the Scriptures God had given, as a child recognises his father’s voice. The authority comes from God who breathed them out, not from the church that received them.

In everyday life. Read Colossians aloud this week in one sitting, as the Colossians first heard it; it takes about fifteen minutes, and you will hear the flow of the argument as never before.

Should I worry that books were left out of the Bible? No. The so-called “lost gospels” were written long after the apostles, usually in the second century or later, and teach what the apostles never taught. The early church did not suppress them out of fear; it recognised that they lacked the apostolic voice. The books we have were received widely and early because they came from the apostles and their companions and agreed with the faith once for all delivered. God, who inspired his word, has also preserved it. You can read your Bible as complete.

Where Christians differ: lost letters and the canon. The canon (the word means a measuring rule) is the list of books that are Scripture, the rule by which the church’s faith is measured. If an apostolic letter is lost, is the New Testament incomplete?

This commentary’s view: no. God in his providence preserved the books he intended for the permanent canon. Not every apostolic letter was meant to be Scripture for all time; or, if the letter from Laodicea is Ephesians, it was not lost at all. The canon is not everything the apostles ever wrote; it is what God caused to be kept, and it is complete and sufficient for all things necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (the Westminster Confession 1.2–3, 6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.2–3, 6).

Uncertain wording. “The letter from Laodicea” is most naturally a letter of Paul’s that the Laodiceans had received and would pass on, not one they wrote; but we do not know which letter it was. It may simply be lost, which need not alarm us, since Paul wrote at least one other letter to Corinth that we do not have (1 Corinthians 5:9). Many have thought it is the letter we call Ephesians, written as a circular to several churches and reaching Laodicea before Colossae; some early manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in Ephesians 1:1. A later forged Epistle to the Laodiceans was never widely received as Scripture, and rightly so.
verseByVerse.note: The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be the letter we know as Ephesians.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Archippus is publicly urged to carry through to the end the ministry the Lord has entrusted to him. His is the only name in the roll call handed a charge of its own.

Archippus. We meet Archippus once more, in the letter to Philemon, where Paul calls him “our fellow soldier” and names him alongside Philemon and Apphia (Philemon 2). He was probably of that household (many guess their son), and had some ministry in the church, perhaps leading it while Epaphras was away; we are not told what. Something had stalled; there is no rebuke in the words, but the charge would not be needed if all were well.

Say to Archippus. Paul does not write privately to Archippus; he tells the whole congregation to say it to him. A man who has gone quiet in his work is better served by a room full of people who expect something of him than by everyone politely looking away.

Fulfil the ministry that you have received. The ministry is one he has received, a trust handed to him by Christ, not a career he chose. A job you chose you may resign; a trust is someone else’s property left in your hands. And he is to fulfil it (plēroō), literally to fill it full, to carry it through to the end: not to maintain it respectably, but to finish (2 Timothy 4:5).

The household on the road. Archippus belongs to Philemon’s household, exactly where Onesimus is walking back to as this letter travels (v. 9). Whatever ministry had stalled, it had stalled in the one home in Colossae about to be tested hardest, the home that must decide how to receive a returning runaway. Paul does not join the two threads for us, and we should not force them.

The finished work. The pattern is Christ’s own. On the night before he died he said to the Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). He too had received a work, and he carried it through to the cross. He did not leave his work half done, and he will not leave ours. Every ministry in his church is a small trust handed down from that finished one.

The charge turns to face us. The one charge swings the list round to face the reader, and it lands on an ordinary Christian whose ministry we cannot even identify. You have been given something too. See that you finish it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Archippus was in serious sin or being publicly shamed; the tone is encouragement to persevere. Nor does it mean only ordained ministers have a ministry to fulfil. Every member of the body has been given gifts and work by the Lord (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10).

How do I know what ministry I have received? Begin with what is already in your hands, the people God has placed around you and the gifts he has given you: the children you are raising, the Sunday school class, the elderly neighbour, the friend who is struggling, the work you were asked to do and said yes to. Ask mature believers where they have seen God use you, notice the needs others miss, and look at what you have started and let slide. That may be the very thing the Lord is asking you to finish.
verseByVerse.note: Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul signs with his own chained hand, asks them to remember his chains, and leaves them in grace.

With my own hand. Paul usually dictated his letters (Romans 16:22) and took the pen himself at the close. His handwriting authenticated the letter against forgeries (2 Thessalonians 3:17), and it was pure affection, his own hand reaching across hundreds of miles to a church that had never seen his face.

Remember my chains. Roman custody often meant a wrist chained to a guard, so the hand that took the pen may well have been in iron. The man who wrote that Christ is the image of the invisible God wrote as a prisoner. It is a plea for prayer (v. 3) and a call to solidarity (Hebrews 13:3), but the chains are also an argument. People do not usually wear irons for what they know to be a lie. A church being offered a more sophisticated religion by teachers who risked nothing had received the gospel from a man paying for it with his chains.

Grace be with you. The letter opened with grace (1:2), and everything between, the supremacy of Christ, the new life, the transformed household, the page of names, stands inside grace. To a congregation being told they could climb nearer to God by rules, festivals, visions and severity to the body, the final word is the first word: not effort, not secret knowledge, but grace, the free gift of God in the Christ in whom they have already been filled.

He wore the chains of our sin. The hand that wrote this greeting was chained for the sake of a Saviour who was himself bound and led away, so that his people might be set free; he wore the chains of our sin so that grace might be with us for ever. Grace will be the last word of history too, when the Lord Jesus comes and every chain falls away.

In everyday life. End your own day where Paul ended his letter. Whatever you did well or badly, whatever you finished or left undone, you go to sleep inside grace.

How do I remember the chains of Christians today? Paul’s request outlived him. Many believers today are imprisoned, beaten, or cut off from family and work for Christ. Remember them first in prayer, by name and country where you can, using the requests published by those who serve the persecuted church. Write to prisoners where it is safe, support their families, and speak up for them. Let their faithfulness shame our complaints and strengthen our courage. The same grace that held Paul in chains is holding them.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add Amen.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself.

He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord.<sup>8</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,<sup>9</sup>and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.<sup>10</sup>Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him),<sup>11</sup>and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.<sup>12</sup>Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.<sup>13</sup>For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.<sup>14</sup>Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.<sup>15</sup>Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.<sup>16</sup>And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.<sup>17</sup>And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”<sup>18</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. keyVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.
keyVerse.note: Epaphras’s prayer gathers up the whole letter in one petition: that believers already filled in Christ may stand firm, grow up into him and be fully sure of him, without looking for anything beyond him. It also shows the chapter’s first command in action, prayer as steadfast, strenuous labour (v. 2), and reminds us that behind every faithful intercessor stands Christ, who prays that his people may stand.

4.reflection:
Paul tells masters that they “also have a Master in heaven” (v. 1). Where do you hold power over others, at work, at home, in church or elsewhere, and how would remembering your own Master change the way you use it?

Verses 2–4 call us to steadfast, watchful, thankful prayer, and to pray for open doors and clear words for those who preach. What makes persistent prayer hard for you, and what would it look like for our group to pray this way for a missionary or pastor we know?

Paul wants our speech to be “gracious, seasoned with salt” (v. 6). Which do you tend to lack, grace or salt? Share an opportunity you have had, or missed, to speak about Christ, and what you learned from it.

The names in vv. 7–17 include a runaway slave, a restored deserter, a faithful doctor and a man who would later leave. Which of these stories speaks most to you, and what does this page of names show about how Christ deals with his people and how we should welcome one another?
